tive to the mark. Moreover, capital would flow more readily from countries with
low interest rates to countries with higher interest rates. Similarly, the interest
rates on private bonds and bank loans would be lower relative to the interest
rates on comparable securities available in Germany.
A fourth advantage is that the relationship between the profitability of pro-
ducing similar goods in different countries would change far less dramatically,
and for two related reasons. The changes in the relationship between domestic

226 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
price levels and foreign price levels would be smaller because inflation rates
would be similar if not identical because these countries would have the same
monetary policy – and the prices of the monies of the other countries partici-
pating in monetary union would not change in terms of domestic currency.
These benefits from developing a common currency were not without costs.
One of the major costs that is that each country would lose the ability to use
monetary policy to reduce its inflation rate or to expand employment – although
each could influence the common monetary policy for the group of countries.
Financing a fiscal deficit would be much more difficult because a government
would no longer have a captive national bank that would ‘automatically’ be a
buyer of its IOUs. Moreover, each country would not be able to change the price
of its currency to reduce an extended period of high unemployment if it had a
payments deficit or an extended period when it might be required to advance
credit to others if it had a payments surplus.
The economic trade-off for each country contemplating membership in the
currency union was whether the increase in employment and in its GDP from
the integration of its market for goods and securities with those of other coun-
tries would be larger than the decline in its GDP because it would no longer be
able to change its interest rates and the price of its currency.
Skeptics believed that that the move to a common currency in the 1990s
was premature because labor markets in Europe were still too segmented and
payments imbalances would not automatically self-correct; as a result, there
would be extended periods when one group of countries would have high levels
of unemployment and large payments deficits. Another group believed that fis-
cal integration was a necessary prior step before monetary integration, perhaps
because a central fiscal authority would be necessary to finance the payments
deficits of countries with persistently high rates of unemployment.
The move to adopt the euro was motivated by the political elite that believed
that the establishment of a currency union would be a major step toward greater
political integration. This group may not have understood the economic condi-
tions that would have to be satisfied if the monetary union were to advance the
economic well-being of the residents of each member country.
The Maastrict Treaty
A practice in diplomacy is to identify a treaty with the city where the representa-
tives of the participating countries signed the basic document; the treaty that estab-
lished the International Monetary Fund is known as the Bretton Woods Agreement
from the village in northern New Hampshire where representatives from forty-four
countries signed the documents before returning to their national capitals for the
country-specific ratification process.

EUROMANIA AND EUROCRASH 227
The Maastricht Treaty of 1992, named after the capital of the southernmost
province in the Netherlands, advanced the agenda for a political union among the
participating countries, which was signified by the adoption of the name European
Union as the successor to the EEC (‘economic’ was no longer the part of the name of
the institutional arrangement; ‘union’ suggests greater integration than community).
Individuals in the participating countries would have a European passport and the
EU would develop its own foreign policy. Moreover the conditions – which became
known as the convergence criteria – that an EU member country must satisfy before
it was deemed qualified to join the monetary union were specified. One condition
was that its inflation rate would be no higher than 3 percent; a second, that the ratio
of its fiscal deficit to its GDP would be no greater than 3 percent and the third that
the ratio of government indebtedness to GDP would be no higher than 60 percent.
The treaty also established the European Central Bank (ECB) and the European
System of Central Banks. Each country would contribute to the capital of the
bank in proportion to its population and its GDP. Initially each member central
bank would engage in a ‘swap’ with the ECB, and transfer some of its government
securities to the ECB and receive in exchange a deposit denominated in the euro
at the ECB. Payments imbalance would be financed by a transfer of deposits
at the ECB. If Italy had a payments deficit in the euro area and Germany had a
payments surplus, the imbalance would be settled – automatically – by a transfer
of deposits from the account of the Bank of Italy at the ECB to the account of the
Bundesbank.
The mechanics of the transition from the German mark, the French franc,
the Italian lira, and the currencies of the other EU countries to the euro were
straightforward. The first problem was to establish the price relationship
between each national currency and the euro. A synthetic unit of account, the
European Currency Unit (ECU), had been established as the weighted average
of the currency of each country several years earlier.
On 1 January 1999 assets and liabilities denominated in the currency of each
of the participating member countries were re-dominated in terms of the euro
at the price of the ECU in terms of each country’s currency. At the beginning of
2002, households and firms exchanged currency notes and coins denominated
in each of the national monies into euro currency notes and coins.
THE SCORECARD ON THE EURO
All appeared to go well with the euro and the Eurozone countries from its
adoption at the beginning of 1999 until the onset of the 2008 crisis. Then, five
countries – Ireland, Spain, Greece, Portugal, and Cyprus – experienced finan-
cial crashes in the next fifteen months; the owners of the IOUs of the banks in

228 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
these countries and of the bonds of these countries took haircuts. France and
Italy appeared subject to economic stagnation; both had rates of unemployment
above 10 percent and high ratios of government indebtedness to GDP.
One of the paradoxes is that, although the US and British banking crises
in 2008 were much more severe than those in the Eurozone as a whole, the
rates of economic growth in the United States and Britain in the post-crisis
years have been significantly higher than in the countries that shared the
euro. The GDPs in the five countries with crashes account for 10 percent of
the GDPs of the Eurozone GDP, while the GDPs in the five US states that
had the most severe real estate crashes account for 25 percent of US GDP.
The key question is whether the sluggishness in economic performance in
the Eurozone countries is due to adherence to a common currency; Japanese
growth has seemed somewhat anemic, even though the country has its own
currency.
The banking crisis in Ireland and the one in Spain in 2008 followed from
the collapse of real estate booms similar to those in Florida and Georgia. Both
countries had high rates of economic growth. Homeowners and real estate
developers had borrowed lots of money from their domestic banks, which in
turn had borrowed from banks in other Eurozone countries. The Irish and
the Spanish economies boomed, the fiscal deficits of their governments were
modest as a ratio of the GDPs and their ratios of government indebtedness to
GDP were below 60 percent. When the booms in Ireland and Spain ended, real
estate prices declined sharply, and many homeowners and property developers
defaulted on their loans.
All of the banks in Ireland failed and were taken over by the Irish govern-
ment, which borrowed euros from the ECB to obtain funds so the banks could
repay their loans to foreign creditors, mostly banks in other Eurozone coun-
tries. The ratio of indebtedness of the Irish government soared to 90 percent of
the country’s GDP; Ireland experienced a surge in unemployment.
The financial implications of the collapse of real estate prices in Spain were
less dramatic than in Ireland; some financial institutions that specialized in
mortgage lending collapsed, but the large commercial banks did not fail. The
unemployment rate increased to above 20 percent and government indebted-
ness soared.
Greece had a sovereign debt crisis; its fiscal deficit surged to more than 10
percent of the country’s GDP after having satisfied – or having appeared to sat-
isfy – the convergence criterion that the ratio of its government debt to its GDP
was not excessively high. Moreover, Greece had a current account deficit that
was 12 percent of its GDP. The increase in spending by the Greek government
led to increases in costs and prices.

EUROMANIA AND EUROCRASH 229
Portugal also had a sovereign debt crisis. Greece and Portugal developed
fiscal deficits because ‘the money was there’; fiscal deficits could be readily
financed by the sale of government bills and bonds to banks and other investors
that were seeking higher rates of return.
Soon after the global credit freeze of 2008, the demand for the IOUs of the
Greek and Portuguese governments declined sharply, which meant that they
would not have enough money to pay their civil servants, police, the army, and
pensioners and at the same time make the interest and principal reduction pay-
ments on their indebtedness. The ECB bought the IOUs of the Bank of Greece
and the Bank of Portugal; otherwise, both governments would have defaulted
on their debt service payments, which would have led to large haircuts for banks
in France, Germany, Austria, and other countries that had bought the IOUs of
these two governments. And even if the governments had stopped their debt
service payments, their tax receipts and other revenues would have been smaller
than their domestic expenditures.
The banking crisis in the Republic of Cyprus was triggered by events in
Greece. Several of the banks in Cyprus had sold large amounts of deposits to
Russians and to other non-residents and used much of the money to buy the
bonds of the Greek government. When the prices of these bonds declined, the
banks in Cyprus incurred large revaluation losses; if they had been obliged to
‘mark to market’, they would have been bankrupt.
The ECB was reluctant to provide cash to the banks in Cyprus, because the
principal beneficiaries would have been the owners of the deposits issued by the
banks in Cyprus. The banks in Cyprus ‘froze’ deposits that were larger than
100,000 euros.
What was the cause of these crashes – when does history begin? The surge
in the indebtedness of the banks in Ireland and Spain to foreign banks would
have been much smaller if these countries had not joined the euro. Similarly, the
surge in the indebtedness of the Greek and Portuguese governments would have
been smaller. The banks that were the lenders to both the Irish and the Spanish
banks and to the Greek and the Portuguese governments were more eager to
lend because the borrowers were part of the European Monetary Union, and
there was a smaller risk of losses because these governments could no longer
reduce the price of their currencies at least until they left the monetary union.
Central banks were established to provide liquidity to banks and private
lenders in moments of stress when depositors fly to safety because they are con-
cerned about the solvency of the banks. If it had not been for the loans from the
ECB to banks in Greece, Ireland, and Portugal, the banks that were the lenders
would have incurred large losses. In effect, the ECB has moved beyond the role
of a lender of last resort and become an informal deposit insurance agency.

230 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
That the countries with high rates of unemployment have payments deficits
and large fiscal deficits and the countries with payments surpluses have lower
rates of unemployment suggests that costs and prices are mis-aligned with the
price of each currency (which are implicitly one) – and that there is a fundamen-
tal disequilibrium within the European Monetary Union.
The tragedy in Athens
Consider the list of countries that are prone to financial crises. Argentina owns one
of the top positions on this list. So do Greece, Nigeria, and Turkey. Venezuela and
the Philippines are on the list. Their common feature is that their governments are
unable or unwilling to adhere to the terms of their IOU indebtedness contracts; the
governments sell their IOUs because they want to spend money to win friends and
influence people and they make strong commitments to the lenders that they will
manage their economies to ensure that the lenders will be repaid. Often they have
managed their borrowing so the increase in their indebtedness is larger than the
interest payments on the indebtedness – a non-sustainable trajectory for the increase
in their indebtedness. The defining characteristic of these countries is that they have
reduced the prices of their currencies with greater frequency and by larger amounts
than their trading partners.
Greece’s initial application to join the euro in 1999 was rejected because it had
not satisfied the convergence criteria; Greece joined in 2002. The government of
Greece engaged in some hanky-panky or window-dressing that involved a forward
transaction that temporarily removed some government debt from its balance
sheet so the convergence criteria would be satisfied. Now, the chatter is that some
bureaucrats in Brussels knew about this window-dressing, but that they were eager
to increase the number of countries in the monetary union.
Once Greece was a member of the euro, interest rates on the debt of the Greek
government and other borrowers in Athens declined significantly; these borrowers
increased their sales of their IOUs, and many of the buyers were banks in Northern
Europe. The primary deficit of the government of Greece surged in 2003, almost
immediately after it joined the euro. After the Lehman crisis, the demand for the
IOUs of the Greek borrowers declined sharply, and the Greek government was in a
bind; its commitments to pay the army, the police, pensioners, and the owners of its
IOUs were larger than its tax receipts.
One choice for the Greek government was to stiff some of those to whom it had
made commitments – the military, the pensioners, and so on. Another was to stiff
foreign creditors. A third was to borrow from the ECB and anyone else that would
provide a loan. Before Greece had joined the euro, the government would have relied
on the Bank of Greece to finance its fiscal deficit if it could not sell its IOUs to private
investors. Once the Bank of Greece had become a vassal of the ECB in Frankfurt,
the choice was straightforward; either the ECB would provide the money that
would enable the government of Greece to pay its bills, or the government of Greece

EUROMANIA AND EUROCRASH 231
would default on some of its payment commitments, or it could leave the euro and
re-establish its own currency.
If Greece left the euro, the authorities in Brussels, Paris, and other European
capitals would be embarrassed. And the banks in Germany, France, Italy, and other
countries that had purchased the IOUs of the government of Greece would lose a lot
of money. The ‘strength’ of the bargaining position of the government of Greece was
that a default would impose large losses on others.
The almost universal view was that Greece’s fiscal problem could be readily solved
by more effective tax collections and squeezing government expenditures. There was
an extensive minuet in which the authorities in Northern Europe received a lot of
commitments from the government of Greece that tax rates would be increased and
tax revenues would be enhanced by greater penalties for those who did not pay and
government payrolls and subsidies would be reduced if the cash was provided that
would enable the government of Greece to avoid default. The cliché was that there
was a lot of ‘low-hanging fruit’, relatively low-cost measures that could be adopted to
reduce the fiscal deficit of the government of Greece.
The problem had been mis-diagnosed as a fiscal problem, which was really
a symptom; the problem was primarily a competitiveness problem – costs and
prices in Greece had become too high. A reduction in the fiscal deficit would lead
to an increase in unemployment and have a modest impact in reducing costs and
enhancing competitiveness.
The unemployment rate in Greece is still above 20 percent seven years after the onset
of the crisis and real GDP is 20 percent below its value at the peak. The fiscal deficit
has declined, and Greece now has a primary surplus. The current account deficit has
declined because of the decline in GDP and the decline in consumption spending.
The continued high unemployment rate suggests that there has been minimal decline
in costs and prices. If the continued high unemployment had led to a decline in costs
and prices, the current account deficits would have declined significantly and the
increase in net exports would have led to an increase in employment and a decline in
the fiscal deficit because of higher taxable incomes and larger tax revenues.
The chatter is that the Maastricht Treaty has no provisions for a country to leave,
either temporarily or permanently. Treaties come and go. If the government in Greece
decides that the costs of continued membership are too high, and that many years
will pass before unemployment leads to significant decline in cost, the government
will leave, and the lawyers will be brought in to sort through the details.
The traditional explanation for an extended payments imbalance is lax financial
management in the country with the payments deficit. But tangos always involve
two individuals and payments imbalances always involve at least two countries.
If the conventional approach is correct and the deficit country has initiated
the payments imbalance, then the countries with the surpluses have passively
adjusted, perhaps either by increasing their saving or by allowing their saving to

232 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
be re-allocated from domestic investment to foreign investment. Alternatively,
one of the countries may have experienced large productivity gains and declines
in the prices of export goods and a payments surplus, which means that at least
one other country had developed the counterpart payments deficit.
Real life is more complicated. The initial imbalance may have been induced
by the countries that had developed high levels of unemployment and increas-
ingly large deficits. But these deficits could have developed only if some other
countries had experienced a counterpart increase in their surpluses. But the
surplus countries may have adjusted and are reluctant to accept a reduction in
their surpluses – which makes it more difficult for the deficit country to reduce
its deficit.
If a deficit cannot be financed, adjustments will occur to reduce the deficit.
Adjustment incurs costs – the unemployment rate and the inflation rate both
increase. Some adjustments involve changes in the alignment of price levels;
some involve adjustments in income and employment. Greece has sought to
adjust by securing a reduction in costs and prices as a result of the decline in
employment and income, but the decline in costs has been modest relative to
the amount that would be needed to achieve a satisfactory payments balance at
a high level of employment.
If Greece were to take a ‘holiday’ from the euro, and the adjustments associ-
ated with a decline in the price of the new euro drachma led to a smaller pay-
ments deficit, then Germany, Austria, Finland, and the Netherlands would
experience a decline in their payments surpluses, or the payments deficits of
some Eurozone countries would increase. Subsequently, employment and
income in Greece would increase, and Greece would be able to finance a larger
fiscal deficit because its growth rate would be higher.
An analogy to the persistent imbalances problem within the Eurozone
economies is that of a country with domestic saving that is larger than domestic
investment opportunities; there is too little domestic demand. There are many
firms and households that would like to borrow and they would spend more if
they could borrow more, but they are considered insufficiently creditworthy,
perhaps because they already have high levels of indebtedness.
THE CRASH OF THE EURO?
There is a sharp contrast between the promises that were made when the euro
was adopted and the subsequent relatively dismal economic performance of the
countries that share the currency. The perennial problem is that of persistent
payments imbalances, which reflects that the alignment of the prices of national
currencies – which is implicit in a monetary union – is not consistent with the

EUROMANIA AND EUROCRASH 233
alignment of national costs and prices. The problem was evident in the mid-
1920s soon after the British pound was anchored to gold at the pre-1914 parity,
even though British prices had increased significantly relative to the US price
level during and in the first several years after World War I. The mis-alignment
problem re-appeared at the end of the 1960s, with the difference that the US
price level was then too high relative to the price levels of its trading partners in
Europe and Japan at the then alignment of the prices of the US dollar in terms
of these foreign currencies. The adjustments initiated to correct the early 1970s
mis-alignment led to the abandonment of the Bretton Woods arrangement of
adjustable parities.
The persistence of imbalances leads to centripetal forces. The high levels
of unemployment in countries with deficits provide an opportunity for outsid-
ers in these countries to challenge the established government leaders. These
outsiders are nationalist, and their message is that the economic integration has
gone too far. The outsiders could also be in countries with persistent surpluses
who criticize the continued loans to ‘deadbeat’ countries.
There are a large number of possible outcomes of this initiative of monetary
integration, which involve both the extent to which the membership remains
intact and the rates of growth of GDP in the countries that share the currency.
The most optimistic is that the membership remains intact and the rate of eco-
nomic growth increases to 2 percent a year. That outcome might occur because
price levels increase significantly in the countries with the persistent surpluses.
Or there might be some other ‘miracle’ that leads countries to adjustments that
reduce their payments imbalances.
The second possible outcome is that the membership remains intact but
that the rate of economic growth remains sluggish. This outcome would involve
persistent payments imbalances, and the countries with the persistent deficits
would continue to have high levels of unemployment. But there would also be
slower than desired growth. The third outcome would involve the departure of
one or two member countries, most likely those with high and persistent rates of
unemployment. The departure could be a temporary holiday, with the anticipa-
tion that the country would again adopt the euro after an effective decline in the
price of its currency. Greece appears most likely to take a holiday. But the man-
agement of the euro will frown on this tactic, and say a holiday is not feasible,
in part because it would be a recognition that their analysis of the cause of high
levels of unemployment was incorrect and in part because they are worried that
a holiday would set an unfortunate precedent.
A fourth outcome is that the EMU fractures into a Germanic euro and a
Latin euro; the countries with the persistent surpluses would be in the Germanic
euro. The price of the Germanic euro in terms of the Latin euro would increase.

234 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
Greece would be a member of the Latin euro club, and it would still have a pay-
ments problem; it might choose to use the occasion of this split to take a holiday
from a monetary union. The Latin Monetary Union probably would establish
its central bank. The technical problem of establishing a Latin euro is modest;
France and Italy might agree to leave the euro at the same time and to peg their
new currencies to a new synthetic currency unit.
A fifth outcome is that one or two countries that have persistent surpluses
would decide that they are tired of subsidizing the countries with persistent
deficits. They would allow their currencies to float. The likelihood of this out-
come seems low unless these countries have higher than desired inflation rates
at the time that they have larger persistent surpluses.
A sixth outcome is that the euro ‘disappears’. Individual countries might
leave the euro and re-denominate the assets and liabilities in their jurisdictions
in their new national currencies. Some of these countries would be debtors to
the ECB; their IOUs would remain denominated in the euro. Similarly, other
countries would be creditors to the ECB; in effect, their deposits in the ECB
would be larger than their liabilities to the ECB. The euro is around as long as
the ECB remains in business – and even if every member country would leave
the ECB, many years would pass before the eventual settlement between the
ECB’s creditors and debtors.
One of the remarkable initiatives of the European Central Bank is its
attempt to induce an increase in the rates of economic growth through a more
expansive monetary policy. The policy may lead to a higher level of spending,
but the likelihood that the growth rate will increase significantly is modest if
the underlying problem is that the structural payments imbalances in the mon-
etary union are too large.
The likelihood that the crash of the euro will involve its disappearance
is small; instead the growth rate will be sluggish. The countries that have net
claims on the ECB will remain attached in the effort to protect the value of
their claims while at the same time limiting the increases in their holdings of
claims on the euro. The likelihood is high that some countries with high levels
of unemployment will leave the euro.

11
POLICY RESPONSES: BENIGN
NEGLECT, EXHORTATION,
AND BANK HOLIDAYS
I
f many financial crises have a stylized form, should there be a standard policy
response? Assume plethora, speculation, panic; what then? Should the gov-
ernment authorities intervene to cope with a crisis and if so when? Should they
seek to forestall increases in real estate prices and stock prices as their price
increases expand so the subsequent crash will be less severe? Should they prick
the bubble once it is evident that the prices of property and corporate shares
are so high that it is extremely unlikely that increases in rents and in corporate
earnings could be sufficiently rapid and large to ‘ratify’ these lofty prices? When
the prices of securities begin to fall, should the authorities adopt measures to
dampen the decline and ameliorate the consequences?
Virtually every country has established a central bank to prevent or mini-
mize shortages of liquidity, especially during a banking crisis. Many countries
have a deposit insurance arrangement to reduce the likelihood of runs on their
banks by small depositors and to forestall what otherwise could be a self-fulfill-
ing prophecy that a shortage of liquidity would cascade into a solvency crisis as
firms eager to boost their holdings of cash sold securities, whose price would
then decline. Even when there is no formal insurance for bank deposits, indi-
viduals in many countries believe that their governments will ensure that they
will not incur losses if the banks should fail – in effect, the banks will be nation-
alized and the government will become the owner of the banks.
Chairman Greenspan of the Federal Reserve initially took the view that the
Fed should focus monetary policy on the achievement of a stable price level for

236 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
goods and services – or at least a low inflation rate – and the macro-employment
objectives. Then, as the US financial system imploded in the last few months of
2008, he seemed more open to the idea that the Fed should have paid more
attention to increases in real estate prices that had been ongoing since 2002.
The management of banking crises is the focus of this chapter, which first
deals with regulatory measures that might be adopted to reduce the susceptibil-
ity of financial arrangements to manias and then with the approach to panics.
The next chapter focuses on the domestic lender of last resort and the following
one on the lender of last resort in an international context.
The Austrian view is that the best remedy – the most efficient response – for
a panic is to ‘leave it alone’ – to let it run its course, and to allow the economy
to adjust to the decline in household wealth, the de-capitalization of the banks,
and the slowdown in household and business spending that follow from the
declines in the prices of real estate, stocks, and commodities.
The moral hazard argument is the primary rationale for non-interfer-
ence by the government; the proposition is that the more interventionist the
authorities are in the current crisis, the more intense the next mania will be
because some of the lenders and investors will extend credit in the belief that
that they will be bailed out if the prices of securities and real estate should
decline sharply. The argument is that government intervention to dampen
the sharp decline in prices of securities skews the risk and reward trade-off
in the minds of many investors – both the shareholders in banks and perhaps
some of the creditors of the banks, including those who own bonds or other
fixed price claims on the banks – by reducing both the likelihood and scope
of future losses. A second rationale for this view – essentially the Austrian
position – is that if the adjustments to the imbalances created by the sharp
decline in the prices of securities and real estate are delayed, the subsequent
economic recovery will be slower than it would have been if the government
had not intervened.
The moral hazard argument usually does not distinguish between those
who own shares in a bank and those who own the bonds that are claims on
the bank. Shareholders in Lehman Brothers and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
lost virtually all their money when these firms failed, as did the shareholders
of the Icelandic banks. The shareholders of Northern Rock, the Royal Bank of
Scotland, and Lloyds TSB lost most of their money – probably 90 to 95 percent.
Similarly the shareholders of AIG and Bear Stearns lost more than 90 percent of
their money. Moreover, a substantial part of the personal wealth of the employ-
ees of both Lehman and Bear was in the shares of their firms and in options
to buy more shares; some senior management officials lost 60 or 70 percent or
more of their personal wealth.

POLICY RESPONSES 237
At times the concern about moral hazard is expanded beyond the share-
holders to include the creditors of the financial firms, including both the
bondholders and those who have short-term claims on the banks; unlike the
shareholders, these creditors have no significant upside gain if the banks’ strate-
gies prove immensely profitable. The returns of these creditors are skewed – if
the banks fail, these creditors will incur substantial losses and if the banks are
successful, the creditors do not share in these gains. Creditors may be lulled
into complacency about potential losses because they believe that the banks will
not be allowed to fail – but the failure of a bank is not an unambiguous event.
If the shareholders lose 90 or 95 percent of their money before the government
provides financial assistance to ‘save the bank’, has the bank failed? Most of the
shareholders are unlikely to agree with the statement that they have been bailed
out if they have lost 90 or 95 percent of their wealth. The bondholders may
receive somewhat higher interest rates because the managers of the banks believe
that they are ‘too big to fail’ and undertake somewhat riskier investments – and
the banks will be able to pay higher interest rates to the bondholders, at least
for a while. The ‘too big to fail’ doctrine may have the same impact as deposit
insurance – unless the authorities reduce the value of the claims of the creditors
below their face value if the banks are closed and re-organized with government
assistance. Thereafter the owners of the deposits that are much larger than the
amounts covered by insurance may withdraw their money whenever there is
modest skepticism that the bank is solvent.
The choice for each country is whether to design a system that would allow
large institutions to fail, with losses to those who own shares in the bank and
losses to those who own the bonds sold by the bank, and losses to those involved
with counterparty risk or instead to provide some form of effective insurance
for all of those with claims on the banks to reduce the likelihood of runs during
periods of distress. And then who should pay the insurance premiums, either
explicitly or implicitly?
FINANCIAL REFORM: BANK REGULATION AND SUPERVISION
Can financial crises be forestalled by strict regulation and supervision? Some
observers advocate more comprehensive regulation. Most of the rules for sound
banking are already incorporated in the regulations or are implicit in banking
tradition. Many of these rules are ignored by both the banks and the regulators.
Banks are supposed to ‘mark to market’, that is, to value their loans and invest-
ments each day (or each week or month) at the prices that they would realize
if they sold these securities today rather than at their historic costs. Reserves
should be established against ‘problem loans’ and write-offs against ‘doubtful’

238 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
ones. As a bank’s loan losses increase and its capital declines, a bank might be
required to raise more capital or be closed under the traditional rules. As an
illustration of the unusual character of banks following these rules, the press
was full of the news in the spring of 1987 when Citicorp wrote down the value of
its loans to borrowers in the developing countries and the Federal Savings and
Loan Insurance Corporation (FSLIC) allowed 500 insolvent banks to remain
open in the hope that they would become sufficiently profitable to rebuild their
capital. The FSLIC was concerned that if it closed these banks, the amount of
losses that it would have to make good would be larger than its assets. As part
of the regulation process, the Federal Reserve began to collaborate with other
central banks in the Group of Ten countries to strengthen bank structures
worldwide by applying the same risk-based capital requirements to banks head-
quartered in each country.
The emphasis that bank regulators attached to capital requirements as a
percentage of assets or bank liabilities led some banks to develop ‘off-balance
sheet’ operations, which generate fees and commissions and interest income for
the bank, but the assets and liabilities are contingent and are shown only as a
footnote on the bank’s balance sheet. The banks established special investment
vehicles (SIVs) that circumvented formal capital requirements; hence the SIVs
enabled the banks to increase their effective leverage. The demand for the IOUs
of each SIV depended on the reputational capital of the bank that had estab-
lished the SIV. These off-balance sheet transactions include interest rate and
currency swaps, futures contracts, options, underwriting risks, ‘repos’ (sales of
securities with a guarantee to repurchase them at a later date), and note-issuing
facilities. Each of these positions can be valued as an option and included among
the bank’s assets when calculating its appropriate required capital.1
A strong case can be made for stricter regulations and supervision of banks
to forestall lending in euphoric periods that may morph into a banking crisis.
Responsibility for bank examination in the United States was divided among
the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Reserve Banks, and the state bank-
ing commissions. In one view there was competition in regulation rather than
in deregulation.2 ‘Divided responsibility,’ said a famous German banker-pol-
itician, ‘is no responsibility.’3 The astute examination personnel needed when
the prices of securities tumble are unwilling to submit to the boredom of long
periods of calm between crises. The mis-management of a bank is often hard to
detect before a crisis. In booms, entropy in regulation and supervision permits
the build-up of vulnerable positions that burst only after the prices of securities
decline. If the bank’s capital declines below the required minimum, the regula-
tory authorities then have to decide whether to close the bank, or arrange for the
bank to be sold. or to stall and hope for a miracle.

POLICY RESPONSES 239
The paradox is that although banks have been regulated for more than
three hundred years, the universal response to failure or near failure of banks
is that more regulation or more effective regulation is needed. The problems
of Bear Stearns, Lehman Brothers, and other US investment banks have been
attributed to the decision of the US Securities and Exchange Commission to
relax the restraints on the capital requirements or the leverage of the investment
banks. At times the collapse of an investment bank has been attributed to the
repeal of the Glass-Steagall Act – which conveniently neglects the failures of
hundreds of financial firms in the 1980s and the failures of banks in Britain,
Iceland, Ireland, and many other countries.
Regulation imposes costs. History shows that increases in regulations
applied to established institutions create incentives to develop new institutions
that are outside the scope of regulations – and yet they are similar to regulated
firms. A universe of ‘shadow banks’ was established to circumvent regulation
– and the costs of regulation. Money-market funds were developed as a way to
pay interest on demand deposits when the banks were prohibited from paying
interest on deposits; the deposits in the money market funds are not guaran-
teed by the US government. The offshore market in bank deposits developed
to avoid the costs that domestic banks incur in the form of reserve requirement
and deposit insurance premiums; the offshore branches of US banks could pay
higher interest rates on their deposit IOUs than the domestic branches of these
banks could pay on their IOUs.
Manias are macro phenomena and result from the excessively rapid growth
of credit. Regulation is a micro phenomenon. Regulation is not likely to affect
whether a mania develops, although it will impact some institutions and it
might impact the pace of the development of the mania.
What is the problem with bank regulation?
Governments have regulated banks for at least three hundred years. The list of reg-
ulations would fill a small phone book and includes capital requirements, reserve
requirements, liquidity requirements, portfolio diversification regulations, limits on
the maximum size of a loan to any one borrower, limits on the loans to insiders, and
limits on trading risky securities. Limits or ceilings have been placed on interest
rates that banks can pay on deposits. At one stage, banks were limited in their ability
to expand beyond their local market area, although most of these limits no longer
exist.
Moreover, US banks and those in many other countries are examined to ensure
that their assets and liabilities correspond with the values that they report.
The pattern is that each crisis leads to a new set of regulations. The banking crisis
of 1907 led to the establishment of the Federal Reserve. The banking crisis of the
early 1930s led to the establishment of federal deposit insurance, the Glass-Steagall

240 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
Act, which led to the separation of investment banking activities from commercial
banking activities, and to the establishment of the Securities and Exchange
Commission which would regulate the investment banks and trading in securities.
The 2008 banking crisis led to Dodd-Frank, which further limited the lending
activities of banks.
These regulations impose costs on banks, which means that they have to charge
higher interest rates when they lend money and pay lower interest to their depositors.
One impact of the costs imposed by these regulations is that near-banks have
developed to circumvent the regulations; some of these unregulated lenders are
owned by the regulated lenders.
Now, it may be that there would have been many more crises if there had not been
these regulations, but the inference from the historic record is that the likelihood
that the Dodd-Frank regulations will forestall the next systemic crisis is small. The
source of the problem is that in the two, three, or four years prior to the crisis, a
surge in the supply of credit leads to a sharp increase in the prices of securities,
at a rate that is too rapid to be sustained. For a while, the increase in the prices of
securities and currencies may be driven by momentum traders. But then when the
prices begin to decline, the investors and the banks will incur losses. The severity of
the losses that the banks as a group will incur depends primarily on two factors –
one is scope and sharpness of the increase in the prices of securities and real estate
in the several months and years prior to the banking crisis, and the other is the
date that the government decides to commit its own capital and credibility to the
banks to forestall the runs of their deposits, liabilities, and shares. The scope of the
increase in the prices of securities and real estate in the years and months prior to
the crisis depends primarily on the magnitude of the increase in the supply of credit.
If the banks are required to hold relatively more capital, then more of the credit will
be allocated by non-bank lenders. Once the prices of real estate and securities start
declining, the run to cash is likely to accelerate until the government indicates in an
unequivocal manner that it will provide unlimited capital.
BENIGN NEGLECT
Many economists believe that the panic will work its own cure, and that ‘the fire
can be left to burn itself out’.4 ‘Cool if not very imaginative heads in the Bank
[of England] parlour thought it in the nature of panics to exhaust themselves.’5
Lord Overstone maintained that support of the financial system in crisis is not
really necessary because the resources of the system are so great that even in
times of the utmost stringency, those that offer a sufficiently high rate of interest
could borrow a large amount of money.6 In 1847, an increase in the discount rate
to 10 and 12 percent in London stopped the flow of gold to the United States; a
small sloop was sent to overtake a ship that had already sailed for New York and
got it to turn around and unload £100,000 in gold.7 Testifying before the 1865

POLICY RESPONSES 241
French Enquête (inquiry) into monetary circulation, Baron James de Rothschild
stated that increases in interest rates could be relied upon to reduce speculation
in commodities and in securities. He added: ‘If speculators could find unlimited
credit, one can’t tell what crises would ensue.’8
The moral hazard dilemma is that policy measures undertaken to provide sta-
bility to the system during the current crisis may encourage much more specula-
tion during the next expansion by those who seek exceptionally high returns and
who have become convinced that there is a strong likelihood that the government
will adopt measures to prevent the economy from imploding – and so their losses
on the downside will be limited. A ‘free lunch’ for the speculators today means
that they are likely to be less prudent in the future. Hence the next several financial
crises could be more severe because the lenders would have taken on riskier posi-
tions during the boom years. The moral hazard problem is a strong argument for
non-intervention as a financial crisis develops to reduce both the likelihood and
the severity of future crises. Will the policymakers be able to devise approaches
that penalize individual speculators while minimizing the adverse impacts of their
imprudent behavior on the rest of the economy? Even then the cost-benefit ques-
tion is whether the benefit to the economy from not allowing the panic to run its
course is worthwhile in terms of the undeserved reward to the speculators.
The losses incurred by shareholders of Bear Stearns, Fannie Mae and
Freddie Mac, AIG, Citicorp, and Bank of America were immense. Moreover, the
leadership and directors of these institutions were replaced. The top manage-
ment was replaced, and many of the top officers lost most of their wealth. Each
of these firms continued in business, but for all practical purposes they failed.
Individuals who invested on the assumption that these institutions were ‘too big
to fail’ incurred large losses. The major beneficiaries of government interven-
tion have been the bondholders and those with counter-party positions.
The view that a panic should be allowed to pursue its course has two ele-
ments. One element takes pleasure in the troubles – or enjoys schadenfreude
– that the investors or speculators encounter as retribution for their excesses;
this puritanical view welcomes hellfire as the just deserts for the excessively
greedy. The other sees panic as a thunderstorm ‘in a mephitic and unhealthy
tropical atmosphere’ that clears the air. ‘It purified the commercial and finan-
cial elements, and tended to restore vitality and health, alike conducive to regu-
lar trade, sound progress and permanent prosperity.’9 One powerful statement
of this position was made by Herbert Hoover as he characterized – without
approval – the view of Andrew Mellon:
The ‘leave-it-alone liquidationists’ headed by Secretary of the Treasury
Mellon felt that government must keep its hands off and let the slump

242 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
liquidate itself. Mr. Mellon had only one formula: ‘Liquidate labor, liq-
uidate stocks, liquidate the farmers, liquidate real estate.’ He insisted
that when the people get an inflationary brainstorm, the only way to
get it out of their blood is to let it collapse. He held that even panic was
not altogether a bad thing. He said: ‘It will purge the rottenness out of
the system. High costs of living and high living will come down. People
will work harder, live a moral life. Values will be adjusted, and enter-
prising people will pickup the wrecks from less competent people.’10
The neo-Austrian economic historian Murray Rothbard added: ‘While phrased
somewhat luridly, this was the sound and proper course for the administration
to follow.’11 The conservative historian Paul Johnson commented: ‘It was the
only sensible advice Hoover received during his presidency.’12
The opposing view conceded that while it is desirable to purge the system of
bubbles and manic investments there is the risk that if the government does not
intervene to staunch the crisis and then a deflationary panic would spread and
wipe out sound investments by conservative investors who would not be able to
obtain the credit they need.
One feature of many liquidity crises is that interest rates seem extremely
high for private borrowers, especially because they are expressed as annual per-
centage rates, they are really premiums for liquidity for one, two, or at most
a few days. The more fundamental question is whether money is available at
these high interest rates or whether the credit market is cleared by non-price
rationing. The evidence from many crises is that it is difficult and sometimes
impossible to borrow in a panic and that the quoted interest rates are irrelevant
because credit is not available.
● After first Arend Joseph and then DeNeufville failed in 1763, and
panic broke out on 22 July, a succinct, not very informative or con-
vincing report commented: ‘Panic even on securities and on goods,
no money was to be had.’13
● The statement in 1825 was: ‘A panic seized upon the public, such as
had never been witnessed before: everybody begging for money –
money – but money was hardly on any condition to be had. “It was
not the character of the security,” observes the Times, “that was con-
sidered, but the impossibility of producing money at all”.’14
● The interrogation of Thomas Tooke before the Select Committee on
the Commercial Crisis in 1847: Question 5421: ‘For several days, if
not some weeks, the Bank of England was the only establishment
that was discounting?’ Answer: ‘Yes.’ Question 5472: ‘The Governor

POLICY RESPONSES 243
of the Bank of England said he could not sell £1 million of stock
[English government bonds] in the week after October 14, if there
had been no letter. Do you think it possible?’ Answer: ‘No, perfectly
impossible, taking the word impossible to signify with the excep-
tion of such a reduction in price as could not be contemplated.’15
● The evidence of Mr Glyn in the same inquiry: Question: ‘Are you
aware that it was the opinion of the Bank broker that a very large
sum might have been sold without materially affecting the prices of
Consols [English perpetual bonds]?’ Answer: ‘I was not aware that
the Bank broker had stated that. I should say, from what I saw at
the time, that a sale of a million or two million, which were the fig-
ures talked of, would have been almost impossible without knock-
ing down the funds to such a price as would have created a further
panic.’
● Mr Browne, MP, did not think such sales could have been effected,
unless at a great sacrifice, adding that ‘if the panic had been equal
to what we might suppose it might have been, under such circum-
stances, I doubt whether they could have been sold at all.’16
● Then in 1857, ‘At one stage during the crisis it was impossible to
negotiate paper at all, the charge under the most favorable circum-
stances being 12 and 15 percent.’17
● A letter from Liverpool: ‘Bills of exchange of the first Quality in
themselves, and to which this and other Banks were willing to add
their Endorsement, were absolutely inconvertible into Cash, and it
is my Belief that many Houses, who were not merely solvent but able
to pay 40s and 60s to the Pound, must have stopped had not the
Government letter been issued.’18
● ‘Commercial confidence in Hamburg is entirely at an end. Bills of
only three or four of the first houses are negotiable at the highest
rate of interest ... A government bond advance of 15 million marks
banco payable by banks failed to help. The panic was so great that
government bonds could not be discounted, and on no security
whatsoever would capitalists part with their money ... When it was
known on December 12 that assistance would help all, the panic
ceased. Government bonds which had not been discountable at
15 percent on the first of the month were readily taken at 2 and 3
percent.’19
● Edward Clark in New York wrote to Jay Cooke in Philadelphia
before Cooke left Clark’s firm to start his own firm: ‘Money is not
tight – it is not to be had at all. There is no money, no confidence &

244 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
value to anything. A week more of such times and the Bks [sic] will
fail.’20
● Then in 1866 ‘The Bank court raised the discount rate to 9 per-
cent and intimated that loans on Government securities were avail-
able at 10 percent. Before that announcement it was impossible to
sell either Consols or Exchequer bills. Jobbers in other securities
refused to deal.’21
● During the 1873 crisis in New York the ‘National Trust Company of
New York had eight hundred thousand dollars worth of government
securities in its vaults, but not a dollar could be borrowed on them;
and it suspended.’22
● And finally, in 1883, ‘The growing demand for money finally led
to a money famine. Time loans were unobtainable, call loans were
72 percent in June, 72 percent on July 28th, 51 percent on August 4.
First-class commercial paper was quoted 8 to 12 percent nominal,
with a very small amount of money available.’23
The evidence is not unambiguous, since the sale of government bonds is some-
what qualified by such remarks as ‘with the exception of such a reduction in price
[i.e., increase in the rate of interest] as could not be contemplated’. Moreover,
there is occasional information on the other side of the argument, especially in
the United States under the national banking system, in which a lender of last
resort was unavailable. In 1884:
To add further to the discomfiture of dealers, money became exceed-
ingly stringent, and at one time commanded as much as 4 percent for
24 hours’ use. This caused a further sacrifice of stocks since few could
afford to pay the high rate asked. The exorbitant charge was, of course,
the direct result of the distrust prevailing, since there was no actual
scarcity ... It was to ... the desire to realize and obtain cash that the large
decline on Thursday and Friday of nearly 7 percent on United States
Government bonds is to be attributed. There was no loss in confidence
in these, nor was there in good railroad bonds and stocks.
One result of the phenomenal and temporary rise in rates for money
was to bring a vast amount of foreign capital to the market. Some of it
was sent here to buy stocks at their depressed prices, and more to loan
on stocks or on any other good securities at the high rates of interest.
The effect of this was to completely turn the foreign exchanges which
had been running so heavily against the US.24

POLICY RESPONSES 245
This statement in its turn is not unambiguous, since the panic started before an
acute liquidity shortage had developed.
The International Monetary Fund acted as a lender of last resort in the Asian
crisis of 1997 – although long after the prices of the Thai baht, the Indonesian
rupiah, and other currencies had declined sharply – and insisted that the gov-
ernment in each of the Asian countries balance its budget and that the central
bank in each country increase interest rates. Some economists objected to these
contractive measures because they would lead to an increase in unemployment,
especially among the poor, while the financial problems had been set in motion
by comfortable officials and well-to-do bankers.
Some support for orthodoxy, however, came from the Japanese experience
in the 1990s when the combination of an expansive monetary policy and the
decline in the price of the yen produced a ‘liquidity trap’. Both Japanese inter-
est rates and bank loans decreased after the declines in stock prices and real
estate prices, and the inference was that there was a ‘credit crunch’. Banks were
reluctant to lend because their loan losses had eroded their capital and firms
were reluctant to borrow because of the sluggish growth in the demand for their
products.
The decline in short-term interest rates in Tokyo to 1 percent and below
led to a surge in the ‘carry-trade’; US hedge funds borrowed yen, which they
sold to buy US dollars which were used to buy US dollar securities that yielded
3 or 4 percent. The ‘carry-trade’ transactions led to an increase in the flow of
funds from Tokyo to New York and to a decline in the price of the yen that in
turn led to an increase in the Japanese trade surplus and increases in Japanese
output and employment. The increase in the Japanese trade surplus was a useful
response to the liquidity trap and an effective supplement to expansive Japanese
fiscal and monetary policies. The carry-trade transactions would remain profit-
able for the US hedge funds as long as any increase in the price of the yen was
smaller than the excess of the interest rates on US dollar securities over the
interest rates on yen loans.
MORAL SUASION AND OTHER EXHORTATORY DEVICES
The dominant argument against the a priori view that panics can be cured by
being left alone is that they almost never are left alone. The authorities inter-
vene to forestall further decline in the prices of securities. In panic after panic,
crash after crash, crisis after crisis, the authorities or some ‘responsible citizens’
try to halt the panic by one measure or another. The authorities may be unduly
alarmed and the position might correct itself without serious harm. The author-
ities may be stupid and unable to learn. (The Chicago School assumes that the

246 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
market participants are always more intelligent than the authorities, in large
part because the authorities are motivated by short-term political objectives.)
The uneven distribution of intelligence cannot be tested against crisis manage-
ment because the authorities and leading figures in the marketplace both exert
themselves to halt the spread of declines in the prices of securities, bankruptcy,
and bank failures. If there is a learning process at work – and the assumption of
rationality requires one – the lesson has been that a lender of last resort is more
desirable and less costly than relying exclusively on the competitive forces of the
market.
One insight from the historical record is that there are many examples when
the authorities initially were resolved not to intervene but eventually did so reluc-
tantly. Lord Liverpool threatened to resign as Chancellor of the Exchequer in
December 1825 if an issue of Exchequer bills was provided to rescue the market
after he had warned against excessive speculation six months earlier.25 William
Lidderdale, Governor of the Bank of England at the time of the Baring crisis,
refused categorically to accept a ‘letter of indemnity’ to permit the Bank to exceed
its lending limit.26 On both occasions, face was saved by finding some other
approach to avert the panic. The initial strong stand not to intervene was reversed
on many other occasions as the panic escalated. These included the intervention
of Frederick II in the Berlin crisis of 1763,27 the Bank of England’s refusal to dis-
count for the ‘W banks’,28 and the US Treasury’s decision in 1869.29
The view of the US authorities in September 2008 was that Lehman Brothers
should be allowed to fail, even though the government had blessed JPMorgan
Chase’s purchase of Bear Stearns and the conservatorship of Fannie Mae and
Freddie Mac. One explanation is that the then Secretary of the Treasury, Henry
Paulson, did not want to become known as ‘Mr Bailout’. A day after Lehman
closed, the ‘policy’ was reversed in response to the massive run on AIG. In effect
a new policy of 100 percent deposit insurance was implicitly provided to all
large financial firms.
STALLINGS
In a run, each depositor rushes to get his or her money from the bank before the
doors are closed because the bank’s money holdings are likely to be too small
relative to the demand of the depositors who want their money. Banks are often
reluctant to pay the depositors that want their money because the banks’ hold-
ings of cash or money are much smaller than their short-term deposit liabilities.
During the Great Depression, banks took their time to pay off depositors, hop-
ing like Micawber for something to turn up. The technique goes back to the
eighteenth century.

POLICY RESPONSES 247
Macleod’s Theory and Practice of Banking describes how the Bank of
England defended itself in September 1720 against a run brought on by its
reversal of a promise to absorb the bonds of the South Sea Company at £400.
The Bank organized its friends in the front of the line of depositors that wanted
their money and paid them slowly in sixpence coins. These friends brought the
coins back to the Bank through another door. The money was deposited, again
slowly counted, and then again paid out. The run was staved off until the feast
of Michaelmas (29 September). When the holiday was over, so was the run, and
the Bank remained open.30
A second story, which may well have the same origin and is likely to be more
accurate, is that the Sword Blade Bank, a supporter of the South Sea Company,
resisted attempts to redeem its paper with silver coins. When the run started on
19 September, the bank brought up wagonloads of silver that it paid out ‘slowly
in small change’. One depositor is reported to have received £8000 in shillings
and sixpences before the bank closed its doors on Saturday 24 September.31 The
circumstances suggest one story; the dates, two. Since the Sword Blade Bank and
the Bank of England were mortal enemies, it is unlikely that they cooperated.
The lessons of 1720 were not lost on the Bank of England a quarter cen-
tury later. The Young Pretender (Charles Edward, grandson of James II) landed
in Scotland in July 1745, unfurled his banner in September, invaded England
in November, arrived in Carlisle on 15 November, and reached Derby on
4 December. Panic broke out on Black Friday, 5 December 1745. British Consols
fell to 45, the lowest price on record, and a run began on the Bank of England.
The Bank resisted, partly by paying off its notes in sixpence coins; the Bank
used the time gained to induce London merchants to proclaim their loyalty and
readiness to accept Bank of England notes. The second half of the prescription,
collecting pledges of faith in notes, was used again in similar circumstances
when the French landed at Fishguard in 1797. On that occasion, 1140 signatures
of merchants and investors in government securities were collected in a sin-
gle day.32 The time gained in 1745 by both the slow payout and the petition of
support enabled the government to organize the army that defeated the Young
Pretender at Culloden in April 1746.
COMPLETE SHUTDOWNS AND BANK HOLIDAYS
One way to stop a panic is to close the market so trading stops. Trading on the
New York Stock Exchange was halted in 1873, and in London and many other
centers at the outbreak of war in 1914. In both cases, the motivation was to
stop a run by providing the market participants with more time to think about
whether it was necessary or desirable to sell their securities at depressed prices.

248 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
However, closing the market may drive the trading underground and inten-
sify the panic. Moreover, short-run and long-run goals are in conflict. Closing
the stock market during one panic may exacerbate the next, as investors sell their
stocks or withdraw their money from the call-money market because they are
fearful that trading soon will be halted. A financial editor suggested that fear that
trading on the New York Stock Exchange might be halted in October 1929 has-
tened the withdrawal of call money by out-of-town banks and other market par-
ticipants, who were aware that the market had been closed in 1873.33 The closing
of stock exchanges in Pittsburgh and New Orleans for two months in 1873 had
fewer serious consequences, since they traded only the securities of local firms.34
The New York Stock Exchange and the other US stock exchanges were
closed for a week after the bombing of the World Trade Center towers on 11
September 2001 because the communications and the technical support sys-
tems were inoperative. Many of the same securities could have been traded on
the regional stock exchanges in the United States, although these exchanges
would have been overwhelmed by the volume of trading.
The declaration of a legal holiday by the government is another technique
for closing the market, which was used during the panic of 1907 in Oklahoma,
Nevada, Washington, Oregon, and California.35 The declaration of bank holi-
days started in various US states in the autumn of 1932 and then was adopted
at the national level on 3 March 1933, the day that Franklin D. Roosevelt was
inaugurated as president. (A bank holiday closes only the banks, while all busi-
nesses are closed on a legal holiday.)
Another device is to suspend the publication of bank statements, as in
1873, in the hope that ‘what you don’t know won’t hurt you’. The technique was
designed to hide the large losses of a few banks since the fear was that accurate
news would reduce depositor confidence further.36
Some commodity and financial markets set daily limits on the maximum
change in prices; when the limit is reached, trading is suspended for the rest of
the day. Specialists in individual stocks often have taken a ‘time out’ whenever the
imbalance between the buy orders and the sell orders has been exceptionally large.
This ‘circuit breaker’ was recommended for US stock markets after the meltdown
of Black Monday, 19 October 1987. The proposal for the New York Stock Exchange
was to postpone trading for a stated interval – such as twenty minutes – in those
stocks whose prices increased above or declined below the limit.
Time has been gained by moratoriums on payment of all debts or on partic-
ular types of obligations, such as bills of exchange that have less than two weeks
until they mature. The most ubiquitous measure of this sort is that the bank
examiners ignore the bad loans that banks own as long as they can – an implicit
moratorium on marking the loans to their market value. Regulatory forbearance

POLICY RESPONSES 249
was used in the US savings and loan debacle in the 1980s. The International
Monetary Fund and the World Bank continued to allow the indebtedness of
many African countries to increase by the amounts of the interest that were due;
if the Fund or the Bank had declared the loans in default, they would have had
to recognize the losses on their loans to these countries. The banks that were the
lenders to the Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs), landlords of mortgaged
shopping centers, and the owners of mothballed Boeing 747s allowed the inter-
est on their bank loans to compound because they wanted to delay the recog-
nition of the loan losses to a more propitious moment when their own capital
would be larger. But the lenders need forbearance from the bank examiners.
Official moratoriums may be less effective than informal ones, how-
ever. A moratorium on the settlement of differences in payments due on the
1873 Vienna Stock Exchange lasted a week, from the stock market collapse to
15 May. A guarantee fund of 20 million gulden was put together by the Austrian
National Bank and the commercial banks.37 Another moratorium was noted in
Paris after the July Monarchy when the municipal council decreed that all bills
payable in Paris between 25 July and 15 August should be extended by ten days.
This moratorium sterilized the commercial paper in banking portfolios and but
it did not discourage a run by holders of notes.38
CLEARING-HOUSE CERTIFICATES
The major device used in the United States to cope with bank runs prior to
the establishment of the Federal Reserve System was the clearing-house cer-
tificate, which was a near-money substitute that was the liability of a group of
large banks in each city. A bank subject to a run could pay the depositors that
wanted their money with these certificates rather than with coin. The New York
Clearing House was established in 1853, and the one in Philadelphia a year after
the panic of 1857. During the panic of 1857, New York banks failed to cooper-
ate to halt the run. The Mercantile Agency of New York took the position that
if four or five of the strongest banks had come to the assistance of the Ohio Life
and Trust Company so that it could meet its obligations, the business and the
credit of the country would have been preserved.39 By 1873 the New York banks
were ready to accept Clearing House certificates as payment on cleared checks.
The advantage of these certificates was that they reduced the incentive for any
bank to bid deposits away from its competitors. Sprague insisted that this sys-
tem had to be accompanied by an agreement to pool bank reserves; otherwise,
a bank that was not subject to a net drain might be forced to suspend payments
after it paid cash to its own depositors if it had not received cash in settlements
from other banks.40 In 1873 reserves were pooled.

250 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
One serious drawback of clearing-house certificates was that they were
acceptable only in the local area – New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore. Thus
these certificates helped maintain domestic payments such as payrolls and
retail sales within a city but they dampened the effective flow of payments
between cities. In the 1907 panic, 60 of the 160 clearing-houses in the United
States used these certificates to facilitate local payments. Nevertheless, Sprague
claimed that the dislocations of the domestic exchanges were as large and dis-
ruptive as they had been on previous occasions. The prices of New York funds
in Boston, Philadelphia, Chicago, St Louis, Cincinnati, Kansas City, and New
Orleans between 26 October and 15 December 1907 varied from a discount of
1.25 percent in Chicago on 2 November to a 7 percent premium in St Louis on
26 November, an increase from 1.5 percent the previous week.41 In December
1907 Jacob H. Schiff wrote: ‘The one lesson we should learn from recent experi-
ence is that the issuing of clearinghouse certificates in the different bank centers
has also worked considerable harm. It has broken down domestic exchange and
paralyzed to a large extent the business of the country.’42
Other devices of the same general character were clearing-house checks
and certified checks that were close substitutes for money and increased the
means of payment in circulation.
Non-bank groups have also organized to mitigate a panic. Consider, for
example, the stock market consortium. On 24 October 1907, a bankers’ pool,
headed by JP Morgan, loaned $25 million at 10 percent in call money in an
attempt to stem the collapse of the stock market.43 Twenty-two years to the day
later, on Black Thursday in 1929, Richard Whitney went from post to post on
the floor of the New York Stock Exchange and placed bids to buy stocks on
behalf of a syndicate headed by JP Morgan and Company.44
BANK COOPERATION
Banks have also collaborated through rescue committees (as in Vienna in May
1873 and earlier), loan funds, funds for guarantees of liabilities, arranged merg-
ers of weak banks and firms, and other devices whereby the strong banks support
the weak and failing banks.45 Three examples include the role of the Paris banks
in the 1828 crisis in Alsace, various devices employed by Hamburg in meeting
the difficulties of 1857, and the Baring Brothers loan guarantee of 1890.
The Alsatian crisis of 1828
Three firms in the textiles industry in Mulhouse failed in December 1827. The
Paris banks then refused to accept any Alsatian paper, and the Bank of France
set a limit of 6 million francs on the amount it would support, a figure that was

POLICY RESPONSES 251
‘scarcely the fortune of two Alsatian houses’. The Bank of France then decided
against accepting any paper with Mulhouse or Basel endorsements and that deci-
sion precipitated a panic. On 19 January, two more Mulhouse merchants failed.
On 22 January in Paris there were rumors of the failure of two Schlumberger
firms. The Paris banks sent Jacques Laffitte as an emissary to Mulhouse; he
arrived on 26 January and offered to lend 1 million francs on the consignment
of merchandise. Before he came, however, two textile merchants, Nicholas
Koechlin and Jean Dollfuss, had left Mulhouse for Paris. To raise cash, these
merchants had been selling inventories of goods at discounts of 30 to 40 percent
below their traditional market prices. Nine houses failed from 26 January to 15
February. Lévy-Leboyer wrote that it could have been worse. At the last minute
a syndicate of twenty-six Paris banks, presided over by J.C. Davillier, extended
a credit of 5 million francs to Koechlin and Dollfuss, who returned to Alsace
on 3 February and distributed 1 million francs to those of their colleagues who
offered guarantees and kept 4 million for themselves. These measures restored
confidence.46 Those who qualified for neither the Koechlin-Dollfuss fund nor
the Basel money failed.47
The Hamburg crisis of 1857
The background of the crisis of 1857 in Hamburg was that trade had expanded,
particularly because the Crimean War had led to an expansion of credit.
Hamburg was the ‘all-English’ city of Germany, but had close relations with
the United States in sugar, tobacco, coffee, and cotton, and with Scandinavia.
When the deflationary tidal wave swept across the Atlantic, Hamburg was inun-
dated. The panic touched off by the failure of Ohio Life on 24 August arrived in
Hamburg three months later (following price declines of 30 percent) with the
suspension of Winterhoff and Piper, a firm that was engaged in the American
trade.48 Daily dispatches from the British consulate in Hamburg by date tell the
story:
21 November: Some of the leading merchant houses and two banks
plan for relief.
23 November: Two major houses engaged in the London trade fail, and
the Discount Guarantee Association grows more cautious in endors-
ing Hamburg bills.49 On one authority the Discount Guarantee
Association is exhausted in three days.50
24 November: A Discount Guarantee Association (Garantie-Diskontverein)
is formed, initially with a capital of 10 million marks banco, later raised
to 13 million (about £1 million), of which the sum of 1 million marks is
to be paid in immediately.

252 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
28 November: The chamber of commerce and leading merchants
induce the Senate to call parliament (Burgerschaft) to arrange to
issue government bonds in order to lend 50 to 66 2/3rds percent of
the value of hypothecated goods, bonds, and shares to merchants in
distress.
1 December: With the suspension of Ullberg and Cremer, ten to
twelve houses in the Sweden trade have gone down. The Discount
Guarantee Association will not issue any more guarantees. Business
is at a standstill.
2 December: A suggestion is made to change the laws of bankruptcy to
enable creditors to share in attachment of goods.
7 December: A proposal is made to establish a state bank for discount-
ing good bills to the amount of 30 million marks banco (about £2.4
million). Parliament rejects this, wanting instead to issue 30 million
marks banco of paper currency as legal tender. The senate rejects
this, insisting on clinging to the silver standard.
In the end, a compromise was reached for a State Loan Institute fund of 15 mil-
lion marks that included 5 million marks banco of Hamburg government bonds
and 10 million in silver to be borrowed in foreign financial centers.51 The story
of the silver train (Silberzug) is recounted in Chapter 13 as an early example of
an international lender of last resort.
One observer totaled the sums available for rescue operations to 35 million
marks banco, which included 15 million in the Discount Guarantee Association,
15 million in the State Loan Institute, and 5 million from the chamber of com-
merce. He compared this amount with 100 million marks banco of protested
bills and noted that if merchants speculated with capital equal only to one-sixth
the value of their goods, a 17 percent decline in prices of these goods would be
sufficient to wipe out their capital position. To the suggestion that the senate
was 300 years behind the times, he reported with approval the senate’s answer:
The merchants have been 300 years ahead of the times in issuing debt. State help
in these cases, he insisted, merely means assistance for speculation and perpetu-
ation of higher prices at a cost to the consumer.52
Guarantees of liabilities: the Baring crisis
The most famous guarantee of liabilities was that worked out by William
Lidderdale when he was Governor of the Bank of England during the Baring
crisis of 1890. Similar guarantees had occurred earlier in Britain. In December
1836 the private bank Esdailes, Grenfell, Thomas and Company, which served

POLICY RESPONSES 253
as London agents for seventy-two country banks, was in financial difficulty.
The view was that this firm could not be allowed to fail because of its relation-
ships with the country banks; moreover, its paper included all the best names in
the City. The assets of the bank far exceeded its liabilities, and the London bank-
ers offered guarantees. The Bank of England led the list with £150,000. Esdailes
survived, but only for two years.53
The guarantee was worked out as an alternative to a letter of indemnity
that permitted suspension of the Bank Act of 1844. The letter was offered by the
Chancellor of the Exchequer, Lord Goschen, to Lidderdale, who refused on the
ground that ‘reliance on such letters was the cause of a great deal of bad banking
in England’.
While Lidderdale refused to quiet the market by the usual means that had
been employed in 1847, 1857, and 1866, he did not ‘let the market take its medi-
cine’. In August 1890, he warned Baring Brothers that the firm would have to
moderate its acceptances for its Argentine agent, S. B. Hales. Baring Brothers
revealed its acute distress to Lidderdale on Saturday 8 November. Fearful of a
panic when Barings’ condition was made public, the Bank of England met with
the Exchequer on Monday 10 November, turned down the letter of indemnity,
prepared for the problem by seeking assistance from foreign countries (a subject
for Chapter 13), and formed a committee headed by Lord Rothschild to address
the question of the large overhang of Argentinean securities.
As the days passed, the rumors circulated and Barings’ bills were increas-
ingly discounted at the Bank of England. By Wednesday, Lidderdale had learned
that although Baring was solvent it would need £8 to £9 million of financial
assistance. On Friday John Daniell, the leading man at Mullens and Co., used
by the Bank of England in open-market operations, came to Lidderdale, crying
‘Can’t you do something, or say something, to relieve people’s minds: they have
made up their minds that something awful is up, and they are talking of the very
highest names – the very highest!’54
On 14 November Lidderdale met with two cabinet ministers who repre-
sented the Exchequer, Lords Smith and Salisbury. They agreed that the British
government would increase its balance at the Bank of England immediately and
that the government would share with the Bank in any losses suffered on Baring
Brothers’ paper discounted by the Bank between 2pm Friday and 2pm Saturday.
On the basis of this agreement, Lidderdale met with eleven private banks to get
them to contribute to a fund that would guarantee Barings’ liabilities, and he
got the State Bank of Russia to agree not to withdraw its £2.4 million deposit at
Barings. The private banks as a group contributed £3,250,000, which included
£1 million from the Bank of England as well as £500,000 from each of three
lenders, Glyn, Mills & Co., Currie and Co., and Rothschild. Lidderdale then

254 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
used these commitments to obtain the agreement of the five London joint-stock
banks to join the guarantee fund for another £3,250,000. On the basis of these
assurances, The Times of 15 November announced that Baring Brothers would
fail but that no creditor of Barings would incur a loss. The work of the guarantee
fund continued on Saturday because the directors of the joint-stock banks had to
meet to approve their subscriptions, which was done by 11am. Then other banks
and financial institutions raised the fund from £7.5 million in the morning to
£10 million by 4pm; the guarantee fund eventually reached £17 million and was
taken as a measure of the strength of the London financial system. Martin’s
