308 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
The sharp decline in the price of the Thai baht in early July 1997 trig-
gered the contagion effect, and the cross-border investment inflows to other
Asian countries slowed and then were reversed. The President of Malaysia,
Dr Mahathir, blamed foreign speculators and specifically George Soros in the
United States, who in turn asserted that he had not sold the ringgit short while
Malaysia was constructing two new buildings taller than any other buildings
in the world. Malaysia did not seek loans from the IMF but instead imposed
controls on investment outflows and on interest payments to foreign creditors.
Thailand, Indonesia, and South Korea borrowed from the IMF. The amounts of
these loans and those to Mexico in 1994–95 are set forth in Table 13.1 from the
Bank for International Settlements.69
The report of the Bank for International Settlements noted that the $50
billion credit lines for Mexico had a ‘psychological impact on the markets’ and
halted the erosion of domestic confidence.70 These credit commitments also
depleted the funds available for rescue operations in the future. At the end of
1998, the US Congress agreed to the proposal of the Clinton administration to
increase the IMF’s capital and member country quotas. The IMF helped Brazil
when it needed assistance after its currency crisis.
A world central bank would be a more efficient lender of last resort than the
IMF, but the likelihood that many countries would agree to establish a world
central bank seems low. Most large countries outside the European Monetary
Union regard the issue and control of money as a mark of sovereignty; in the
United States, these functions are enshrined in the Constitution.
THE UNITED STATES AND THE DOLLAR
The United States took the lead in the 1940s, the 1950s, and the 1960s in estab-
lishing new international financial institutional arrangements – the IMF and
the World Bank, the General Arrangements to Borrow, the Special Drawing
Rights, the swap network, and the gold pool. Moreover, the United States took
the initiative at the end of the 1980s in assisting Mexico and developing coun-
tries in the reduction in the values of their loans to major international banks
so the governments and other borrowers in these countries might again be able
to sell their IOUs in global markets. As well, the United States took a leadership
role when individual countries like Mexico and Russia and South Korea had
major international payments problems.
One of the major surprises at the beginning of the 1980s was the develop-
ment of a persistent US trade deficit; previously the United States had had a
trade surplus during nearly every year since the beginning of the twentieth

THE INTERNATIONAL LENDER OF LAST RESORT 309
century. The result was a dramatic change in the US international financial
position; in 1980, the United States was the world’s largest creditor country,
with a net creditor position larger than the combined positions of all other
creditor countries. By 2000 the United States had become the world’s larg-
est debtor, and its net debtor position was larger than the positions of all
other net debtors as a group. The US net debtor position has continued to
increase.
The analogy between the persistent US payments deficit in the 1950s and
the 1960s and the persistent US trade deficit in the 1980s and the 1990s and
subsequently is that the value of the US international accounts is the mirror of
the value of the accounts of all other countries as a group. The United States
developed a payments deficit after 1950 because the demand for international
reserve assets on the part of other countries was larger than the increases in the
supply of gold and other new reserve assets from non-US sources. The United
States developed a persistent trade deficit after 1980 because of the demand in
other countries for US dollar securities and US real assets.
The surge in the US trade deficit and the emergence of the United States as
the largest international debtor has led to the question of causation – did the
United States develop a persistent trade deficit because of profligate spending
by American households and the US government, or did this deficit develop
because of the persistent foreign demand for US dollar securities. The United
States had been the most successful economy during the 1990s, with some eco-
nomic analysts suggesting that with low inflation, low unemployment, govern-
ment budget surpluses in the making, and technical progress, it entered a ‘New
Era’ in which the business cycle has been dampened and financial crises tamed.
Not all was completely solid, however. Prosperity relied on increases in US con-
sumer spending and a decline in household saving and, after 2002, a surge in
property prices that proved temporary. Credit card debt reached new heights. So
did household bankruptcies. The increase in US net international indebtedness
may pose problems if foreign confidence in the price of the US dollar declines.
A strong, perhaps overstated warning by a British economist is entitled ‘Seven
Unsustainable Processes’, although the author is unwilling to discuss timing
beyond saying that a downturn from 2015 would be likely within the next five
to fifteen years.71 There is a possibility that the United States and the dollar may
lose their positions in ‘world economic and financial primacy’.72 But the United
States will lose its pre-eminent position only if some other country develops a
pre-eminent position, much as the United States displaced Britain after the First
World War.

310 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
Some political scientists place faith in what they call ‘regimes’, habits
of cooperation built up during periods of leadership (that they in turn call
‘hegemony’).73 Such cooperation worked remarkably well in the 1980s, espe-
cially under the initiatives of Secretary of the Treasury James Baker, who aban-
doned the policy of benign neglect of the price of the dollar and worked out the
Plaza Agreement of September 1985 and the Louvre Agreement of January 1987.
Few observers placed much reliance on the system of summit meetings among
the G-7. These had strong overtones of ceremony and posturing. More suited to
the working out of effective agreements was the G-5 among France, Germany,
Japan, Britain, and the United States.
Can the IMF and the World Bank offer an alternative to declining US lead-
ership? These institutions were established at Bretton Woods to help other coun-
tries with their problems. They work slowly, which is a disability in a time of
crisis that may require decisions in hours, not weeks. Moreover, their funds may
prove too inadequate when there is a massive change in the investor demand for
securities denominated in a foreign currency. Their resources will need to be
supplemented with the financial resources of the G-7 central banks, especially
if there is a run on the US dollar.
Despite the persistent US trade deficit, the US dollar continues to be used
as a unit of account and a medium of exchange, and a storer of value. Under
President de Gaulle, France continually challenged US policies and the domi-
nance of the dollar without, however, great success in dampening the role of
the dollar. The European Union may grow in economic and financial strength,
although there has been a significant and persistent crisis in the Eurozone since
the global meltdown of 2008; growth has been extremely sluggish. Other coun-
tries depend on US leadership for lack of a better alternative; but the United
States has been holding back from taking a leadership role, preoccupied with
its own political and economic problems, and reluctant to pay the cost of pro-
viding international public goods. Regimes work smoothly in quiet times, but
something more decisive in the way of leadership is called for in crisis, and the
likelihood of escaping economic and financial crises in the years ahead seems
small.
The report card on the IMF as an international lender of last resort
The International Monetary Fund is seventy years old. Forty four countries were
represented at Bretton Woods. Now there are 18 members and 2400 employees;
about half of the employees are economists. It was established to serve and advance
the interests of its members, and to reduce the likelihood that international trad-
ing and payments arrangements would fracture much as they did in the 1930s, and
world trade would decline sharply.

THE INTERNATIONAL LENDER OF LAST RESORT 311
The report card on the performance of the Fund cannot be divorced from the
performance of the world economy. Grades on the IMF report card that could be
given include:
● the growth in world trade
● stability in the prices of currencies
● currency protectionism
● monitoring the global economy
● financial assistance
● technical assistance
The growth in world trade has been exceptional, in part because the older
established industrial countries have accepted imports of traditional manufactured
goods from newly industrializing countries. Initially Japan and Taiwan, then South
Korea and Singapore, and Hong Kong, and subsequently China and Thailand,
and Malaysia. Protectionism has flared from time to time in response to the surge
in imports. Various countries have complained about particular US industry
protectionism.
The problem in developing a report card on the performance of the IMF is
distinguishing how many of its perceived shortcomings, relative to the aspirations
of those at Bretton Woods in 1944, should be attributed to the problems of collective
leadership and the member countries, and how many should be attributed to the
leadership of the Fund including the managing director and the staff. Obviously
there is a tension; the Fund as an institution would like additional powers, but the
member countries – and especially the member countries with the most votes – are
reluctant to concede greater power to the Fund staff. The likelihood is high that
there is a tension between the smaller countries that would like a stronger Fund as a
counter to voting strength of the four or five largest countries.
World trade has expanded rapidly, and national tariffs and other restraints on
cross-border trade in goods, services, and securities have declined.
The variability in the prices of currencies in nominal terms and in real terms
has been very large since the early 1970s. The deviations between the market prices
of currencies and the real prices of currencies and the scope of overshooting and
undershooting have been large. The Fund appears not to have made the connection
between the variations in these flows and the changes in economic activity.
The Fund has promoted financial deregulation. Minsky would have considered
financial deregulation a shock, and would have been greatly concerned with the pace
of liberalization, with the impacts of cross-border investment inflows on the supplies
of credit to the domestic borrowers.
A number of countries, especially in Asia, have followed beggar-thy-neighbor
policies. Singapore has been at the top of the list in the efforts to achieve employment
gains by maintaining a low price for its currency, which is evident from its large
and persistent current account surpluses and the cumulative increase in its net

312 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
international creditor position. No large country could have realized such large and
persistent surpluses.
The Fund has lost sight of its original mandate to manage the international
monetary system. There appears to be a modest understanding at the Fund about
the perniciousness of the variability in cross-border investment inflows and the
destabilizing impacts of the variability of these flows on the GDPs of the countries
that experience these inflows.

14
THE LEHMAN PANIC – AN
AVOIDABLE CRASH
T
he bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers Holdings, the fourth largest US invest-
ment bank, in mid-September 2008 triggered the most severe financial
panic and crash in a century. Lehman had been an aggressive buyer of mortgage-
r elated securities; the firm used the money that it obtained from selling its own
short term IOUs to buy long-term mortgages. Every investment bank is highly
leveraged, but Lehman was at the extreme end of the spectrum in terms of its
leverage; its assets were more than thirty times its capital. At times, Lehman’s
leverage may have been as much as forty times its capital; at the end of each quar-
ter, Lehman engaged in ‘window dressing’ so that its reported leverage appeared
smaller than the leverage that it had had in the previous several months.
Lehman’s management had Goldman envy. Goldman Sachs was the most
profitable and the most prestigious of the investment banks, although Lehman
had a much longer history. Lehman was very profitable during the years when
real estate prices were surging because of its high leverage and its aggressive
posture toward risks. Lehman acquired both the credit risk that the borrowers
would default and the duration risk that short-term interest rates would not
increase significantly relative to long-term interest rates.
Leverage is sharp and double-edged. When the economy is prospering and
real estate prices are increasing, the greater the leverage, the greater the profit-
ability. One of the ironies of financial arithmetic is that when property prices
increase, household net worth increases and leverage will appear to decline
because the percentage increase in property prices is larger than the percentage
increase in indebtedness. The borrowers appear wealthier, since the value of their
assets has increased more rapidly than the value of their liabilities. But when

314 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
the boom morphs into a slowdown, the high leverage means that the percentage
decline in the net worth of the indebted households and of the banks may be
three or four times larger than the percentage decline in property prices.
The earliest manias reviewed in this book occurred nearly four hundred
years ago, and many of the manias and panics took place more than one hun-
dred years ago. The 2008 crisis occurred in ‘real time’ – as the sixth edition of
this book was under preparation.
When property prices begin to tumble, the most vulnerable market partici-
pants are those that have expanded most rapidly in the previous several years
and those who have the greatest leverage. US real estate prices peaked at the end
of 2006, and declined in 2007 and 2008. Lehman was subject to two ‘runs’ in the
summer of 2008 – investors and hedge funds sold their Lehman shares, both
those they owned and those they could borrow, because they anticipated that the
price of these shares would decline. And the investors, including many banks
that were lenders to Lehman and owned its IOUs, were increasingly reluctant to
renew these loans as they matured. Both groups were concerned that Lehman
seemed slow in raising additional capital to counter the decline in its net worth
from the fall in the price of its mortgage-related securities. And the President of
Lehman was not the most popular financier in Manhattan; indeed he may have
been one of the least popular. But if bankers are ranked by popularity someone
had to be at the bottom of the hit parade in terms of this attribute.
Would US financial history have been different if the head of Lehman has
been a more popular, engaging, and attractive individual? Almost certainly
yes. But would US financial history have been significantly different if Jack
Armstrong had been head of Lehman; that’s a much more difficult question.
When Lehman failed, global credit markets ‘froze’ – liquidity disappeared.
Trading volumes declined sharply. There was the traditional rush to cash that
occurs when the financial environment suddenly becomes highly uncertain;
the firms with abundant supplies of cash were able to extend credit but were
extremely reluctant to do so because they wanted to maintain their liquidity
and their cash holdings, in part because they might find it difficult to refinance
maturing debt and in part because the shortage of liquidity would mean that
some firms would be obliged to sell securities at prices much below their intrin-
sic value. The firms like Lehman that had relied extensively on borrowed short-
term funds to finance their purchases and holdings of long-term securities
found it increasingly difficult – and extraordinarily expensive – to re-finance
their maturing IOUs. The risk premium embedded in the structure of interest
rates soared; the interest rates in the interbank market increased by a factor of
30 to 40 relative to the interest rates on US Treasury bills, and the interest rates

THE LEHMAN PANIC 315
on high-risk bonds surged relative to those on US Treasury bonds. The credit
shock of 2008 was like the proverbial one hundred year flood; none of the trad-
ers and investors had previously experienced such a meltdown.
The most recent previous episode of financial distress was in the summer of
1998, when Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM), then the largest hedge fund
in the United States, was ‘on the ropes’. LTCM also was highly leveraged, and it had
been highly profitable. But LTCM had made a losing bet, and in the effort to raise
cash, it had to sell securities in a market that was not especially receptive to illiquid
securities. The prices of these securities would decline when they were sold. And
few market participants would be eager to buy these securities because they knew,
or at least suspected, that LTCM would be obliged to sell more of these same securi-
ties as losses eroded its capital, which would depress their price further.
LTCM was on a death spiral because it was obliged to sell some relatively
illiquid securities because it needed cash to repay some maturing short-term
loans that the lenders would not renew. Modest declines in the prices of the
securities meant that LTCM incurred losses on these sales; hence its capital was
declining and its leverage was increasing. But since the lenders would not renew
maturing loans as long as the firm’s leverage was increasing, LTCM had to sell
even more securities.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York took the leadership role to resolve
the problem, and it ‘induced’ fourteen banks that had been lenders to LTCM to
convert some of their loans to buy shares in LTCM. These banks then owned
90 percent of LTCM and the firm continued to shrink.
The policy problem for the US government in the autumn of 2008 was the
familiar one – should new measures be adopted to provide additional liquidity
to the domestic financial system or instead should the US government continue
with a hands-off approach, even though the prices of securities would decline
further, more banks would fail, and the ensuing recession would be steep and
perhaps prolonged? Eventually – perhaps in three or four years – markets would
stabilize, and the next banking crisis might be less severe perhaps because the
lenders would be much more cautious – or at least more cautious. In contrast,
if the US government intervened to stabilize the credit markets, the economic
slowdown would be moderated but the next crisis would be more severe because
lenders and investors would conclude that they would be ‘bailed out’ by the US
government – whatever that means.
THE 2005 SURGE IN US HOUSE PRICES
Sharp increases in the prices of real estate result from rapid increases in the
supply of credit available to those who want to buy real estate. Often the increase

316 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
in the supply of credit has been too fast to be sustainable, because real estate
prices have increased too rapidly relative to household incomes. Some investors
purchased real estate to profit from the anticipated increase in property prices;
in many cases, their interest payments on the borrowed money were larger than
their rental incomes and they relied on the money from new loans to pay some
of the interest on their indebtedness. When the growth of credit slowed, some of
these borrowers would not have enough money for their interest payments, and
they would become distress sellers of real estate. In some cases the prices they
would receive when they sold their properties would be below their mortgage
indebtedness, and they defaulted on their loans.
US house prices peaked at the end of 2006. Between 2002 and 2006, the
market value of US residential real estate had increased from $16,000 billion
to $23,000 billion, or from 110 percent of US GDP to 150 percent of US GDP
– which was 15 percent higher in 2006 than in 2002. The sharp increase in
property prices resulted from the ready availability of mortgage loans and led
to a boom in the construction of new homes and condominium apartments.
Housing starts increased to 2.1 million units a year, or nearly 40 percent more
than the number that was needed to accommodate the growth of the American
population, the demand for second homes, and the replacement of the homes
lost to fires, storms, and highway construction.
The increase in the credit available for mortgages was facilitated by securiti-
zation, which had begun in the 1970s and initially involved depositing mortgages
with similar attributes in terms of maturity and credit risk in a dedicated corpo-
ration in the form of a trust. The managers of the trust then issued new securities
(collateralized mortgage obligations or CMOs) that were claims on the interest
income and the principal of the trust. Securitization accelerated after 2000; the
second round involved ‘slicing and dicing’ groups of CMOs into four or five dif-
ferent tranches, or slices, that differed in terms of whether they had the first,
an intermediate, or the last priority to the interest income and the principal of
the CMOs. Thus the collateralized debt obligations, or CDOs, were the ‘children
of the CMOs’. The initial round of trusts begat a second round of trusts. The
tranches with the first priority to the interest income of the CMOs were placed
in one trust, the tranches with the second priority to the interest income of the
CMOs were placed in a second trust, and so on. Conservative investors could buy
the CDOs that had the first claim to the interest income because they were least
risky, while investors that wanted higher yields could buy those that had lower
priority to the interest income of the CMOs – and hence were riskier.
The intuition is that the CDOs that had the next-to-last or last claim to
the interest income and the principal of the CMOs would be riskier than those
that had the first claim. Somehow, the credit-rating agencies concluded from

THE LEHMAN PANIC 317
‘their models’ that even those CDOs that had the tranches with the last claim
to the income of the CDOs were nevertheless less risky than the CMOs. This
outcome seemed counter-intuitive, and after the collapse of the mortgage mar-
ket, it appeared that the credit-rating agencies had relied on the information
about the riskiness of various CDOs that they had obtained from the investment
banks that were eager to satisfy the investors’ demand for securities that had
high anticipated rates of return and yet were deemed not especially risky. The
demand for free lunches never ends. And the supply of chumps is endless.
The amount of money available for mortgage loans increased as a result of
securitization, because the CMOs and the CDOs were more liquid than individ-
ual mortgages, and accordingly the interest rates on mortgages were somewhat
lower. The increase in investor demand for mortgage-related securities meant
that some borrowers with less attractive credit histories qualified for mort-
gages because ‘the money was there’. Moreover, the investment bankers became
innovative about both the minimal down-payments required of home buyers
and the interest payments on mortgages – there were adjustable-rate mortgages
(ARMs), interest-only mortgages, and negative amortization mortgages (part of
the interest payments that the borrowers were scheduled to make to the lenders
during the first several years of the mortgage was added to the principal of the
mortgages). Some mortgages had ‘teaser interest rates’ – the rates that the bor-
rowers were charged for the first two or three years of the mortgage loan were
exceptionally low, perhaps two or three percentage points below the interest
rates that they would pay during the remaining years of the loan.
These innovations in the terms of mortgage loans were motivated because
the demand for mortgage-related securities was significantly larger than the
supply of loans from creditworthy borrowers – which is typical of the last
several years of an expansive credit cycle.
Selling Money by S. C. Gwynne
Sam Gwynne was a young banker in the 1970s; he had been hired by Cleveland Trust,
one of the leading banks in the city, soon after graduating from college to develop
the international department of the bank. The bank’s management was concerned
that they would lag behind the banks in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, and San
Francisco that were rapidly increasing their loans to foreign borrowers. Cleveland
Trust could readily sell its own IOUs to get the money to lend; its problem as a recent
newcomer in foreign lending was in finding qualified borrowers. And Gwynne was
on the road in Latin America and the Philippines seeking borrowers. The US banks
headquartered on the seacoasts and in Chicago had been searching for qualified
borrowers before Gwynne went abroad, so many of the firms that were interested
in borrowing money from Cleveland Trust previously had been turned down by

318 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
other banks. Cleveland Trust ended up with a portfolio of high-risk borrowers – the
developing-country equivalent of subprime borrowers in California, Nevada, and
Florida.
During the early stages of the credit cycle there are a large number of qualified
borrowers. The supply of credit increases more rapidly than the number of qualified
borrowers. The choice for the Cleveland Trust was to keep dancing as long as the
music was playing, or to sit down and lose market share
Securitization led to ‘financial deepenings’, the supply of mortgage-related
securities increased more than twice as rapidly as the supply of mortgages. For
example, every $100 million of new mortgage loans would lead to an increase of
nearly $100 million of CMOs that in turn would nearly lead to an additional $100
million of CDOs. The investment banks that established the trusts and issued
the CMOs and the CDOs loved the fee income that they earned when they pro-
duced these new securities, since this income did not appear to be related to an
increase in risk. During this financial deepening process the investment banks
carried large inventories of mortgages and mortgage-related securities in their
‘production and distribution pipelines’ awaiting sale to investors; some of these
pipelines were six months long – that is, six months might pass from the day
that an investment bank bought a mortgage until the day that it issued a new
CMO that included this mortgage. A credit risk was attached to these mortgages
as long as they were in the pipeline; some investment banks regularly hedged
this risk.
Some of the investment banks ‘sold’ these mortgage-related securities to
their captive affiliates if they could not be readily sold to non-related investors.
Securitization of mortgages led to an anonymous relationship between
the homeowner borrowers and the mortgage lenders that replaced the tradi-
tional relationship where the lenders knew the borrowers because they lived in
the same neighborhood. Later this anonymity would come to complicate the
‘workout arrangements’ when individual borrowers had problems making their
monthly debt-service payments. The new and anonymous relationship between
the lenders and the borrowers invited fraud in the mortgage-origination proc-
ess. Some of the fraud was on the part of borrowers, who provided incomplete or
misleading information about their incomes, assets, and credit histories (which
were known as ‘liars’ loans’). Some of the fraud was by the mortgage brokers,
who encouraged homeowners to take on indebtedness that was much too high
relative to their incomes. The mortgage brokers knew that some of the borrowers
were fibbing about their incomes and assets and credit histories, but they were
not concerned about the ability of the borrowers to repay because the credit risk
would be transferred to other firms in the mortgage loan-distribution pipeline.

THE LEHMAN PANIC 319
The eagerness of the credit-rating agencies for the fee income attached
to providing an evaluation of the risk of individual mortgage-related securi-
ties ‘clouded’ their objectivity. The charitable interpretation is that they had
‘crooked yardsticks’, but they might lose the business to one of their competi-
tors if they failed to provide the credit rating that the investment banks wanted.
(The investment banks paid the credit-rating agencies to produce the reports
that were intended to guide the decisions of the purchasers of mortgage securi-
ties as investments.)
At some stage it was inevitable that the booms in real estate in the United
States, Britain, Ireland, Spain, and other countries would end, property prices
would decline, new home construction would fall and probably sharply,
and recessions would follow. There was significant disagreement about the
impacts of the recession and the slowdown in construction on house prices
and whether the upward momentum would stall and prices would stabilize
at the higher level or whether instead real estate prices would decline. The
view of many lenders was that property prices would not decline because,
well, ‘US real estate prices had never before declined on a national basis’. (A
factually incorrect statement since US real estate prices declined in the Great
Depression.) Most of those involved in the real estate industry believed that
there would not be a significant reduction in home prices. A second, much
smaller, group – members of the ‘reversion-to-the-mean school’ – believed
that prices would decline until the traditional ratio of the market value of US
real estate to US GDP, plus or minus 10 percent, had been restored. A third
view was that house prices would decline 10 to 15 percent below the tradi-
tional historical ratio because the economy would need to ‘digest’ the large
excess supply of houses that had developed during the boom years when hous-
ing starts were larger than the demographic demand; these declines below the
long-run trend line would be larger in those regions that had experienced the
most overbuilding.
Housing starts began to decline toward the end of 2006, which contributed
to the slowdown in the US GDP growth rate. Still, the decline in the US GDP
growth rate in 2007 and the first eight months of 2008 was modest. The number
of people employed peaked in December 2006, and thereafter the number
declined continuously but modestly. During the first half of 2008, it appeared as
if the United States would experience a prolonged and gradual slowdown until
the excess supply of houses and apartments was absorbed.
Then the bankruptcy of Lehman on 15 September triggered the most severe
banking crisis since the Great Depression. The cost to American families was
immense; the unemployment rate soared and more than ten million families
lost their homes in foreclosure proceedings.

320 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
The Japanese experience in the 1990s suggests that declines in prices of
securities and assets need not lead to a crisis or panic, even though the metric
of the increase in the ratio of household net worth to GDP in Japan was more
than ten times larger than the same ratio in the United States. Both stock
prices and real estate prices in Japan had increased by a factor of five to six
while US real estate prices had increased by 40 percent. Although the banks
and most of the other financial institutions in Japan had negative net worth
in any meaningful mark-to-market test, there never was a run on a major
Japanese bank.
Japan was ‘different’ because it was ‘understood’ that bank depositors would
not incur losses even if a major financial institution were closed. The tradition
in Japan is that many of the types of losses that would fall on individuals in the
United States and in other Western industrial countries are ‘socialized’ – the
government makes good on these losses either by providing additional capital
to the banks or by establishing a new government agency that would buy the
dodgy loans, which meant that the costs would fall on the taxpayers. In effect,
Japan had 100 percent deposit insurance and each of the Japanese financial
institutions was ‘too big to fail’ even though the shareholders in many of these
banks eventually would lose most or all of their money.
The first group impacted by the decline in US real estate prices consisted of
those who had purchased homes in 2005 and 2006, often first-time homeown-
ers with spotty credit histories and modest, if any, down-payments. If these bor-
rowers had difficulties in making their monthly payments, they would sell their
properties and repay their mortgage indebtedness – as long as property prices
continued to increase. But once property prices stopped increasing, they were
‘between the rock and a hard place’ since their mortgage indebtedness probably
was larger than the net amounts they would receive if they sold their proper-
ties. And many or perhaps most of these homeowners lacked the cash to pay the
lenders the difference between the amount of the mortgage indebtedness and
the net proceeds from the sale of homes.
The share of subprime mortgages in total mortgages increased from 6 per-
cent in 2003 and 2004 to 20 percent in 2005 and 2006. Many of these subprime
mortgages required that the interest payments in the first several years be
modest. Once property prices began to decline, many individuals that had pur-
chased properties with minimal down-payments then had ‘upside-down mort-
gages’ – their indebtedness was greater than the market value of their homes.
These homeowners then had three choices – they could continue to make the
monthly mortgage payments, they could engage in a ‘short sale’ and sell the
property and hope that the lender would ‘forgive’ the excess of their indebted-
ness over their sales proceeds, or they could engage in ‘jingle mail’ – return the

THE LEHMAN PANIC 321
keys to the lenders and walk, leaving the lenders with the costs and burdens of
foreclosure. The larger the decline in house prices, the greater the decline in
the net worth of homeowners, and the higher the number of mortgage loans
that would become non-performing.
The second group impacted by the decline in property prices comprised
mortgage brokers that bought the loans from the homeowners with the intent
to sell them to the investment banks, who had twelve to eighteen months to
put these mortgages back to the brokers if the borrowers stopped making their
monthly payments and ask the brokers to return the money they had received
when they sold the loan. A few mortgage brokers that had extended loans to
subprime borrowers failed in 2005; many more failed in the last few months of
2006. The failure of these brokers meant that the investment banks were stuck
with tens of billions of non-performing loans that they had recently acquired
from the mortgage brokers.
The investment banks were the third group that was impacted by the
defaults of the homeowners, and in several additional ways beyond being stuck
with the non-performing mortgages that they had recently acquired. Once real
estate prices began to decline, it became much more difficult to sell mortgage-
related securities because they were much harder to value. As mortgage defaults
increased, the investment banks incurred losses on the tens of billions of mort-
gages and mortgage-related securities, including the CMOs and CDOs that they
had been unable to sell.
Once an investment bank was a distress seller of mortgage-related securi-
ties, their prices declined sharply. The ‘mark-to-market’ convention was that
firms that owned identical securities had to value them at the most recent mar-
ket price. Alpha firm might have a desperate need for cash, and it might have
sold Omega bonds at a price much below the price appropriate given their antic-
ipated income. Beta, Gamma, and every other firm that owned Omega bonds
were then required by the mark-to-market convention to use the market price
accepted by Alpha in valuing their holdings of Omega bonds. The anomaly was
that the market prices of these securities were much lower than the prices based
on their current and prospective cash flows. (All of a sudden, the ‘mark-to-mar-
ket’ convention that had been adopted to reduce the scope for fraud by those
valuing their inventories of securities no longer seemed like such a good idea.)
Subsequently the commercial banks that had acquired significant mort-
gages in California, Georgia, Illinois, and a few other states failed because of
large loan losses. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation closed those
banks that had exceptionally large losses relative to their capital, and sold their
deposits to banks that had a secure capital position; the FDIC either had to take
over some or all of the non-performing loans of these failed banks or pay some

322 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
of the acquiring banks to take over these loans. Nearly two hundred commer-
cial banks had failed by the end of 2009, and another 250 by the end of 2011.
The money that the FDIC had collected from the insurance premium paid by
the banks that was used to ensure that no depositor incurred a loss was being
depleted at a rapid rate.
The FDIC had a $500 billion credit line at the US Treasury; it had rarely
drawn on this line. If this line was exhausted, the Congress almost certainly
would have voted more funds to the FDIC in the form of a loan that eventually
would have to be repaid by the higher insurance premiums on the banks that
remained in business. The FDIC needed cash and it asked the banks to make
advance payments of their insurance premiums. The banks were not happy.
Several of the hedge funds managed by Bear Stearns failed in March 2007;
these funds owned mortgage-related securities and were extensively leveraged.
Then in mid-August, Countrywide Financial, the largest mortgage lender in the
United States, apparently had a liquidity problem; the firm had rapidly increased
its share of the national market for mortgages, and had relied on money bor-
rowed in the commercial paper market to finance about one third of the mort-
gages that it purchased. Countrywide was unable to renew its commercial paper
loans as they matured; initially it drew on the credit lines that it had with com-
mercial banks. Then, Countrywide sold a new issue of preferred shares to Bank
of America, and a few weeks later Bank of America purchased Countrywide.
About the same time, Northern Rock, the largest mortgage lender in Britain,
began to borrow from the Bank of England because it also was not able to re-
finance its IOUs in commercial paper as they matured.
The Bagehot doctrine and insolvent banks
The Bagehot doctrine discussed in Chapter 11 was that a central bank should lend
freely – but at a penalty interest rate – to forestall the likelihood that a liquidity crisis
would cascade into a solvency crisis because a commercial bank would sell securi-
ties and assets to get the cash to meet the demands of their depositors that wanted
their money. The prices of these securities would decline, and some of the banks that
previously had been well-capitalized then might have too little capital as the prices
of the securities in their portfolios fell.
The extension of credit from the central bank to a bank that has a shortage of
liquidity can be viewed as a ‘bail-out’ of the bank’s shareholders; otherwise this bank
might be forced to close and its shareholders would lose most or all of their money.
Bagehot advised against the extension of financial assistance to an insolvent bank.
Assume, however, that Alpha Bank – or Lehman or the Royal Bank of Scotland –
is insolvent. Should the US government provide financial assistance to ensure that
Alpha Bank could continue to operate even if it has a negative net worth – as the US
Treasury did for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in mid-September 2008 when both

THE LEHMAN PANIC 323
were put into ‘conservatorship’ at the US Treasury? In effect, the US government
would have become the majority shareholder because the investors that previously
had owned Alpha Bank would experience a dilution of their share ownership when
new shares were issued to the US Treasury in exchange for its investment to ensure
that Alpha Bank would not close.
If Alpha Bank went bankrupt, the legal procedure is that its securities and assets
would be sold to get the money to satisfy its creditors, the prices of these securities
would decline, and some other lenders that had previously been deemed well-
capitalized that owned the same securities as Alpha Bank would experience a decline
in their net worth and might have too little capital.
The logic that Bagehot used to justify why the central bank should provide credit
to an illiquid bank that is solvent also justifies why the central bank or some other
government agency should provide financial assistance to an insolvent bank. Both
arguments centered on the impacts of the failure of one financial institution on the
solvency of other financial firms.
Early in 2008, Bear Stearns, the sixth largest US investment bank, was subject to
two runs, one on its shares by investors who thought the firm would incur even
larger losses and might go bankrupt, and another by the holders of its short-
term IOUs who were reluctant to renew their loans to Bear. Bear was acquired
by JPMorgan Chase, but only after the Federal Reserve had agreed to take up
to $29 billion of losses on some of the ‘toxic waste’ that had been in Bear’s port-
folio. Then, in the first week of September, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were
taken over by the US Treasury in what was announced as a ‘conservatorship’;
one estimate was that each of these firms had had a negative net worth of $100
billion to $200 billion as a result of the declines in the market values of the mort-
gages and mortgage-related securities that each owned. Hence it might have cost
the US Treasury at least $300 billion or perhaps $400 billion to re-capitalize
both firms.
In September 2008, Washington Mutual (WaMu), one of the largest and
fastest growing mortgage lenders, was subject to a run; the FDIC intervened and
detached the bank from its holding company. WaMu was sold to JPMorgan Chase
without cost to the FDIC; the shareholders of WaMu lost all of their money.
The precarious financial position of Lehman Brothers was well known, which
made it difficult for the firm to obtain more capital; potential investors had no
way to value many of the securities in Lehman’s portfolio and hence no way to
know how much capital the firm needed. These lenders were cautious, since it was
difficult to determine the ‘true’ market value of the securities in their portfolio
at a time when the prices of mortgages and of mortgage-related securities were
declining. The US government tried to facilitate the sale of Lehman to other finan-
cial institutions – but the government officials said no government monies would

324 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
be used to bless the sale. (The credit of the US government was committed to
encourage JPMorgan Chase to buy Bear Stearns, since the Fed agreed to buy up to
$29 billion of dodgy securities that were in Bear’s portfolio. The commitment to
buy these securities had been demanded by JPMorgan Chase to ‘get the deal done’;
otherwise, the US government would have had to cope with the consequences of
the failure of Bear. And the credit of the US Treasury was extended to ensure that
the owners of the bonds of Fannie and Freddie would not incur losses.)
The Secretary of the Treasury subsequently said that the effort to sell
Lehman to Barclays Bank had been prevented by the financial authorities in
London, who were concerned that the British government might have to bail
out Barclays if the losses of Lehman and its need for capital had been underes-
timated. The British government was reluctant to bail out an American bank,
even though Lehman employed six thousand individuals in London.
One day after the failure of Lehman, the US government intervened to
prevent the collapse of AIG, then the world’s largest insurance company.
AIG had sold several hundred billion dollars’ worth of credit default swaps
(CDSs), essentially insurance policies to the buyers of bonds that they would
not incur losses if the firms that had issued bonds defaulted. Many of these
CDSs were purchased by the firms that owned Lehman bonds. Some were
purchased by third parties, who had no direct insurable interest; from their
point of view, the premium required to buy a credit default swap was low
relative to the payoff if the borrower defaulted – a Wall Street version of a
lottery ticket.
Would AIG have failed in the absence of the financial investment by the
US government? The answer depends on whether the US government would
have intervened to prevent or dampen the decline in the prices of securities by
agreeing to provide additional capital – perhaps a very large amount of capital
– so that institutions would not be obliged to sell securities because the losses
on some of the securities in their portfolios might mean that their capital was
too low; they might conclude that the interests of their shareholders would be
better served if they sold securities and became smaller rather than if they tried
to raise additional capital.
Saving Lehman would have meant as a minimum that the bondholders
and those with counterparty positions would not incur any financial loss; how-
ever, the existing shareholders would find that their ownership interest had
been diluted by 99 or 99.5 percent. Top management would have been given
one-way tickets to Outer Slobovia. But the corpus of the Lehman firm and the
credit channels that it managed would remain open, even though subsequently
Lehman’s assets might decline slowly.

THE LEHMAN PANIC 325
One reason that the decision not to save Lehman was so costly was that it
became evident that the US government did not have a policy when the capital
of a large bank had been so depleted that it would be forced to close. In 1984
the US government intervention meant that none of the lenders to Continental

holding company. The US government intervened to ‘save’ Bear Stearns; each

to pay JPMorgan Chase up to $29 billion if the bank incurred losses on toxic
assets. The US Treasury was on the hook for up to $300 billion or $400 billion or
perhaps more to ensure that the investors that owned the bonds of Fannie Mae
and Freddie Mac would not incur losses. These are two episodes in the eight-
een months when the government intervened to protect the bondholders and
other creditors of large financial firms that would otherwise have failed. Bear
was smaller than Lehman, Fannie and Freddie immensely larger. Somehow the
government had enough imagination to save these firms, and then its imagina-
tion disappeared when Lehman was about to fail. Moreover, JPMorgan Chase
paid $10 for each of the shares in Bear, after its arranged marriage was blessed
by allowing Morgan to put up to $29 billion of securities that might be subject

to accept the securities of dubious value. But the US government decided not to

money.
The second factor that contributed to the turmoil and the credit freeze after
Lehman was closed is that the government regulators did not know that Lehman
was the principal dealer in the market for commercial paper, where firms with
excess cash buy the IOUs of firms that are short of cash. Lehman brought the
borrowers and the investors together; the staff of Lehman understood the chan-
nels of credit. When Lehman closed, a lot of information was lost.
Economic history would have been different if the US government had
become the dominant shareholder in Lehman Brothers and had kept it open.
While a recession would have followed from the decline in property prices and
the sharp fall in housing starts, the decline in economic activity would have

The US government officials said that they did not have the authority to pre-

326 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
ensure that the bondholders of Fannie and Freddie would not incur losses. And

Incestuousness and cronyism and bad blood
Henry (‘Hank’) Paulson was US Secretary of the Treasury when Lehman failed.
The chatter in the markets is that Paulson is said to have hated Dick Fuld, head of
Lehman.
One of Paulson’s brothers worked for Lehman in its New York office. A relative of
President George Bush worked for Lehman in one of its regional offices.
One cynic has suggested that Secretary Paulson was concerned that if the US
government intervened to prevent the closing of Lehman, the Bush Administration
would have been accused of ‘crony capitalism’.
Do any of these factors explain why the US government could not find the authority
to prevent Lehman from closing?
Many in the US government were concerned that preventing the failure of
Lehman would have meant that there would be many more Bear Stearns and
Lehmans and Countrywides that would be on the ropes in the next financial
crisis in 2020 or 2025 because their managements had taken on too much risk.
The case that the US financial management team wanted to send a signal seems
much stronger than the case that they did not believe they had the authority to
‘save Lehman’. But the question is, who would have been saved if the US govern-
ment had intervened to prevent the closing of Lehman?
‘TOO BIG TO FAIL’ THE COSTS AND CURSE OF THE CLICHÉ

The implosion of every surge in real estate prices leads to the failure of a Lehman
or of a Northern Rock, usually one of the firms that had expanded rapidly dur-
ing the economic boom that preceded the banking bust. Angelo Mozilo, the
founder of Countrywide Financial, wanted his firm to become the largest mort-
gage lender in the country. WaMu, headquartered in Seattle, was reluctant to
lose market share to Countrywide. The loan officers in the hundreds of branches
of these firms almost always have quotas that indicate how many new loans they
have to book each week in order to satisfy the managers of the branches, who
have quotas to fulfill.
The curse of the cliché ‘too big to fail’ is that it obscures more than it reveals.
If a small bank incurs large losses, the FDIC takes over the bank, and induces
some other bank to buy its deposits and most or all of its loans; the FDIC may

THE LEHMAN PANIC 327
need to throw in some money to attract a buyer as it did with the JPMorgan
Chase purchase of Bear Stearns. But assume that one of the three or four largest
US banks incurred massive loan losses; any bank that tried to buy this failing
bank would incur an indigestion problem. And the same problem would arise
if the fifth largest bank in the country or the tenth largest bank were to incur
large loan losses. ‘Too big to fail’ often is interpreted to mean ‘too big to close’
because of the disruption to the credit channels that it would incur if it went out
of business.
The very largest banks can fail and still remain open; the ownership and
management control would change while the bank remains open and contin-
ues to provide services to its borrowers and its lender. Each bank has at least
six groups of stakeholders, including insured depositors, uninsured depositors,
bond holders, financial firms with counterparty risks, bondholders of the bank
holding company, owners of common stock, owners of preferred stock, senior
managers, and the board of directors. The city where the bank is headquartered
is a major stakeholder. When Continental Illinois failed in 1984, the insured
depositors were protected by the FDIC, and the uninsured depositors withdrew
their money before the bank was taken over by the FDIC. The bondholders
came out whole because the bank was never closed and, similarly, those with
counterparty claims did not lose any money. The common shareholders lost all
their money, the top managers were removed and publicly embarrassed, and
the individuals who were on the Board of Directors lost their sinecures and
their reputations were tarnished. For all practical purposes, Continental Illinois
failed; Continental Bank was not too big to fail.
A number of large banks would have failed and closed in 2008 if the US
Treasury had not made a large investment in these firms. The price of each
common share in Citibank declined to less than $1; in effect, investors were say-
ing that there was a high probability that the shares would become worthless.
The US government provided $45 billion of capital to Citibank by purchasing
newly issued shares and at its peak owned 36 percent of the bank’s shares. The
US government secured a change in management. Similarly Bank of America
remained open only because the US government provided $25 billion of capital.
The Royal Bank of Scotland, the largest bank in Britain, failed; Her Majesty’s
Government re-capitalized the bank and owned about 90 percent of the bank
shares.
If even the largest banks can fail and the shareholders in these banks lose all
or most of their money, what remains of the moral hazard argument that ‘bailing
out’ Lehman in September 2008 would have encouraged increased risk-taking
in the next several decades? This argument is that the private individuals who
take the risks realize large financial rewards if their risk-taking pays off; if the

328 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
r isk-taking doesn’t pay off, the government and hence the taxpayers have to pick
up the chit for the losses. The top managers in both Bear and Lehman lost much
of their personal wealth in the form of the shares of their firms and options to
buy more shares that were in the portfolios; they lost a major part of their fami-
lies’ fortunes.
The traditional debate is among those who believe that the government
should not intervene to save firms that are financially challenged; those who
advance this view believe that if asset prices decline sufficiently sharply, the
markets eventually will stabilize and vulture investors who had been waiting
on the sidelines will then buy the institutions that had lost most of their capi-
tal. Those who support this view subscribe to the moral hazard position that
the next financial crisis will be more severe because the lenders would believe
that they will be bailed out, much as the government intervened to prevent the
closing of firms like Bear. The shareholders in Continental Illinois, Fannie Mae
and Freddie Mac, and Lehman lost much of their wealth when the prices of the
stocks of these companies became worthless. The shareholders in Washington
Mutual and Countrywide Financial lost much of their wealth (although Angelo
Mozilo has retained a lot of wealth).
The challenge to this view is that each crisis is different, and that the eco-
nomic costs of not stabilizing the system are extremely high in terms of the large
number of insolvent firms, the surge in the unemployment rate, and the loss of
production and decline in GDP. Moreover, the moral hazard view fails to dis-
tinguish between government intervention to stabilize a single failing firm, and
intervention to stabilize a group of firms – or a very large group of firms – in
response to a major systemic shock. Is the failure or near failure a result of faulty
management decisions at a time when the economic environment is stable?; in
this case, the failure is idiosyncratic and reflects that management made a faulty
decision. And there is no case for intervening to prevent this firm from closing,
since the adverse impact on other lenders would be trivially small. But if a large
number of banks and other financial institutions are on the ropes at more or less
the same time because of a sharp decline in the prices of securities or real estate,
the failure is systemic; many of the firms that are about to fail formerly had
been considered well-managed. The sharp increase in the number of banks and
other firms that might fail has resulted from a dramatic change in the financial
environment, and what might charitably be called the mismanagement of the
economy by the monetary authorities.
Return to the question ‘Who would be “saved” if Lehman had been saved?’
The purpose of intervention is to ensure that the institution would remain
open so that the channels for the distribution of credit would remain open;
the bondholders and those with counterparty risks would remain whole. The

THE LEHMAN PANIC 329
shareholders in Lehman would have lost all or nearly all of the value of their
shares. The top managers of Lehman would have lost their positions. The Board
of Directors would be shown the door.
Hence the position that saving Lehman would have encouraged exces-
sive risk-taking so that the costs would be even larger implicitly assumes that
the existing shareholders would have been made whole or at least would have
walked away with a substantial proportion of their wealth, which is one possible
outcome but not the only one and a very unlikely one. The likelihood that bank
managements in 2025 would conclude that they could undertake very risky
investments because shareholders of Bear had lost 90 percent rather than 100
percent of their wealth seems very low. The traditional argument about moral
hazard fails to distinguish between saving the banks and saving the bankers;
the banks can be saved as functioning institutions, while the bankers – both
the private shareholders and top managers – walk the plank. The masses in the
country are against bailing out the bankers, and this distinction between bail-
ing out the banks and bailing out the bankers should be clear to most interested
observers.
There are two responses to the view that public money should not be used
to stabilize the financial system. One is that the costs of not saving a Lehman
or an AIG in terms of unemployment and business failures and the increase in
the government’s indebtedness are high. A second is that eventually the govern-
ment will change its policy in the effort to stabilize the financial markets, and
that it would have been less costly if the government had intervened earlier. The
delay in intervention means that prices of securities decline further and that a
larger number of banks would fail.
If the government decides to intervene to stabilize the financial system
before property prices have declined to their long-term equilibrium levels, there
may be a need for a series of injections of government money because the con-
tinuing decline in property prices leads to continuing shrinkage in the capital of
the banks. If, in contrast, the intervention is long delayed, then the loan losses of
the banks will have been larger, and they may need a larger injection of govern-
ment capital to stabilize their balance sheets or they may shrink their assets to
match the decline in their capital. The choice of the optimal date to intervene to
stabilize the system requires a fine touch – and during the moments of stress as
prices of most risky assets are declining, a fine touch is likely to be in short sup-
ply. One implication is that the less risky option may be to intervene early, and
another is that the authorities should have a game plan based on their insights
from playing the financial market counterpart of war games.
Banks traditionally have borrowed at short term and loaned at long term –
one of the risks that they have acquired was that short-term interest rates might

330 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
increase significantly relative to long-term interest rates, as in the early 1980s.
Another was the liquidity risk that depositors might withdraw their money and
that their creditors might be reluctant to purchase more of the banks’ IOUs
when the ones they then owned matured. The prospect was that the depositors
and the creditors would discipline the lending practices of the banks by the
implicit threat to withdraw their money from any bank that appeared to have
a lot of risky assets in its portfolio. Countrywide Financial and Northern Rock
were both disciplined in August 2007, eight or ten months after property prices
started to decline – the discipline was needed several years earlier when they
were rapidly increasing their purchases of mortgage loans.
The implicit threat that depositors – small household depositors – would
withdraw their money was supposed to mean that the prospect of runs would
deter banks from making risky loans. The inference from the data is that the
discipline occurs only after property prices have begun to decline. The Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation was established in 1934 to reduce runs on
banks by owners of small deposits who were concerned that they might lose
their money if their bank failed. In effect, these depositors were provided with
a US government guarantee against loss if the banks failed. Initially, the ceil-
ing on each insured deposit was $2500, which was soon raised to $5000, and
then to $10,000 in 1950, $20,000 in 1969, $100,000 in 1980, and to $250,000 in
2008. Individuals could readily circumvent this ceiling by setting up accounts
in the same bank under the names of different family members and different
combinations of family members, and by opening accounts in different banks.
In effect, deposit insurance was unlimited to anyone who wanted to break up a
large amount of money into $250,000 units.
The institutional innovation of deposit insurance eliminates the ‘discipline’
that depositors might impose on banks, based on the threat that they might rush
to get their money, which would mean that the managers of the banks would be
super-cautious; the belief was that these small depositors were unsophisticated
and would be trigger-happy. The view was that there was no need for insurance
of larger depositors because their owners were believed to be sophisticated, and
much less likely to trigger a run.
The practical issue involved in the decision as to whether to ‘save Lehman’
was which of the stakeholders in the firm would avoid losses if government assist-
ance enabled the firm to avoid bankruptcy. Lehman was significantly larger
than Bear. Lehman was regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission
since it was an investment bank; if, instead, it had been a commercial bank, it
would have been regulated by the Federal Reserve.
One interpretation of ‘too big to fail’ is that a faltering bank is so large that no
other institution has sufficient capital to acquire the firm, much as Bear had been

THE LEHMAN PANIC 331
purchased by JPMorgan Chase; hence, the US government would have to provide
financial assistance to any of the five to ten very large firms because its demise
would have costly consequences both for its competitors and the economy.
One of the concerns implicit in the ‘too big to fail’ cliché is that the one or
several stakeholders in the bank benefit from the proverbial ‘free lunch’ because
they are protected against losses that their counterparts in smaller firms would
have incurred when they failed. The largest bank failure prior to the 2008 crisis
was that of Continental Illinois Bank in 1984, then the seventh largest US bank.
Continental Illinois had incurred large loan losses when the oil price declined
sharply. Continental differed from most of the other banks in the ‘top 10’ in
that it had a relatively small domestic deposit base. There had been a run on
Continental Illinois in 1982, but that had been stanched; the run in 1984 started
after the bank reported very weak earnings. The run started on the offshore
branches of Continental Illinois. Initially, the bank borrowed from the Federal
Reserve, and then it was rescued by the FDIC.
The owners of the common stock of Continental Illinois lost all their
money as their shares became virtually worthless. The top executives and sen-
ior managers lost their positions and a large part of their personal wealth that
was invested in the bank’s stocks – and their professional reputations were shat-
tered. The careers of many managers as bankers were shortened. The directors
of Continental Illinois were publicly embarrassed – and most lost money since
they owned shares in the firm.
Who, then, was ‘bailed out’? The owners of the insured deposits did not
incur any losses because of the FDIC guarantee – but these depositors had paid
for this insurance because the premiums that the banks paid for deposit insur-
ance might otherwise have led to higher interest rates on deposits. The owners
of the uninsured deposits also avoided losses because they withdrew virtually
all of their money before Continental Illinois was taken over by the FDIC. The
owners of the subordinated debentures which had been issued by the bank hold-
ing company for Continental Illinois were bailed out. (There is general agree-
ment that the FDIC made a mistake by providing money so that the owners of
the bonds issued by the bank’s holding company did not incur losses.)
For all practical purposes, Continental Illinois failed even though it
remained in business. Presumably, the only way to ensure that the uninsured
depositors took a ‘haircut’ was that the government regulators would close the
bank before all these depositors had closed their accounts in the bank or had
reduced the amount in each account so that it was no larger than the amount of
the insured deposits.
Compare the costs and the benefits of ‘saving Lehman’ with the costs and
benefits of ‘letting Lehman go’. In August and September 2008, the Secretary of

332 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
the Treasury encouraged other financial firms to acquire Lehman, to invest in
Lehman, or to develop a cooperative arrangement that would acquire some of
the dodgy securities that Lehman owned – but he was adamantly against pro-
viding any US government financial assistance to Lehman because he did not
want to be known as ‘Mr Bailout’.
There were several different models of how Lehman might have been saved.
One was Morgan’s purchase of Bear Stearns; a buyer would have been found for
Lehman after the Federal Reserve agreed to acquire $40 or $50 or $60 billion
of its mortgage-related securities that were believed most likely to default. The
buyer might have been given a put, much like JPMorgan Chase was given a put
when it purchased Bear. The owners of Lehman shares would receive a token $1
or $2 a share from the acquiring firm. Some of the senior executives of Lehman
would be given positions in the acquiring firm, most would not. The owners of
Lehman’s short-term IOUs would be made whole, and perhaps the owners of its
bonds would be made whole like the owners of the bonds of Fannie and Freddie;
alternatively these bondholders might have been given haircuts. The Lehman
name would disappear from the marketplace. The financial cost to the Federal
Reserve might have been $50 billion or $60 billion or $70 billion or even $100
billion that it would have used to buy the toxic securities – but these securities
would have had some value after the economy stabilized.
A second model is provided by the US Treasury’s investment by the Troubled
Assets Relief Program (TARP) in Citibank and Bank of America; the US gov-
ernment would buy 60 or 80 million new shares in Lehman at $1 a share – the
amount needed to re-capitalize the firm. The immediate financial cost would be
the amount that the Treasury would have to lay out to buy enough shares so that
the capital of the revived Lehman would be 4 or 5 percent of its liabilities.
A third model is provided by the US Treasury’s takeover of Fannie Mae
and Freddie Mac; Lehman also would be placed in a conservatorship and the
US Treasury would become its owner. The US Treasury would lend money to
Lehman. At some stage, this loan would be converted to newly issued shares,
and then after the crisis and after the firm had become profitable, the gov-
ernment-owned shares in Lehman would be sold to the public in a series of
public offerings over one or two years. The amount that the Treasury would
need to invest would be determined by the size of the ‘hole’ in Lehman’s capital
structure.
Estimating the cost to the US government of saving Lehman is conjectural
and involves the valuation of its mortgages and mortgage-related securities in
the post-crisis period. (During the crisis, the market values of these securities
would be highly uncertain, and almost certainly far below their intrinsic value
based on the cash flows in a stable environment). Before its collapse, Lehman

THE LEHMAN PANIC 333
had a net worth of $30 billion, and a leverage of thirty, so its assets were about
$900 billion and its liabilities $870 billion. If its loan losses were three times its
capital, then the cost to the US Treasury would have been $60 billion.
As Lehman approached bankruptcy, it was ‘two firms’; one firm continued
to generate operating profits of $10 billion to $15 billion a year, while the other
firm had negative capital as a result of the massive decline in the value of the
mortgages and mortgage-related securities in its portfolio. One advantage of the
use of government funds to re-capitalize the firm is that the ‘good bank’ would
continue to generate $10 billion or $15 billion of annual profits from its trading
and investment activities. The advantage of the second and the third approaches
is that the US government would benefit from the operating income of Lehman,
which would offset some of the earlier losses.
The ‘additional cost’ – always noted by those concerned with the moral
hazard argument – is that the next crisis will be more severe because Lehman
would have been ‘bailed out’. Regardless of the approach taken to prevent
Lehman’s bankruptcy, the Lehman shareholders would have been wiped out,
its top executives would have been replaced and lost much of their personal
wealth, and its directors would have been humiliated by their failure to protect
the shareholders. Three groups of stakeholders would have benefited if Lehman
had not failed – one was employees, perhaps some of those with bonuses that
they were scheduled to collect; the second was the owners of Lehman bonds and
other debt instruments; and the third was the counterparties.
AIG – one of the world’s largest insurance companies – also experienced a
run as efforts were made to avoid the bankruptcy of Lehman. AIG had written
tens of billions of credit default swaps. In effect AIG acquired the credit risk
attached to these bonds in exchange for the premium income; the buyers of the
credit default swaps believed that premiums that they paid were modest relative
to the credit risks that they were inducing AIG to take. The run on AIG was like
the run on Lehman once removed, since AIG would have to reimburse those
who had bought these swaps to protect themselves against losses on their hold-
ings of Lehman bonds when the firm went bankrupt.
The counterfactual is to determine how the financial crisis in the US finan-
cial economy would have evolved if Lehman had been saved in September 2008;
there is some likelihood that the run might have been deflected to other firms,
perhaps Merrill Lynch or Morgan Stanley. One possibility is that the run on
AIG would have continued, perhaps less rapidly. Another possibility is that the
US government would have made it known at the time that Lehman was saved
that it stood ready to assist any other large firm that had a shortage of liquidity
or had depleted capital – which was essentially the policy that was adopted when
AIG was bailed out. The terms of the ‘bail-outs’ would have included that the

334 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
common and preferred shareholders would have lost most or all of their money
and the management and the directors would be replaced.
If AIG had not been saved then it is 99 percent likely that investors would
have withdrawn their money from many other financial firms; better safe
than sorry. Asset prices would have declined further, and other financial firms
that previously had been thought stable and well-managed would have failed.
Lenders would be extremely cautious in making new loans, and in renewing
maturing credits. The US recession would have become much more intense, and
the US economy might have fallen into the debt-deflation trap.
The following paragraph appeared in the sixth edition of Manias:
Thus the amounts needed to save Lehman – the counterfactual – would
have been the $50 billion or $100 billion that would have been the
financial outlay by the US Treasury minus any recovery and the incre-
mental cost of financial crisis in the future because the lenders would
have realized that there was an increased likelihood that they would be
bailed out if they followed a more risky investment strategy. The addi-
tional cost would be the cost of saving other large financial institutions
that had invested too aggressively.
Soon after the September 2008 crisis, these bonds were selling for ten to twenty
cents on the dollar; the bond holders incurred massive losses.
The cost of saving AIG
There are a relatively small number of opportunities to perform experiments with
government policy toward financial institutions. The US government’s investment
of TARP money in the banks can be viewed as an experiment; similarly, its invest-
ment in AIG can be considered an experiment. The US government was eager to
recover its investment in AIG, and the firm was required to sell some of its subsidi-
aries at a time when there was exceptionally large uncertainty in the markets; the
result was that AIG’s receipts from the sale of these subsidiaries were smaller than
they would have been if the sales had been delayed for a year or two until there was
much less uncertainty about financial stability. Nevertheless, AIG appears likely to
repay all of the government investment – and hence there was a ‘two-fer’ in that the
investment contributed to reducing the likelihood of a cascading crisis by a massive
amount and the US government’s investment in AIG was profitable. In effect, the US
Treasury was a successful ‘vulture’ investor. Moreover, the US Treasury investment
in AIG was a ‘public good’ that sharply reduced the likelihood that the crisis would
escalate and that many more banks would fail. And the failure of a larger number of
banks in this counterfactual scenario would have meant that the costs to the FDIC
would have been larger.

THE LEHMAN PANIC 335
The investment of TARP money in the banks has been profitable. (However,
the TARP investment in US auto companies was not profitable.) Similarly, the
US Treasury’s loan guarantee to Chrysler Corporation in the late 1970s was
profitable.
The surprise is that Lehman hovered on the border of bankruptcy, but the
markets were so gun-shy of risks that many of the securities that Lehman owned
were priced below their intrinsic value. The implication is that Lehman had a
liquidity problem; actually, the system had a liquidity-cum-solvency problem.
The intervention of the Federal Reserve led to higher prices for US Treasury
securities, but the impact of the increase in the price of public debt on the price
of private debt was modest.
The following paragraph is reprinted from the sixth edition:
This cost of not saving Lehman must be adjusted to include the addi-
tional outlays that the US Treasury and the Federal Reserve incurred
when they intervened to save AIG, Citibank, Bank of America, and
more than twenty other firms. Estimating this amount is extremely
difficult – the runs on individual institutions would continue until it
was clear beyond the shadow of a doubt that no institution would fail
because of a lack of liquidity. The US Treasury invested more than $400
billion in other financial institutions, and the data suggest that virtu-
ally all of this money will be recovered.
The data now are in. TARP was a very profitable venture for the US Treasury,
the US government was a successful vulture investor. And the rate of return on
its investment in the banks would have been even higher if it had provided capi-
tal in the form of purchasing newly issued common shares rather than in the
form of preferred shares.
The explanation for the success of the US Treasury as a vulture investor was
that its commitment to provide capital to banks to ensure that they would not
fail meant that the risk premium attached to non-government bonds declined
sharply. Only the US government had the ability to provide that assurance. And
if it had provided that assurance several weeks earlier, the Great Recession that
began in 2008 would have been far less severe.
The immediate impact of the decision not to save Lehman was a panic and
crash. Some of the costs of not saving Lehman can be estimated in terms of the
increase in unemployment, the decline in US GDP, and the increase in the US
government’s fiscal deficit. In the first eight months of 2008, employment had
declined by an average of forty thousand jobs a month; in the six months after the

336 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
failure of Lehman, employment declined by six hundred thousand a month – a
multiple of 15.
The striking phenomenon was the surge in interest rates on risky assets –
on LIBOR relative to the US Treasury bills. Those banks with a relatively strong
cash position no longer had confidence in the credit standing of the banks that
had incurred large loan losses. Those banks in a weak cash position were then
obliged to raise cash in other ways and to shrink their assets. ‘Cash was king’
and the banks with a strong cash position were ‘hoarders’ – which raised the
costs of other banks to obtain cash.
The primary costs of not saving Lehman are those associated with the
incremental decline in US GDP because of the surge in interest rates on risky
assets. In August 2008, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office projected
that the US fiscal deficit would be $450 billion in fiscal 2009; six months later,
the projection was $1500 billion, which was ten or fifteen times larger than the
highest estimate of the costs of saving Lehman. Most of the increase in the pro-
jected fiscal deficit was due to the sharp decline in economic activity because
of the dramatic reduction in the willingness of the banks to lend, and because
households and firms hunkered down – as employment declined sharply, spend-
ing declined. Individuals were less confident about their jobs.
‘TOO BIG TO FAIL’ AND MORAL HAZARD
A significant number of large financial institutions had failed prior to the run
on Lehman; the US government had intervened with both Bear Stearns and
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Why was Lehman different?
Banks, mortgage brokers, insurance companies, and other financial institu-
tions can be placed in one of four groups in terms of how they fared in the 2008
crisis. One group consists of those firms that went out of business because they
lost all or virtually all of their capital; the shareowners in these firms lost all or
nearly all of their money and these firms disappeared from the marketplace.
This group includes Indy Mac, Washington Mutual, and Lehman Brothers.
Nearly three hundred mortgage banking firms failed. Nearly five hundred com-
mercial banks were closed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. The
top executives lost their positions, and a great deal of their personal wealth; the
careers of many of these individuals were shortened. The boards of directors of
these firms were disgraced.
A second group comprises those firms that incurred such large losses that
they were acquired by other, better capitalized firms, either with or without
