financial assistance of the US government. Countrywide Financial was in this
group, as were Wachovia Bank, Bear Stearns, and Merrill Lynch. These firms

THE LEHMAN PANIC 337
disappeared from the marketplace and their shareholders lost most but not all of
their money. Similarly, most of the top executives in these firms lost their posi-
tions, and their careers were truncated. In some cases, however, the top officials
still walked away with tens of millions of dollars.
The third group includes the firms that probably would have been forced
to close their doors if they had not had assistance from the US Treasury or the
Federal Reserve. AIG, Citibank, and Bank of America are in this group. So are
some of the regional banks. The prices of the shares of these firms declined
by 80 to 90 percent, although these prices subsequently increased once the US
government became a significant shareholder and the likelihood that the firms
would fail diminished sharply.
The fourth group consists of the firms that did not take any funds from the
US Treasury, or else took these funds because they were instructed to do so by
Secretary of the Treasury Paulson even though they did not want the US gov-
ernment’s money. JPMorgan Chase is in this group, as is Goldman Sachs; both
had been the top tier of US investment banks. Several of the firms in this group
were able to raise capital in the private markets; Morgan Stanley sold new shares
to Mitsubishi Bank.
Why did the failure of Lehman lead to the unprecedented panic in the credit
markets? One view is that the initiatives of the US government to prevent the
bankruptcy of Bear Stearns and subsequently of Freddie and Fannie followed
by the unwillingness to commit government money to save Lehman meant that
there appeared to be no coherent government policy toward providing finan-
cial assistance to weakened large institutions. If two points determine a line,
then measures adopted by the US government to deal with Bear Stearns and the
Freddie and Fannie problem set the policy. But then the ‘policy’ was reversed by
not saving Lehman. And while the initiatives toward AIG represented a reversal
of the reversal, market participants were shaken by the randomness of the US
government’s behavior.
Haircuts for all?
The principal stakeholders that have benefited from the use of government money to
stabilize the banks and other financial institutions have been bondholders and other
counterparties, uninsured creditors, and senior managers. If these firms had gone
bankrupt like Lehman, the bondholders would have taken a haircut, and depending
on the severity of the losses, they might have lost 30 or 50 percent of their money.
The employment contracts of the senior managers would no longer be binding if the
firms failed, and those who had large amounts due because of their success as traders
would find that they were another group of unsecured creditors.
If bondholders are subject to loss if the firm closes, then many would sell their
bonds in anticipation of these losses. Interest rates on these bonds would increase

338 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
sharply, and the banks would not be able to sell new bonds when the existing bonds
mature. The banks would be forced to shrink their assets. Similarly the counterparties
would be reluctant to re-finance existing positions. The likelihood of losses by these
groups could trigger runs.
One position is that bond instruments should be designed so that the bondholders
would incur losses if the firms failed; then they would exercise more discipline
on the senior managers so that they would be more cautious in undertaking risky
investments. Perhaps. The credit-rating agencies already evaluate the riskiness of the
bonds, and it is not obvious that the prospect of haircuts might induce the investors
to be more cautious in buying the bonds of the banks.
The hidden cost of too much discipline is that bankers would be extremely cautious
lenders, and many worthwhile projects would find it difficult to obtain financing.
The design challenge is to ensure that large firms are allowed to fail when the causes
of failure are idiosyncratic to one or two institutions in a stable financial environment.
When the failures are systemic and involve a large number of institutions, the policy
problem differs; failure has many more costly externalities. The capital of financial
institutions as a group declines, and there may be too little capital relative to the
liabilities of these institutions. Either asset values will decline until the ratio of
bank assets to bank capital is at a satisfactory level, or the government must provide
financial investments to the lenders. The nub of the problem is that the value of bank
capital is highly sensitive to changes in the prices of securities because banks are
highly leveraged. And modest changes in capital requirements will have only modest
effects on the relationship between the declines in the prices of securities and the
value of bank capital.
Assume that there had been no rescue program – no TARP money, no Fed
investments, and so on. Then other banks that had been dependent on borrowed
short-term money to carry long-term assets would have failed. Other banks that
had been conservative in their lending policies would have encountered large
loan losses because the recession would have been much more severe.
Fast forward to 2020 or 2025, or whenever the next period of a rapid expan-
sion in the supply of credit begins. How many of the top executives of the major
US financial firms at that time would look back at the government intervention
in the 2008 crisis and conclude they can afford to take greater risks in the allo-
cation of credit because so many large financial institutions had been ‘bailed
out’?
These executives would have observed that the stock prices and market
value of financial firms as a group had declined by 90 percent or more. They
would have observed that the senior executives of most of these institutions
were replaced, and that the directors also lost their positions. They would have
noticed that many managers lost their careers. They would have noticed that
the US investment banking industry had been decimated, with one dominant

THE LEHMAN PANIC 339
firm as a survivor; another of the major firms had to sell about 20 percent of its
shares to a Japanese firm.
‘Too big to fail’ is a catchy cliché. But the slogan obscures much more than it
reveals. And because of the reluctance of government officials to provide finan-
cial assistance to Lehman so that the firm could have avoided bankruptcy even
as its shareholders lost all their money, a market adjustment cascaded into the
most severe crisis in one hundred years.
One of the distinguishing features of the military is contingency plan-
ning; they develop hundreds of scenarios that involve their intended response
to adventuresome activities by foreign belligerents. The mindlessness of the
responses of the US Treasury and Federal Reserve officials to the implications
of the surges in property prices is staggering. The taxpayers of America should
consider a class-action lawsuit to claw back their salaries and their honorary
degrees. Good luck.

15
THE LESSONS OF HISTORY
T
he last four hundred years have been replete with financial crises, which often
followed increases in the supplies of credit, greater investor optimism, and
more rapid economic growth. More and more individuals purchased securities
and assets for short-term profits from the increases in their prices. Households
became wealthier as the market prices of securities and assets increased, and
consumption spending grew. Business firms became more upbeat and invested
more. The external indebtedness of many countries increased, and at a pace that
was too rapid to be sustainable. The domestic counterpart of the rapid increase
in the external indebtedness was that the domestic indebtedness of a group of
borrowers in these countries increased at rates that eventually proved too rapid
to be sustained. Economic booms followed and then euphoria developed. The
increases in the supplies of credit led to sharp increases in the prices of securi-
ties and real estate to levels that proved too high to be sustainable.
The uniqueness of the last forty years is that there have been four waves of
financial crises; each wave was preceded by a surge in the supplies of credit that
involved three, four, or, in some episodes, eight or ten countries. That the prices
of securities and real estate in so many countries increased at about the same
time suggests a common cause, and one external to these countries. The pat-
tern has been that the increases in cross-border investment flows to these coun-
tries led to increases in the prices of their bonds, stocks, and real estate and to
increases in the prices of their currencies – unless the central banks intervened
to limit or prevent the increases in the prices of currencies.
The likelihood that these four waves of surges in external indebtedness and
in the prices of securities and currencies were independent and unrelated events
is low. Instead it seems plausible that there was a systematic relationship among
several of these successive waves, and that the change in the direction and scope

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 341
of cross-border investment inflows associated with a wave of banking crises led
to new pattern of cross-border investment flows that preceded the next wave of
banking crises.
The increases in the supplies of credit generally were provided by banks.
However, the buyers of bulbs during the Dutch ‘tulipmania’ of the 1630s relied
on credit from the sellers of the bulbs; otherwise, they would not have been
able to pay the increasingly high prices. As bulb prices increased, rational exu-
berance morphed into irrational exuberance; the Dutch economy boomed, and
then when bulb prices tumbled, the growth rate slowed. Both the South Sea
Bubble in London and the Mississippi Bubble in Paris in 1720 resulted from
rapid increases in the supplies of credit from newly established banks. The coin-
cidence of these two similar developments reflects that financial innovations in
London were mimicked in Paris.
The ‘mother of all asset price bubbles’ in Tokyo in the second half of the
1980s resulted from the rapid growth in the supply of credit and the relaxation
of regulations that had limited bank loans for purchases of real estate. Once
property prices began to increase by 20 to 30 percent a year, there was a surge in
the demand for real estate, since the anticipated returns from further increases
in the prices of apartment buildings and office buildings and land were so much
higher than the returns in other sectors of the economy. The banks relied on
real estate as the collateral for increased loans; as real estate prices increased,
the value of the collateral increased, and the lenders felt secure in increasing the
supply of credit for purchases of real estate.
The increases in the prices of securities and real estate in Japan were an inte-
gral part of the adjustment process to ensure that Japanese imports increased
and its current account surplus declined. The investment outflow from Japan
surged in the first half of the 1980s in response to the sharp increase in interest
rates on US dollar securities. As the interest rates on these securities declined
and the likelihood of a fall in the price of the US dollar increased, the invest-
ment outflow slowed in more formal terms, the country’s capital account deficit
declined. Adjustments were necessary to ensure that there was a comparable
decline in Japan’s current account surplus. These adjustments included the
increase in the price of the yen and the increase in the prices of securities and
real estate in Japan, which led to a increase in consumption spending.
The sharp increases in the prices of real estate in the United States, Britain,
Spain, Ireland, and Iceland that began about 2003 resulted from the increase in
the cross-border investment inflows to each of these countries, which contributed
to the increases in the supplies of credit available for the purchases of homes and
commercial properties. The prices of the British pound and the Iceland krona
increased. Ireland and Spain were members of the European Monetary Union,

342 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
and hence they could not adjust to the increase in investment inflows by an
increase in the prices of their currencies in nominal terms, and, hence, the intui-
tion is that the increase in the price of securities and real estate was accordingly
larger. The increases in the prices of securities and real estate was an integral part
of the adjustment process to ensure that the changes in the current account bal-
ance of each country corresponded with the changes in cross-border investment
inflows; when these inflows increased, adjustments were necessary to ensure
that there was a corresponding increase in their current account deficits. And
when the investment inflows slackened, adjustments were necessary to ensure
that the current account deficits of these countries declined. Hence the changes
in the prices of securities and, where possible, currencies in Mexico, Iceland, and
other countries during each of these waves were an integral part of the adjust-
ment process induced by changes in the cross-border investment inflows, which
required a corresponding change in net imports of goods and in the trade deficits
of these countries. Higher prices for securities and real estate led to higher levels
of household wealth and to more spending on both domestic and foreign goods.
And the increase in spending on foreign goods led to the larger trade deficits that
corresponded with the increase in the investment inflows.
Each of the waves of banking crises was triggered once one or several of
the lenders concluded that the borrowers’ indebtedness was too large relative to
their incomes or was increasing too rapidly. Or, one or several of the lenders may
have concluded that the country’s external indebtedness was too large relative to
its GDP or was increasing too rapidly. The pattern is that in the previous several
years the cross-border investment inflows had accelerated, and the prices of the
currencies of the indebted countries had increased. The trade deficits of these
indebted countries increased as the prices of their currencies increased. Once
the lenders slowed the pace of their purchases of the borrowers’ IOUs, some of
the borrowers then could no longer depend on the money from new loans to pay
some of the scheduled interest payments on their outstanding loans. They had
to adjust. If they were unable to adhere to the terms of their loan contracts, they
would be bankrupt. The crises in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries often
followed a sharp decline in commodity prices, which meant that the incomes
of farmers had declined so sharply they did not have enough money to pay the
interest on the loans that had enabled them to purchase seeds and real estate. At
other times the crises developed in response to sharp declines in stock prices.
Crises generally were infrequent, often about once a generation – the United
States had one crisis in 1907, and then a severe one in the early 1930s; however,
in the first half of the nineteenth century a crisis occurred almost every ten
years. Four waves of crises in the thirty years since the early 1980s, each involv-
ing three, four or more countries, seems exceptional.

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 343
The sharp increase in US stock prices in the 1917–1929 period followed an
economic boom that featured a surge in the production of automobiles and the
expansion of highways, the electrification of millions of households, and the
rapid expansion of telephones. Investor optimism surged; stock prices increased
threefold between 1927 and 1929. The Federal Reserve had made credit more
readily available to reduce the likelihood that the surge in productivity would
lead to declines in the prices of goods and services. Real estate prices trended
upward, although not as rapidly as stock prices.
The increase in interest rates on US dollar securities in 1928 led to a reduc-
tion in American purchases of foreign bonds and complicated the ability of cen-
tral banks in Europe and in Latin America to maintain the parities for their
currencies because they lacked the money to finance their trade deficits. Some
of these countries stopped pegging their currencies to gold. A series of currency
crises followed in the early 1930s; initially speculators targeted the Austrian
schilling. The Austrian central bank stopped supporting the schilling in May
1931, and the decline in the price of the schilling triggered the contagion effect,
which initially involved that speculators sold the German mark because they
believed that the parity between the mark and gold could no longer be main-
tained. Then the speculators targeted the British pound; the Bank of England
stopped supporting the pound in September 1931. After the price of the British
pound declined sharply, speculators sold the US dollar in the belief that the US
government would no longer adhere to the $20.67 parity.
The US government established a new parity for the US dollar of $35 in
March 1933. Then speculative pressure was directed at the currencies of the
‘gold bloc’ countries – the French franc, the Swiss franc, the Italian lira, and the
Dutch guilder, whose convertibility into gold was suspended in 1936. At the end
of the 1930s, the alignment of the prices of currencies was and significantly dif-
ferent from where the alignment was ten years earlier.
There were episodic currency crises between the late 1940s and the early
1970s as investors became increasingly skeptical that governments would incur
the costs to maintain the parities for their currencies, which had been set at the
end of World War II. Patterns of production and trade had been disrupted by
the massive destruction of factories and of infrastructure during the war. Many
European countries reduced the prices of their currencies in September 1949
to adjust for more rapid increases in their price levels than in the US price level
during and after World War II and the constraints on their ability to increase
their exports.
The French franc was devalued by 10 percent in 1959. The British pound was
subject to speculative pressure in 1964, and the price of the pound was eventu-
ally reduced by nearly 20 percent in the autumn of 1967. There was speculation

344 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
that the price of the German mark would be increased in 1969 and that the
price of the French franc would be decreased at about the same time. Then in
1970 the speculative pressure was directed at the US dollar; investors antici-
pated that either the prices of the currencies of other industrial countries would
be increased, or that the US dollar price of gold would be increased while the
implicit price of gold in terms of those other currencies would be retained or
increased by a smaller amount.
Most of the currency crises in the 1950s and 1960s were preludes to the
declines in the prices of currencies by 10 to 20 percent; none was associated
with a banking crisis and none involved defaults on liabilities denominated in
foreign currency. Speculative pressure did not lead to excessively large changes
in the prices of currencies relative to the prices projected from differences in
inflation rates.
One of the unique features of the period since the early 1980s is that nearly
all of the banking crises have been associated with currency crises. The prin-
cipal exception is that the financial crisis in Japan in the first half of the 1990s
was not associated with a crisis about the price of the yen, because Japan had a
current account surplus. Moreover, the banking crisis in Ireland in 2008 and
2009 and the one in Spain at the same time were not associated with a currency
crisis because both countries were members of the European Monetary Union.
The financial crisis that involved the debt of the Greek government in the spring
of 2010 was centered on the ability of the Greek government to reduce its fiscal
deficit and make its debt-service payments in a timely way and thus was a credit
crisis; however, the price of the euro declined because some of the investors were
concerned about its viability as a monetary union.
The wave of cross-border investment inflows to Mexico and other devel-
oping countries that began in the early 1970s was too rapid to be sustained,
because the external indebtedness of these countries was increasing much
more rapidly than their GDPs. The domestic counterpart of the increase in
external indebtedness of these countries was an increase in the indebtedness of
the governments and government-owned firms. The first impact of the slow-
ing of investment inflows to these countries was that the prices of their cur-
rencies declined; at the same time, the domestic counterpart of the US dollar
liabilities of the governments and government-owned firms increased in pro-
portion to the declines in the prices of their currencies. These declines were
often large because some domestic residents sought to increase their holdings
of US dollar or other foreign securities at about the same time as the invest-
ment inflows were slowing. Hence, the borrowers were squeezed between the
decline in money from new investment inflows and the increase in their debt-
service payments.

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 345
The coincidence of the waves of banking crises with currency crises since
the early 1980s reflects that initially the increase in investment inflows led to
higher prices for securities and for currencies; then when the inflows slowed,
the prices of securities and the prices of currencies declined. The increase in
the prices of currencies dampened inflationary pressures in the goods market
which enabled central banks to continue their expansive policies for an extended
period. The subsequent declines in the prices of currencies and securities were
responses in different markets to the slowing of investment inflows. The decline
in the prices of currencies contributed to the severity of the banking crises, since
the increase in domestic equivalent of liabilities denominated in the US dollar
led to the bankruptcy of some domestic borrowers.
When the cross-border investment inflows slowed and the prices of curren-
cies declined, some of the borrowers in these countries became distress sellers
of securities and real estate because they could no longer obtain enough money
from new loans to pay the interest on their indebtedness. Their sales depressed
the prices of securities and real estate. Moreover the reduction in investment
inflows led to increases in interest rates on domestic securities, which contrib-
uted to the declines in the prices of securities and real estate. The failures of
banks – the financial crises – followed from the large losses incurred by exten-
sively indebted firms and individuals; the value of the collateral pledged to the
banks declined sharply relative to the value of the bank loans.
Domestic financial crises became less frequent in the last one hundred
years after central banks were established to act as lenders of last resort – they
were able and willing to provide cash to banks in response to sharp declines in
investor demand for speculative securities and real estate.
One feature of banking crises in the twentieth century was that central
banks often had to choose between whether they should give priority to main-
taining the price of their currencies or instead to give priority to domestic
financial stability. Initially a central bank would increase interest rates to con-
vince investors that it had an unshakable commitment to its parity; higher
interest rates led to sharp declines in the prices of securities and real estate and
slowed economic activity. Then, the central bank might give up maintaining
the price of its currency because of the high costs in terms of the increases in
unemployment and business bankruptcies. The contagion effect in the 1930s
was triggered by the initial mis-alignment between the prices of individual
currencies and national price levels; the decision of Britain in 1925 to again
peg the price of the pound to gold at its 1914 parity is now recognized to have
been a major mistake because the price level in Britain had increased more
rapidly than the US price level. The decision of the French government to peg
the franc to gold at the end of 1926 at a price that was one fifth the 1914 price

346 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
intensified the decline in British competitiveness, since the price of the franc
was then too low. The series of currency crises reflected that investors became
concerned that each central bank would not maintain the anchor for its cur-
rency in terms of gold after one of its major trading partners had allowed the
price of its currency to decline. Each central bank then would conclude that
the costs of retaining its parity was too high in terms of business failures and
unemployment.
The contagion effect in 1997 was triggered by the sharp decline in the price
of the Thai baht in July; investors suddenly realized that investment flows to
Thailand’s neighbors and to other emerging-market countries would decline
sharply and that the central banks in these countries would no longer support
their currencies because of the surge in investment flows from these countries
in anticipation of the subsequent declines in their prices. Immediately, specula-
tive pressure shifted to one or several other currencies that still retained their
pre-crisis prices.
This sequence of large declines in the prices of the currencies both in the
1930s and then in the second half of the 1990s leads to the question of whether
an international lender of last resort would have enabled countries to avoid the
deflate-and-devalue cycle. Domestic lenders of last resort can provide abundant
credit to reduce the likelihood that a liquidity crisis will cascade into a solvency
crisis. The problem in both the 1930s and the 1990s was that currencies were
not appropriately aligned with national price levels, and that once the price of
the currency of one country declined, speculative pressure was deflected to the
currencies of its trading partners.
The counter-factual question is whether an increase in the supply of inter-
national reserve assets in the early 1920s when the potential shortage of gold was
first recognized would have obviated some of the sharp declines in the prices
of currencies in the interwar period. National price levels had increased much
more rapidly in some countries than in others during and after World War I,
with the result that the prices of currencies were not aligned with national price
levels. The price of the German mark was too low after the post-hyperinflation
stabilization, while the price of the British pound was too high, and the price of
the French franc was too low after it was pegged at the end of 1926. A larger vol-
ume of international reserve assets would have made it possible for the adjust-
ment of prices of currencies to occur over a longer period. But neither a larger
volume of international reserve assets nor an international lender of last resort
would have obviated the need for the adjustments of mis-aligned prices of cur-
rencies. But a larger volume – or perhaps a much larger volume – might have
reduced the frequency and severity of speculative attacks like the ones on the
French franc in 1924 and 1926.

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 347
During the interwar period central banks were committed to pegging their
currencies to gold, initially at their pre-war parities, while the general view since
the early 1970s is that currencies should float – although central banks in some
countries in Asia have intervened extensively to limit increases in the prices of
their currencies.
The large variability in the prices of securities and real estate and in the
prices of currencies, and in the number and severity of banking crises since
the early 1980s, suggest that the lessons of the interwar period have been over-
looked – if they have been remembered. One of the lessons was that cross-border
investment inflows distort national competitiveness in the short and medium
run – for three, four or more years. Another was that currencies ‘overshoot’ and
‘undershoot’ their long-run average prices unless central banks are committed
either to parities for their currencies or to limiting the variability in the prices of
currencies. A third is that if some countries are no longer committed to main-
taining parities for their currencies, some, and especially those in Asia, have
managed the prices of their currencies to secure a competitive advantage in the
goods market. ‘Permanent undershooting’ is a form of currency protectionism
and invites critical responses from trading partners.
The three decades since the early 1980s have been the most tumultuous in
monetary history in terms of the number, scope and severity of banking cri-
ses. More national banking systems collapsed than in any previous comparable
period; the loan losses of banks in Japan, in Sweden and Norway and Finland,
in Thailand and Malaysia and Indonesia, in Mexico (twice), in Brazil and
Argentina, and in the United States and Britain and Iceland and Ireland ranged
from 10 to 50 percent of their assets. In some countries the costs to the taxpayers
of providing the money to fulfill the implicit and explicit government guaran-
tees on bank deposits and other bank liabilities amounted to 15 to 20 percent of
their GDPs. The loan losses in many countries were much greater than those in
the United States in the Great Depression of the 1930s.
Occasionally the failure of a bank was firm-specific; Franklin National
Bank of New York City and then Herstatt AG of Cologne lost the large bets that
they had made on changes in the prices of currencies. However, most of the
bank failures since the early 1980s have been systemic events that have occurred
in waves and involved large numbers of lenders in different countries because
of the sudden dramatic changes in the international financial environment. In
some episodes virtually all of the banks in a country failed. Usually these coun-
tries experienced sharp declines in real estate values after periods when these
prices had increased rapidly.
The dominant pattern, evident in Mexico, Argentina, Thailand, Malaysia,
Russia, and many other countries was that a banking crisis and a currency crisis

348 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
occurred at the same time, after several years when the increase in cross-border
investment inflows led to increases in the prices of securities and real estate and in
the prices of their currencies. The subsequent sharp declines in the prices of cur-
rencies simultaneously led to an inflationary shock as the prices of tradable goods
increased and at the same time a deflationary shock as interest rates surged.
The dominant shock at the beginning of the 1970s was an increase in the
inflation rates in the United States and every other country. Investors shifted
from monies and securities into ‘hard assets’ like gold, silver, art, and collecta-
bles and from securities denominated in the US dollar to securities denominated
in various foreign currencies. The closing of the US Treasury’s gold window in
August 1971 was interpreted to mean that the United States no longer had a
strong commitment to a low inflation rate. The decline in the price of the US
dollar in the currency market was much larger than the excess of the US infla-
tion rate over the inflation rates in the major US trading partners; the prices of
their currencies then overshot.
The second major monetary shock was the adoption of a severely contrac-
tive monetary policy by the Federal Reserve in October 1979. The market inter-
est rates on US dollar securities surged and real interest rates, which had been
negative, became very positive. The US dollar price of gold peaked about ten
weeks later. Prior to this shock, investors had sought to adjust their portfolios
to an increase in inflation rates; subsequently they began to adjust to a decline
in the anticipated US inflation rate. The US dollar price of gold and the prices
of other hard assets began to decline, while the price of the US dollar began to
increase. Many banks in Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana failed when oil prices
declined sharply while small banks in Iowa, Kansas, and other states in the agri-
cultural Midwest also went under because the sharp declines in the prices of
cereals led to even larger percentage declines in the prices of farm real estate.
Several thousand US thrift institutions failed in the early 1980s when short-
term interest rates surged relative to long-term interest rates as a result of the
October 1979 monetary shock.
The price of the US dollar continued to increase until the middle of 1985 –
or, what is the same thing, the price of the Japanese yen, the price of the German
mark, and the prices of every other currency declined in response to the sharp
increases in foreign purchases of US dollar securities. Then the price of the US
dollar overshot. As interest rates on US dollar securities declined and as the
price of the US dollar increased, the incentive to move funds from foreign finan-
cial centers to New York declined; by the mid-1980s the foreign demand for US
dollar securities had fallen and the price of the US dollar began to decline.
As the price of the Japanese yen increased, the foreign demand for Japanese
stocks increased sharply. Investors were motivated by the prospect that the price

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 349
of the yen and the price of Japanese stocks would continue to increase. The price
of the Japanese yen appeared to be overshooting.
Japan experienced a major banking crisis in the early 1990s, after the surge
in the prices of securities and real estate in the 1980s, and especially in the sec-
ond half of the decade. The Japanese economy was adjusting to the decline in
Japanese purchases of foreign securities and the increase in the foreign pur-
chases of Japanese securities. As the Japanese capital account deficit declined,
market forces ensured that there was a corresponding decline in the country’s
current account surplus.
The increase in the price of the Japanese yen during its early 1990s banking
crisis led to a surge in Japanese investment in Thailand and nearby countries in
the effort to reduce production costs. Banks in these countries increased their
borrowing in offshore markets. The prices of the securities in these countries
increased, and the prices of their currencies increased in real terms. The curren-
cies of these countries were overshooting.
Many banks in Thailand, South Korea, and Indonesia failed in the Asian
Financial Crisis; a sudden sharp decline in the prices of their currencies led
from trade deficits to trade surpluses. Then in the late 1990s, soon after the
financial debacle in Russia, Long-Term Capital Management, then the largest
US hedge fund, collapsed and would have failed if the Federal Reserve had not
mandated that its largest creditors invest equity capital in the firm.
The range of movement in the prices of currencies since the early 1970s was
much larger than in any previous period. Moreover, the deviations between the
market prices of currencies and long-run average prices has been much larger
than when currencies were anchored to parities. When cross-border invest-
ment inflows to a country increased, the price of its currency increased relative
to the long average values in a pattern described as overshooting. And when
these inflows slowed or reversed, the price of the currency declined in a pat-
tern described as undershooting. Initially, these large swings in the prices of
currencies were attributed to the lack of familiarity of market participants with
freely floating exchange rates. Then the large changes in the prices of currencies
were explained because of the inherent lags before the supplies of tradable goods
could increase in response to changes in the relationship between domestic and
foreign prices and costs. The more appropriate explanation is that these large
swings in the prices of currencies result from changes in the investor demand
for foreign securities. Moreover, the scope of overshooting and undershoot-
ing of currency values was much larger than in any previous period. Thus the
increases in the prices of the German mark and the Japanese yen in the late
1970s were much greater than the increases that would have been projected
based on the excess of the US inflation rate over the inflation rates in Germany

350 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
and in Japan. Then in the early 1980s the prices of both currencies declined
sharply even though the US inflation rate remained higher than their inflation
rates. In the late 1990s the US and European inflation rates were similar but
the price of the newly established euro – the successor to the German mark,
the French franc, the Italian lira, and the currencies of the other countries that
joined the European Monetary Union – declined by 30 percent slightly after its
establishment at the beginning of 1999.
Overshooting and undershooting are an integral part of the adjustment
process in response to changes in cross-border investment flows when curren-
cies are floating. These changes must be accompanied by corresponding changes
in the cross-border movement of goods and in trade balances. Countries that
experience investment inflows must develop larger trade deficits, which result
from increases in demand for imports because the prices of their currencies
have increased, and from increases in consumption spending because of the
higher levels of household wealth.
The increases in the flows of money to countries are like increases in the
savings available in these countries, which can adjust by counterpart increases
in household consumption, business investment, and larger government defi-
cits. Household consumption accounts for 60 to 70 percent of GDP in most
countries; as a result most of the adjustment to an increase in investment
inflows involves increases in household consumption – or what is the same
thing, reductions in household savings. The increases in the availability of for-
eign savings lead to higher asset prices and more consumption spending and
less domestic saving.
The large swings in the prices of US dollar, the Japanese yen, the euro, the
Swiss franc, and other currencies result from the reversal in the direction of
cross-border investment inflows. Increases in the inflows of money often lead
to real increases of prices of 20 or 30 percent and hence to overshooting. Then
when the shock occurs and the pace of investment inflows slows or is reversed,
the prices of these currencies may decline by 40 or 50 percent.
The increases in cross-border investment inflows often followed from
an institutional innovation, especially the relaxation of financial regulations.
These movements may have been reinforced because the increases in the prices
of currencies enhanced the anticipated rates of return available to investors that
incurred the cross-border risks. However, as a group, these investors failed to
appreciate the end-game, and that the prices of the currencies eventually would
decline because the borrowers’ indebtedness had been increasing too rapidly.
Thus, each of the banking crises followed from the reversal in the pattern of
cross-border investment inflows that had accelerated during one, two, or more
years prior to the crisis. When the cross-border investment inflows slowed, some

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 351
of those who had borrowed to finance the purchases of real estate or stocks or
some other assets became distress sellers because they needed to raise cash to pay
the interest on their indebtedness. The prices of the Mexican peso, the Brazilian
real, the Argentinean peso, and the currencies of many other developing coun-
tries plummeted in the early 1980s when the investment inflows diminished
sharply. The decline in the prices of these currencies led to large revaluation losses
by domestic firms and banks that had liabilities denominated in the US dollar.
The scope of the overshooting and undershooting of the currencies of the
emerging-market countries has been even larger than for the industrial coun-
tries. The price of the Mexican peso fell by nearly 50 percent during that coun-
try’s presidential transition at the end of 1994 and the beginning of 1995. The
prices of the Thai baht, the Malaysian ringgit, the Indonesian rupiah, and the
South Korean won declined by 50 to 70 percent in the last six months of 1997.
The price of the Russian ruble fell by more than 50 percent in August 1998.
The four waves of banking crises in the thirty years between 1980 and 2010
were more than in any other comparable period. The first wave followed from
increases in bank loans to the governments and government-owned firms in
Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and other developing countries in the 1970s; their
external indebtedness increased from $125 billion to $800 billion. The second
wave followed the surge in the prices of securities and real estate in Japan in the
1980s; household wealth surged, and the economy boomed. Finland, Norway,
and Sweden experienced sharp increases in the prices of securities and real
estate at about the same time. The third wave of banking turmoil was the Asian
Financial Crisis; the prices of securities and stocks had increased sharply in the
previous five-plus years. In most of these countries, the increases in real estate
prices begat the increase in stock prices because many of the companies listed on
the stock exchanges owned large amounts of property. US stock market wealth
doubled in the late 1990s and the market values of the stocks of the firms in the
dot.com and information technology industries increased fourfold. The fourth
wave involved sharp increases in the market value of real estate in the United
States, Britain, Ireland, Spain, Iceland, and South Africa after 2002.
One feature of each of these banking crises was that the external indebted-
ness of each of these countries had increased by 20 to 30 percent a year during
the previous three, four or more years; Japan was the major exception to the
pattern that there was a surge in external indebtedness in the several years prior
to the crisis. Moreover, the counterpart of the increase in the external indebt-
edness was that the indebtedness of a group of borrowers in these countries
increased rapidly. The rapid increases in indebtedness enabled some of the bor-
rowers to use money from new loans to pay the interest on their outstanding
loans. The indebtedness of these borrowers could increase more rapidly than

352 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
their GDPs for a few years, but eventually the lenders became more cautious in
extending new loans, and some of the borrowers then had to scramble to get the
money to pay the interest. Since the increases in the prices of securities followed
from larger cross-border investment inflows, declines in the these inflows led to
the declines in the prices of the currencies of the indebted countries.
The sharp increases in the prices of securities and real estate and the sub-
sequent failure of banks were systematically related to the overshooting and the
undershooting of currencies, and resulted from changes in the amounts and
direction of cross-border investment inflows. The four waves of crises followed
from the sharp declines in the prices of currencies which automatically led to
increases in the indebtedness of the domestic firms that had debts denominated
in the US dollar, the Swiss franc, or some other foreign currency. The almost
universal surges in interest rates as the prices of the currencies declined trig-
gered sharp declines in the prices of real estate and of stocks during the crash
phase of the cycle.
Most of these banking crises were ‘predictable’ events, since increasing reli-
ance on money from investment inflows to pay the interest on outstanding for-
eign indebtedness was not sustainable indefinitely; the uncertainty involved the
sharpness of the declines in the prices of the currencies when the investment
inflows slowed. Thus, the mania phase of the expansions in Mexico and the other
developing countries in the 1970s and in Thailand and Malaysia and Indonesia in
the 1990s could not continue because the external indebtedness of each of these
countries was increasing too rapidly relative to its GDP, and because the indebted-
ness of the borrowers in these countries also was increasing too rapidly relative to
their incomes. It was inevitable that the lenders would become more cautious in
increasing their loans to these borrowers, although the details and the timing of
these moves could not have been predicted. As the flow of cash from new loans
diminished, the borrowers would need a new source of money for some of their
interest payments. The likelihood that these countries could adjust to the decline
in the investment inflows without the decline in the prices of their currencies was
low. Similarly, at some stage it was inevitable that Japanese real estate prices would
stop increasing; many of those that had recently borrowed money to buy proper-
ties would encounter a cash bind because the interest payments on their loans
would be larger than their rental incomes.
THE CAUSES OF FINANCIAL TUMULTUOUSNESS
The financial tumult since the early 1970s resulted from the impacts of mon-
etary shocks and credit market shocks on the direction and scope of cross-bor-
der investment inflows. One monetary shock involved an increase in investor

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 353
demand for foreign securities. Another monetary shock involved unanticipated
changes in the rates of money supply growth and the accompanying impacts
on anticipated inflation rates and on interest rates. The credit market shocks
involved the relaxation of financial regulations that allowed the banks to increase
their loans to specific groups of borrowers, who then became more attractive to
lenders. In several cases, a monetary shock and a credit shock occurred at the
same time and had complementary impacts on investment inflows.
An increase in the investment inflow to a country induced both an increase
in the price of its currency and an increase in the price of securities which often
moved above their long-run equilibrium prices. The investment inflows fre-
quently were so large that they could not be sustained indefinitely; the subse-
quent decline in the investment inflows almost always led to a decline in the
price of its currency and often triggered a crash in the prices of securities of 50
or 60 percent or more.
The first major shock in this extended period was the increase in the annual
US inflation rate to the range of 5 and 6 percent in the second half of the 1960s;
in the previous twenty years this rate was almost always below 3 percent and
usually less than the inflation rates in Germany and its neighbors in Western
Europe. Annual US payment deficits surged at the end of the 1960s as it seemed
increasingly likely that the prices of the European currencies and the Japanese
yen would increase. Investors and firms increased their purchases of non-dollar
securities to profit from an increase in the price of various foreign currencies.
Because the United States was reluctant to increase the US dollar price of gold
and France and Japan were unwilling to increase the prices of their currencies,
the payments imbalances became larger and the international reserve assets
owned by Germany and Japan and other countries with payments surpluses
increased more rapidly. Then in 1971, when the US economy slowed and the
inflation rate declined, the Federal Reserve adopted a more expansive mone-
tary policy, and the decline in interest rates on US dollar securities led to larger
investment flows from New York to foreign centers.
The global inflation in the early 1970s was an unprecedented peacetime
event that followed from the combination of the more rapid growth of the US
money supply after the Federal Reserve eased monetary policy and the more
rapid growth in the money supplies in Germany and in Japan in response to
their increasingly large payments surpluses. Investors interpreted the closing of
the US Treasury’s gold window to mean that Americans no longer had a strong
commitment to a low inflation rate. The more rapid increase in the US inflation
rate meant that a realignment of the prices of national currencies was inevitable.
Because the US inflation rate exceeded the inflation rate in Germany by more
than 2 percent, the Bretton Woods system of adjustable parities was no longer

354 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
viable and the abandonment of parities for the German mark, the Japanese yen,
and the currencies of other industrial countries became inevitable.
Interest rates on US dollar securities increased as the US inflation rate
climbed; however interest rates on US dollar demand deposits were subject to
ceilings that the Federal Reserve had adopted to limit competition among banks.
These ceilings did not apply to interest rates on US dollar deposits in London
and other foreign financial centers, which increased and induced investors to
move funds from domestic to offshore financial centers. The rapid increases in
money supply growth in the United States and other industrial countries in the
early 1970s contributed to sharp increases in demand for primary products, and
in the prices of oil, wheat, and other commodities. The rates of growth of GDP
in the countries that produced these primary products increased. The Saudi
Arabian embargo on oil shipments to the United States and the Netherlands
following the Yom Kippur War of October 1973 triggered a sharp increase in
the demand for petroleum and the oil price surged. The decline in oil supplies
following the Iraqi invasion of Iran in 1980 had a much larger impact on the
price of oil and global inflation. Investors increased their purchases of gold and
other precious metals, collectibles, real estate, and other ‘hard assets’ as infla-
tion hedges.
THE FIRST WAVE OF CREDIT BUBBLES
The increase in the rates of economic growth in the primary producing coun-
tries in the 1970s led to the growth of bank loans to governments and govern-
ment-owned firms in Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and other developing countries
of 30 percent for about ten years; the external indebtedness of these coun-
tries increased by 20 percent a year. Banks headquartered in Canada, several
European countries, and Japan used US dollars that they borrowed in the off-
shore deposit markets in London, Zurich, and Luxembourg to fund these loans
and to ‘poach’ on what had been the turf of US banks. The US banks responded
aggressively to minimize the decline in their market share. Moreover, US and
foreign banks wanted to circumvent the regulations that limited the growth of
their domestic loans and assets. The increase in the flows of money to Mexico,
Brazil, Argentina, and other developing countries enabled these countries to
finance larger trade deficits.
The change in the operating procedures of the Federal Reserve in October
1979 (the so-called ‘Volcker shock’) was the next major monetary shock.
Previously, the Federal Reserve had stabilized interest rates and market forces
had determined the growth of credit; under the new policy, the Fed sought to
limit the growth of credit, and market forces determine interest rates – which

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 355
surged. In effect, this monetary shock was adopted to offset the dominant mon-
etary shock in the 1970s and the increase in the US inflation rate and the run
on the US dollar. The US dollar price of gold peaked ten weeks after this policy
change; the anticipations that the US inflation rate would continue to increase
were shattered. Investment spending fell, a recession followed, and the prices of
petroleum and other commodities dropped sharply.
The combination of the much higher interest rates on US dollar securities
and the sharp reduction in the anticipated US inflation rate led to an increase
in investor demand for US dollar securities, and the prices of the German mark,
the Japanese yen, and other currencies declined. Mexico and other developing
countries were squeezed by the scissors-like increase in the interest rates on
their US dollar indebtedness and the decline in both the volumes and the prices
of their exports. Banks in Texas were similarly impacted by higher interest rates
and lower oil prices. Interest rates paid by US thrift institutions on their short-
term deposits increased rapidly and in many cases began to exceed the interest
rates on their long-term mortgage loans.
THE SECOND WAVE OF CREDIT BUBBLES
As the price of the US dollar increased in the first half of the 1980s and interest
rates on US dollar securities declined, the incentive for investors to buy US dol-
lar securities diminished. As the investment outflow from Japan diminished,
the price of the Japanese yen began to increase. The Bank of Japan bought US
dollars to dampen the increase in the price of the yen, and its holdings of US
dollar securities surged, which led to a rapid increase in the money supply.
The Japanese financial system had been extensively regulated with the intent
to provide loans to corporate borrowers at very low interest rates. Moreover,
administrative guidance required that these banks extend loans to firms in the
industries that the government bureaucrats believed were strategically impor-
tant. One motive for financial liberalization was that the industrial demand for
bank loans had declined so that it was no longer necessary to allocate credit
among borrowers on a preferential basis; another was that the US authorities
demanded that US banks and other financial firms have access to the banking
and capital markets in Tokyo on terms comparable to the access available to
Japanese banks in New York.
Financial deregulation enabled the banks headquartered in Tokyo and in
Osaka to increase their real estate loans at a rapid rate. Because of building
restrictions and the time consumed in assembling larger lots for construction,
the increase in the demand for real estate had a much larger impact on the price
of land than on the supplies of living space and office space. Many of the firms

356 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
that were listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange were real estate investment com-
panies; the increases in real estate prices contributed to sharp increases in the
values of their assets and in the prices of their shares. The increase in the prices
of the shares of the firms traded on the Tokyo Stock Exchange together with
the increase in the price of the Japanese yen attracted Americans and investors
based in other industrial countries.
Restrictions on the foreign investments of Japanese banks and firms were
relaxed in the effort to limit the upward pressure on the yen. These banks rap-
idly increased the number of their branches and subsidiaries in London, New
York, Zurich, and other financial centers. The flow of savings from Japan to the
United States and various European countries surged; the cliché in both New
York and Tokyo was ‘Where will the US Treasury get the money to finance
its fiscal deficit if the Japanese stop buying US government securities?’ These
newly established foreign branches of Japanese banks increased their loans in
their host countries; in part they used the funds obtained in the offshore deposit
market. The newly established foreign branches of the offshore banks charged
lower interest rates than their host-country competitors because they wanted to
increase their market shares. Moreover, Japanese investors began to purchase
real estate – office buildings, apartment buildings, golf courses, and ski resorts
– in the United States and in other industrial countries; most of these purchases
were funded with money borrowed from the branches of Japanese banks in
London, Zurich, and other offshore financial centers.
Financial liberalization in Finland, Norway, and Sweden enabled banks
headquartered in these countries to source for domestic loans by borrowing
in the offshore market. Stock prices and real estate prices in these countries
increased sharply in response to the investment inflows.
The decision of the newly appointed Chair of the Board of the Bank of Japan
at the end of 1989 to restrict the growth of bank loans for real estate pricked the
asset-price bubble; heavily indebted borrowers could no longer obtain enough
money from new loans for their scheduled interest payments. Stock prices
declined by 30 percent in 1990 and by 25 percent in 1991. The growth of the
Japanese economy slowed dramatically. The price of the Japanese yen continued
to increase as the country’s exports increased relative to its imports. Japanese
firms responded to the adverse impact of the increase in the price of the yen
on the profitability of domestic manufacturing by increasing their investments
in manufacturing facilities in China and Thailand and other countries in
Southeast Asia that would be used primarily as sources of supply for markets in
Japan, the United States, and other industrial countries. Japanese banks rapidly
increased their loans to the subsidiaries of Japanese firms and to other firms in
these countries.

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 357
THE THIRD WAVE OF CREDIT BUBBLES
The development of the Brady bonds in 1989 and 1990 enabled Mexico and
other developing countries to convert bank loans that had been in default
into long-term bonds that were partially guaranteed by the US government,
which effectively ended their financial isolation (‘the lost decade’) from the
global capital market. Mexico began to prepare for membership in the North
American Free Trade Agreement; the Bank of Mexico adopted a contractive
monetary policy to reduce the inflation rate, hundreds of government-owned
firms were privatized, and government regulations on international trade
and business practices were liberalized. Foreign direct investment in Mexico
surged as US, European and Japanese firms increased their manufacturing
facilities in Mexico. US money market funds bought peso securities because
the interest rates were high and attractive. US pension funds and mutual
funds increased their purchases of stocks of a new asset class – ‘emerging
market equities’. Mexico’s current account deficit increased to 6 percent of
its GDP.
Similarly the investment inflows to Brazil, Argentina, Thailand, Malaysia,
and other emerging-market countries (which had been re-christened after hav-
ing been known as developing countries for several decades) increased rapidly.
The prices of the currencies of these countries increased in nominal and real
terms, and their trade and current account deficits increased.
Then, at the beginning of 1994, several political incidents in Mexico – an
Indian uprising in the southernmost province and then the assassination of the
leading presidential candidate of the dominant political party – led to a decline in
investment inflows, which meant that the Bank of Mexico needed to buy pesos to
manage the decline in its price. When its holdings of US dollars were so depleted
that it could no longer support the peso, the price declined sharply. The invest-
ment inflows to Thailand slowed significantly in late 1996 because the non-bank
finance companies that had been established by the banks to circumvent regula-
tions on consumer loans were incurring large loan losses – which were the losses
of the banks once-removed. The Bank of Thailand was unable to maintain the
price of the Thai baht once its international reserve assets had been depleted
at the beginning of July 1997. The decline in the price of the baht triggered the
contagion effect that rippled through the Asian countries as well as to Brazil,
Argentina, and Russia; the imports of the Asian countries declined relative to
their exports by $150 billion.
Several of these shocks were true surprises: the political events in Mexico
in the first few months of 1994 could not have been foreseen. However, the
Mexican current account deficit was too large to be sustained and some trigger

358 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
eventually would have led to a decline in the investment inflow and the decline
in the price of the peso. Similarly the current account deficits of Thailand and
Malaysia in 1996 were too large to be sustained. Some event would have led to
declines in investment inflows, although the catalyst for these declines could not
have been foreseen. The implosion of the bubbles in real estate prices and stock
prices in Thailand and Malaysia was inevitable when the investment inflows to
these countries declined.
THE FOURTH WAVE OF CREDIT BUBBLES
The striking feature of the period between 2002 and 2007 was the sharp
increases in the prices of residential and commercial real estate in the United
States, Britain, Spain, Ireland, Iceland, South Africa, New Zealand, and sev-
eral other countries. The prices of residential real estate in several of these
countries more than doubled. The increases in prices of residential real estate
in the United States were smaller than in other countries; however, these US
price increases occurred primarily in one-third of the states, those in the south
and along both seaboards, and the prices in some of these states more than
doubled.
Each of these countries experienced an increase in investment inflows and
the price of the currencies of each country (except for Spain and Ireland which
were members of the European Monetary Union) increased. The increase in
indebtedness was too large to be sustained; when the investment inflows to the
United States and Britain declined, the supplies of credit available for real estate
purchases fell, and real estate prices tumbled. The prices of mortgage-related
securities declined, and many banks and other financial institutions in the United
States and in Britain failed. Ireland had experienced a massive construction
boom; its banks failed when the bubble burst. Iceland had experienced a spectac-
ular increase in stock prices during the years when there were large investment
inflows; when these inflows slowed dramatically, stock prices declined sharply
and the currency lost half of its value.
US real estate prices peaked at the end of 2006 and then began to decline.
One of the large investment banks was merged into one of the largest com-
mercial banks with a wedding dowry provided by the Federal Reserve that
might have reached nearly $30 billion depending on its loan losses. In mid-
September 2008, two of the large government-sponsored mortgage lenders
that owned 50 percent of US mortgages were effectively taken over by the US
Treasury; the owners of their common stock and their preferred stock lost all
their money. The owners of the bonds of these mortgage lenders were ‘bailed
out’ by the US Treasury; otherwise they would have incurred losses of several

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 359
hundred billion dollars. Several days later, Lehman Brothers, the fifth larg-
est US investment bank, failed; the efforts to negotiate the sale of the firm
were not successful. A massive credit panic and crash followed; the interest
rates of corporate bonds surged relative to the interest rates on US Treasury
securities. A few months later there were runs on the bonds of the govern-
ments of Greece and Portugal. The fiscal deficit of the Greek government was
more than 12 percent of its GDP, and its total indebtedness was more than 125
percent of its GDP. The large international banks had been willing to acquire
the bonds of these governments, which enabled them to finance fiscal deficits
that were much too large to be sustained. The total indebtedness of the Greek
government had surged in part because one or several previous governments
had not been fully forthcoming with information about its total indebtedness.
Nevertheless the indebtedness of these governments had surged because the
‘money was there’ – the banks were willing to buy the bonds which enabled
the governments to finance large deficits. Then the crisis occurred when the
bank lenders suddenly became much more cautious, and the governments did
not have enough cash to pay the interest on their indebtedness and meet the
government payrolls.
THE PATTERNS IN THE DATA
The identity of the borrowers in each of the waves of credit bubbles differs.
The borrowers in the first wave were governments and government-owned
firms in Mexico and ten other developing countries. The borrowers in the
second wave were homeowners and real estate companies in Japan and banks
and homeowners in Finland, Norway, and Sweden. The borrowers in the third
wave often were banks in emerging-market countries, who used external
sources of funding because they were less costly than the domestic sources.
The borrowers in the fourth wave were primarily homeowners and property
developers.
Several large banks were lenders in more than one wave. Banks headquar-
tered in the United States, Canada, Japan, Britain, and France were among
the lenders in the first wave. Japanese banks were the primary lenders in their
domestic real estate bubble in the 1980s. US banks as well as banks based in
Britain, Ireland, Iceland, and Spain were among the lenders in the fourth wave.
Several of the US banks that encountered large losses during this wave also had
incurred large losses in the first wave.
Despite the differences in the identities of the borrowers and the lenders in
these several waves, there was remarkable similarity in the pattern of cash flows.
Most of the countries that were identified with credit bubbles also experienced

360 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
an increase in the price of their currency and an increase in their current
account deficit. Japan is an exception in that it had a current account surplus;
however, the price of the yen increased and its trade and current account sur-
plus declined as the prices of real estate and stocks surged. The increases in the
investment inflows to these countries contributed to the increases in the prices
of securities.
The increase in the prices of the currencies of these countries and the
increase in the prices of securities and real estate were responses to the increase
in investment inflows and components of the international adjustment prob-
lem; domestic consumption had to increase to ensure that the increase in the
net imports of these countries more or less matched the increase in invest-
ment inflows. The higher levels of consumption spending induced by the sharp
increases in the prices of securities led to economic booms. The governments in
some of these countries – including the US government in the late 1990s – real-
ized fiscal surpluses in response to the sharp increase in spending although sev-
eral governments increased their spending almost as rapidly as their revenues
increased.
The pattern of cash flows between lenders and borrowers in each wave was
Ponzian – the increase in the indebtedness of the borrowers was several times
higher than their interest payments on their indebtedness. For three, four or
more years, the borrowers incurred no burden in their debt service payments,
since there was more than enough cash from new loans to pay the interest on
their indebtedness. However, the pattern of cash flows was not sustainable; at
some stage it was inevitable that the lenders would become more cautious in
extending new loans, perhaps because their loans to this group of borrowers
were becoming a larger share of their loan portfolios. And the slowing in the
growth of cross-border loans to this group of borrowers would lead to declines
in the prices of their currencies – which might contribute to greater cautious-
ness by lenders. The borrowers would incur a real debt-servicing burden for the
first time when the increase in their indebtedness declined below their interest
payments; then they would need to find some other source of money for part of
their interest payments. Governments would need to increase their taxes rela-
tive to their expenditures to get the money to make the interest payments – or
they would default.
In a world with perfect foresight, the lenders would have foreseen that the
inevitable decline in the prices of the currencies of the indebted countries would
lead to massive revaluation losses by the borrowers on their liabilities denomi-
nated in the US dollar or some other foreign currency, which might spill over to
large losses by the lenders. The losses by the lenders were so large that the rea-
sonable conclusion is that the lenders had less than perfect foresight; they failed

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 361
to ask ‘Where will the borrowers get the money to pay the interest on their out-
standing indebtedness if there are not enough new loans to provide the money?’
The likelihood is high that these several surges in the external indebtedness
of these countries and in the prices of securities were not independent events;
instead there was a systematic relationship between one wave of banking crises
and the increase in indebtedness that was the beginning of the next wave. When
the surges in the external indebtedness of Mexico and other developing coun-
tries slowed in the early 1980s, the prices of the currencies of Mexico and the
other developing countries declined sharply, and their trade deficits morphed
into surpluses. The countries that had developed large trade surpluses when the
credit bubbles were expanding would experience a real increase in the prices of
their currencies and decline in their trade surpluses.
The Japanese were reluctant to accept the decline in their trade surplus in the
second half of the 1980s because of the adverse impacts on profits and employ-
ment in their export industries; the intervention by the Bank of Japan to dampen
an increase in the price of the yen led to the surge in the reserves of the Japanese
banks and the increase in the money supply. Regulations that constrained domes-
tic and foreign transactions were liberalized to limit the increase in the price of
the yen; banks were able to increase the supply of credit available for real estate
purchases, which led to higher property prices.
When stock prices and then real estate prices in Japan began to decline in
the early 1990s, the price of the Japanese yen increased; Japanese firms then
increased their investments in Thailand, Malaysia, and nearby countries in
anticipation that production costs for low-value-added activities would be below
the domestic costs. About the same time, investment flows to the emerging-
market countries increased rapidly because investment banks had discovered
‘emerging market equities as a new asset class’. Many countries were involved in
extensive privatization activities, which attracted firms based in the industrial
countries.
When property prices and stock prices in Thailand and its neighbors fell
sharply in the summer of 1997, the prices of their currencies declined and their
trade deficits morphed into trade surpluses. The counterpart was that there
was a surge in investment inflows to the United States which contributed to the
increase in the US trade deficit and to increases in US stock prices.
After US stock prices began to decline in the spring of 2000, the price of
the US dollar began to decline. The investment inflows to the United States,
Britain, and other countries increased from about 2002, the prices of securities
in these countries increased, and the prices of the currencies of most of these
countries also increased. Thus, the large changes in the cross-border invest-
ment inflows led to large changes in the prices of currencies and in the prices

362 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
of securities and real estate. The increases in real estate prices in the United
States, Britain, and other countries after 2002 were responses to the increases
in investment inflows. It is as if there is a pool of international credit that can be
tapped by borrowers in various countries when they conclude that the net inter-
est costs are lower than the costs of obtaining funds in their domestic markets.
Many of these borrowers incur currency exposure but presumably they have
concluded that the reduction in their interest payments more than compensates
for this risk.
THE IMPACTS OF MONETARY SHOCKS,
AND CREDIT MARKET SHOCKS
The striking feature of the last forty years has been the sharp variability of cross-
border investment inflows. The prices of the German mark and the Japanese
yen increased throughout most of the 1970s and then declined sharply in the
first half of the 1980s. When investment inflows to Mexico increased in the
early 1990s and its economy was booming, the price of the peso increased sig-
nificantly after adjustment for differences in inflation rates, and the Mexican
trade deficit reached 6 percent of its GDP. When investment inflows slowed
sharply in 1994, the price of the peso declined sharply, money was withdrawn
from Mexico, and the Mexican trade surplus reached 4 percent of its GDP. This
change in the direction and scope of cross-border investment inflows was mas-
sive and sudden, and had powerful impacts on the price of the peso, the inflation
rate in Mexico, the prices of peso securities and of real assets, and the solvency
of Mexican firms, households, and banks.
Financial market events in Thailand, Norway, Indonesia, Iceland, and
many other countries were similar to those in Mexico. The Minsky story of the
cyclical variability in the supplies of credit in domestic economies is dramati-
cally evident in the global economy in the variability in cross-border invest-
ment inflows. In domestic economies, increases in the credit supply contribute
to economic booms and euphoria, which in turn lead investors to become more
optimistic and encourage lenders to extend more credit. Increases in invest-
ment inflows lead to increases in the prices of their currencies and to dramatic
increases in the prices of securities and other assets. Investor optimism led lend-
ers to provide more credit to domestic borrowers and economic booms often
followed.
Some of the credit market and monetary shocks led to increases in invest-
ment inflows to countries and to increases in the prices of currencies, stocks,
and real estate. As long as the prices of currencies were increasing and the prices
of securities and real estate also were increasing, the rates of return on these

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 363
currencies and securities were high and increasing; optimism about economic
futures increased. Then another shock would trigger a decline or reversal in
cross-border investment inflows, and the prices of currencies, securities, and
other assets crashed.
These manic-type shocks resulted from extensive changes in the prefer-
ences of investors for securities and other assets denominated in different cur-
rencies. Investors became concerned that the US inflation rate would increase
in the 1970s; they sold US dollar securities and bought securities denominated
in the German mark, the Swiss franc, and the British pound, and the prices of
these currencies increased by much more than the excess of the US inflation rate
over the inflation rates in these major US trading partners. During the 1970s
the US dollar price of gold increased ‘because gold was a good inflation hedge’,
although the annual percentage increases in the price of gold in the second half
of the 1970s were many times larger than the percentage increases in the US
price level. Early in 1980 investors became convinced that the US inflation rate
would decline; they sold securities denominated in the German mark and other
foreign currencies and the prices of these currencies declined sharply.
One explanation for the greater variability of cross-border investment
inflows in the last thirty years is that shocks, and especially those that involved
changes in the stance of monetary policy, have been larger than in earlier peri-
ods when currencies were pegged or when there was a commitment to parities
for national currencies. One of the major arguments in the case for floating
exchange rates is that central banks then have greater independence to change
their monetary policies and the rates of growth of their money supplies and
their interest rates to achieve their domestic economic objectives. In effect the
commitments to parities for national currencies constrained changes in the
central banks’ monetary policies and especially the adoption of more expan-
sive monetary policies; these commitments meant that national inflation rates
could not differ significantly from the inflation rates in the countries’ major
trading partners. In the absence of a commitment to parities, the policies
adopted by central banks have led to changes in the current and anticipated
inflation rates that in turn induced large changes in cross-border invest-
ment inflows. Hence the much greater variability in cross-border investment
inflows in part reflects changes in national monetary policies, and the changes
in anticipated inflation rates have been much larger than when currencies have
been pegged.
The much greater variability in cross-border investment inflows in part
reflected that monetary shocks have been greater than when currencies had been
pegged; these shocks led to changes in investor estimates of the inflation rates in
different countries and hence in the anticipated prices of currencies at various

364 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
future dates. The expansive US monetary policies of the late 1960s and the early
1970s led investors to revise upward their estimates of the US inflation rate and
also to revise upward their estimates of the anticipated prices of the German
mark and the Japanese yen. Investors sold US dollar securities and bought secu-
rities denominated in the German mark, the Swiss franc, and the British pound,
which led to the sharp increases in the prices of these currencies.
If, as a group, investors increase the proportion of non-dollar securities in
their portfolios, then the United States would develop a larger current account
surplus (or a smaller current account deficit), which would require that the price
of the German mark – or the euro as its successor – and the price of the Japanese
yen, and other foreign currencies, increase less rapidly than would be inferred
from the difference in national inflation rates. These foreign currencies would
overshoot the values inferred from the differences in national inflation rates as
long as investors increased the rate at which they acquired foreign securities.
The adoption of a more contractive US monetary policy in the autumn
of 1979 led investors to reduce their estimates of the US inflation rate and to
revise downward their estimates of the prices of the German mark, the Japanese
yen, and other foreign currencies. The increase in their purchases of US dollar
securities led to the sharp declines in the prices of the German mark and the
Japanese yen.
Overshooting was inevitable whenever investors wished to increase their
holdings of securities denominated in a particular currency; similarly, under-
shooting was inevitable whenever investors wished to decrease their holdings
of securities denominated in this currency. The earlier clichés applied to large
and rapid deviations between the currency values and those that were consistent
with the differences in national inflation rates – the ‘vicious and virtuous cycle’
and ‘destabilizing speculation’ – reflected the impacts of sudden changes in the
