direction of cross-border investment inflows. Changes in anticipated inflation
rates – more precisely, changes in the differential in national inflation rates – led
to overshooting and undershooting because the impact of the changes in these
differentials on the anticipated prices of currencies induced changes in cross-
border investment inflows.
Because the sharp increases in the prices of Japanese stocks and real estate
attracted US and other foreign investors, the price of the yen increased. Credit
market shocks impact the prices of individual currencies as they affect inves-
tor demand for securities denominated in different currencies. The credit mar-
ket shocks in the last thirty years have had major impacts on the prices of the
Mexican peso, the Thai baht, and many other currencies because they led to
changes in the amounts of the securities denominated in these currencies that
investors wished to hold.

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 365
A second, complementary, explanation for the greater variability in cross-
border investment inflows is that when currencies are not pegged, a shock of a
given magnitude in the form of an increase in demand for securities denomi-
nated in a currency has a larger immediate impact on the country’s GDP as a
result of the increase in the prices of its securities and real estate. When curren-
cies were pegged, the immediate impact of increases in the flows of money to
countries was that their central banks’ holdings of international reserve assets
increased and their monetary liabilities increased correspondingly. The price of
securities available in the country also increased in response to the purchases
by the foreign investors.
When currencies were not pegged, comparable increases in the foreign
demand for securities denominated in these currencies initiated the adjustment
process to ensure that the countries’ trade balances changed by the amounts
that corresponded to the increases in the investment inflows. The invisible hand
operated to ensure that the immediate impact of the increases in the flows of
money were that domestic investment spending increased as the cost of capi-
tal declined and consumption spending increased in response to higher levels
of household wealth. Household consumption spending is three or four times
larger than investment spending in most countries, and accounted for most of
the increase in total spending. The inevitable outcome of the adjustment process
was that domestic saving declined in the countries that received large invest-
ment inflows.
The invisible hand led to increases in the prices of the currencies of the
countries that experienced larger investment inflows and to increases in the
prices of securities and real estate in these countries. Moreover, the invisible
hand led to higher rates of growth of GDP as the prices of securities and house-
hold wealth increased and consumption spending climbed. Thus the increases
in the variability in ratios of changes in trade balances to GDP that resulted
from the initial increase in the investment inflows to countries induced changes
in the adjustment process that led to higher rates of return on their securities
and other assets. The increases in household wealth contributed to the economic
boom. In effect there was a feedback mechanism from the initial increases in
the investment inflows to the higher rates of return that induced further invest-
ment inflows. The economic booms were prolonged and pervasive; many of
the participants may have failed to recognize that the cross-border pattern of
investment inflows could not be sustained. One of the patterns in the data is
that increases in the investment inflows to countries were associated with eco-
nomic booms, which were evident in Mexico and other developing countries in
the 1970s, in Mexico, Thailand, and other Asian countries in the first half of the
1990s, and in the United States in the second half of the 1990s. The increases

366 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
in the prices of their currencies reduced the inflationary pressures associated
with a robust economic expansion and the increase in export prices relative to
import prices led to higher rates of economic growth. The investment inflows
were also associated with a non-sustainable pattern of cash flows because some
of the borrowers in these countries obtained the cash to pay the interest to their
creditors from new loans. The continuation of the economic booms may explain
why the lenders – at least a large number of them – failed to recognize that even-
tually there would be costly adjustments.
COULD AN INTERNATIONAL LENDER OF LAST
RESORT HAVE MADE A SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE?
Might the financial tumultuousness of the last thirty years have been mitigated
if there had been an international lender of last resort? Central banks were
established as lenders of last resort to reduce the likelihood that the increase in
the demand for money would lead to distress sales of assets and trigger solvency
crises; these banks would increase the supply of money in response to the excep-
tional increase in demand. During the expansion phase of the cycle, investors
took on greater risks in anticipation of higher returns – and they reduced their
estimates of the risks attached to various securities. And at the same time, many
lenders became less cautious in the effort to increase their share of the market
for mortgages, and for loans to business and governments.
Could an international lender of last resort have made a significant dif-
ference and reduced the frequency and scope of financial crises since the early
1980s? Or could a more active international lender of last resort have made a
significant difference? The source of the problem – one source of the prob-
lem – is that the cross-border investment inflows have been much larger than
when currencies were attached to parities, and more highly variable. Would
an international lender of last resort have moderated the volume of cross-
border investment inflows that have led to exceptional increases in the sup-
plies of credit, or is it possible that investors’ demand for foreign securities
would have been even larger because they would have had greater confidence
that the central banks would be more ambitious in their efforts to moderate
the changes in the prices of currencies? The answer depends on the responsi-
bilities and the financial resources available to the international lender of last
resort and its willingness to extend credit to central banks whose currencies
may depreciate sharply, perhaps because of the decline in investment inflows.
Would the international lender of last resort have the authority and be will-
ing to caution central banks about the volume and variability of cross-border
investment inflows?

THE LESSONS OF HISTORY 367
The variant of the moral hazard argument is that efforts to stabilize the
changes in the prices of currencies in response to the sharp variations in cross-
border investment inflows might lead investors to incur larger cross-border
risks because they would have greater confidence that the range of movement
in the prices of currencies would be smaller. The lender of last resort might
seek to moderate the investment inflows to various countries – but the like-
lihood that countries would agree that the international lender could place
limits to investment inflows seems low. The lender might be empowered to
provide cautionary statements that the cross-border flows are non-sustaina-
ble. National governments would seem more likely to agree to an arrangement
that would enable them to have access to more money from an international
lender to moderate the undershooting when the direction of the money flows
is reversed – if they could agree on the source of the money for the interna-
tional lender.
Most of the currency crises since the early 1980s have resulted from the
reversal in cross-border investment inflows. In virtually all of these countries
the pace of the investment inflows was too high to be sustained because the bor-
rowers’ indebtedness was increasing too rapidly. During the manic phase, the
increase in investment inflows led to increases in the prices of currencies that
overshot long-run average prices. The inevitable first sign of a modest slacken-
ing of the pace of investment inflows would have led to declines in the prices of
the currencies, which would feed back to much sharper declines in the inflows
and then to massive declines in the prices of currencies.
Overshooting and undershooting were an inevitable part of the process of
adjustment to the changes in the volume and direction of cross-border invest-
ment inflows. In some countries, the severe decline in the price of their cur-
rency associated with undershooting would imperil the solvency of domestic
firms that had liabilities denominated in foreign currencies because of the sharp
increases in the domestic currency equivalent of their interest and amortization
payments. The bankruptcy of these firms could imperil the solvency of domes-
tic banks and other financial institutions.
A domestic lender of last resort might on occasion make some public state-
ments that stock prices were increasing too rapidly and that the market was
characterized by irrational exuberance. Similar statements might be made
about prices in the markets for residential and commercial real estate; the cen-
tral bank might advise banks to limit the increases in their real estate loans. The
counterpart is that an international lender of last resort might provide private
and even public statements that increases in the external indebtedness of one or
several countries were too rapid to be sustained and that the eventual adjust-
ment to sustainable values could be costly and perhaps messy. Investors and

368 MANIAS, PANICS, AND CRASHES
other market participants would be left to draw their own conclusions about the
implications of these statements.
The International Monetary Fund was established in the 1940s to assist
countries in financing their balance of payments deficits and thus to reduce the
pressure on countries to reduce the prices of their currencies because of a short-
age of funds to finance their cyclical or otherwise temporary payments deficits.
The motive for establishing the IMF was the belief that much of the financial
instability in the 1920s and especially in the 1930s could have been avoided
or mitigated if there had been an international lender of last resort. Fund staff
visit each of the member countries once or twice a year to discuss the country’s
economic policies. The Fund is a large repository of data and country experi-
ences about the changes in asset prices and changes in international indebted-
ness of individual countries. It has rarely sounded the alarm that the external
indebtedness of member countries was increasing too rapidly – that their cur-
rent account deficits were too large, and that the transition to sustainable values
for their current account balances would be costly in terms of economic stabil-
ity – and that was more likely a ‘hard landing’ than a ‘soft landing’. Nor has the
IMF been able to provide the credits at the time of crash to avoid extensive and
debilitating undershooting.
Many of these countries used money from the Fund to limit the declines in
the prices of their currencies after the advent of a currency crisis. Some countries
were reluctant to accept money from the IMF because the conditions attached
to acceptance would deflate their economies.
The US Treasury became a lender of last resort to Mexico at the time of
that country’s financial crisis at the end of 1994, because the financial resources
from the IMF were too small; the IMF and several foreign governments also
provided assistance. The announcement that this money would be available
limited further declines in the price of the peso. If a comparable initiative had
been taken one or several weeks earlier, the undershooting of the peso would
have been smaller, and the adverse impacts of the decline in the price of the peso
on the Mexican economy would have been less severe.
Whether the shortfall in the performance of the IMF relative to the ambi-
tions that led to its establishment has resulted from the failures of analysis or
policy or member country truculence is a topic for another book.

EPILOGUE
T
he economic achievements in China since the early 1980s have been brilliant,
and probably unparalleled by those in any other country. Three hundred to
four hundred million people – perhaps one third of the country’s population
– moved from huts with dirt floors on farms and villages to apartments in the
cities and near factories; they have a middle-class lifestyle ‘with clean water in
and dirty water out’. The rate of economic growth averaged nearly 10 percent
for nearly thirty years. China is the world’s second largest economy and even if
its growth rate were to decline sharply, China will eventually surpass the United
States as the world’s largest economy.
China has produced an exceptionally large number of billionaires and tens
of thousands of millionaires. Perhaps six or seven hundred thousand Chinese
students attend colleges and universities in the United States, Britain, Japan,
Australia, Germany, and other foreign countries.
Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and several other countries have had high
rates of economic growth for three or four decades. A number of factors must
come together if a country’s GDP is to grow by 8 or 10 percent a year for two or
more decades. The country must be able to increase its exports; the firms that
sell abroad must be able to capture market share from more established foreign
firms so they will need a price advantage. High levels of investment in facto-
ries that produce products for domestic and foreign markets must be financed,
which means that the country needs a high savings rate; most countries that
have grown rapidly have supplemented their high level of domestic saving with
a modest amount of foreign saving; they have become international debtors
during their rapid growth years. High rates of growth require massive invest-
ment in infrastructure – in electric power, water supply, roads and railroads and
airports, and urban accommodation. A flexible financial system is required to
bring together the divergent needs of business borrowers and household savers.
High rates of growth of urban areas can occur only if there is a massive increase
in food production or increased dependence on imported foods. High rates of
growth require a rapid increase in the supply of managers and the number of
entrepreneurs.

370 EPILOGUE
China has two handicaps that these other countries did not have, since it
had been a command economy for the previous thirty years with two bizarre
and destructive detours; one was the ‘backyard furnaces’ and the other was the
‘cultural revolution’. The state owned the means of production and the land that
families had farmed for generations. Economic activity was organized around
major government-owned firms and government agencies, which often pro-
vided housing, medical services, and education for the children of their employ-
ees. Competition was limited, and the quality of industrial products and of most
services was low by the standards of other newly industrializing countries.
The second handicap is that China had a much larger population than any
other country, with only India coming close. It is much more difficult for a
country to capture a share of the world market than for a small country, since
the displacement impact on foreign producers is much larger.
China entered the modern period with a massive supply of unskilled labor
that was large, mobile, and adaptable and eager for improvement in its living
standards. Households saved an extremely high proportion of their incomes
because of the need to accumulate the financial wealth necessary to buy living
accommodation and partly for retirement. There was a massive supply of latent
entrepreneurs. The respect for intellectual property rights was modest.
Some of the state-owned enterprises in China have been privatized. Much
of the growth of the economy has depended on the success of foreign-owned
firms. One of the brilliant decisions of the Chinese government in the early
1980s was to invite foreign firms to produce in China, partly for export and
partly for the domestic market. These firms had established brand names and
supply chains and distribution networks, which meant that China encountered
a less severe external constraint than Japan and other countries that had been
reluctant to allow foreign firms to invest on their turf. Often these firms were
required to have Chinese-owned joint venture partners.
The rapid expansion of Chinese exports drove the growth of cities and
urbanization. Factories needed to be built near ports, and infrastructure had to
be developed so that the factories had access to water and to electric power and
transport. Roads and railroads and seaports and airports were necessary to facil-
itate the movement of raw materials to factories and finished goods to ports and
airports. As long as exports were increasing, migration to the cities continued.
Productivity in the urban industrial sector was much higher, initially per-
haps three to four times as high, as productivity on farms and in the country-
side. Thus the shift in the allocation of labor from farms to factories would
automatically have led to an increase in GDP, even in the absence of any gains
in output per unit of labor in the industrial sector. Perhaps two to three per-
centage points of the GDP growth rate resulted from the re-allocation of labor.

EPILOGUE 371
Moreover the re-allocation led to productivity gains in the rural sector as
redundant labor left.
One of the decisions that Deng Xiaoping made in the early 1980s was
to adopt the Japanese style of financial regulation that had been used in the
immediate years after World War II to quicken the rate of economic growth.
The dominant features of this model were ceilings that kept interest rates that
the banks could pay to household savers low; the interest rates that the banks
could charge business borrowers were also low. Because the maximum interest
rate that the banks could pay household savers often was less than the annual
increases in the price level, the purchasing power of accumulated saving
declined; the consequence was that households saved an exceptionally large
proportion of their income to build up the wealth necessary to buy a home.
But because property prices were increasing by more than 10 percent or more a
year, people needed to save a large amount each year so their financial wealth
would increase more rapidly.
Moreover, the demand for credit at the maximum interest rate that the
banks could charge business borrowers was much larger than the supply, so the
banks needed a mechanism to determine which borrowers would be the first
to receive credit. The banks in Japan received directives from the Ministry of
Finance about the identity of the borrowers that should receive priority in receiv-
ing bank loans, which almost always went to business firms that were thought
by the bureaucrats to be those that would be the ‘winners’ in global industrial
competition. Real estate was considered a consumption good, and relatively
modest amounts of credit were available for purchase and construction.
A curb market in bank credit developed in Tokyo; the borrowers in this
market were the firms that were denied credit by the banks or received less credit
than they wished. The suppliers of loans were the firms that were able to bor-
row from the banks; these firms received an economic rent. Some of the firms
that were able to borrow directly from the banks loaned the money to firms that
were not favored or were able to borrow a smaller amount than they wished.
Because interest rates that the banks charged the favored borrowers often
were below the rate of economic growth, a pattern of ‘evergreen finance’ devel-
oped. In effect, these firms paid the interest on their outstanding indebtedness
with the cash from new loans.
During the 1960s and the 1970s, property prices had increased somewhat
more rapidly than the rate of growth of nominal GDP. Many of the companies
that were listed on the stock exchanges were property companies. As property
prices increased, stock prices increased. Japanese firms believed that their cost
of capital was low; they were much more interested in maintaining or increasing
their market share than in the profitability of their investments.

372 EPILOGUE
As the property market boomed, the Japanese financial sector also boomed.
The Japanese banks owned significant amounts of stocks and of real estate, and
as stock prices and real estate prices increased, their capital increased, and they
were then able to increase their loans. The Japanese banks based loan values on
the value of the collateral offered by the borrowers; as property prices increased,
the value of collateral and bank capital increased. Japan seemed to have the
financial counterpart of a perpetual motion machine.
The Japanese growth rate began to slow in the second half of the 1980s, and
the Ministry of Finance began to relax various regulations, including those that
had limited bank loans for real estate. Moreover, controls on Japanese foreign
investment were relaxed to limit the increase in the price of the Japanese yen.
Much of the real estate investment in Japan consisted of upgrading or
rebuilding the cities. Japan had extremely fragmented ownership of property,
which meant that developers had an arduous – and expensive – task of assem-
bling the land required for modern office and apartment buildings.
The massive increase in the prices of real estate and stocks in Japan in the
second half of the 1980s was an integral part of the adjustment to the decline in
the investment outflow from Japan, and to the reduction in the country’s capi-
tal account deficit. The invisible hands were at work to ensure that there was a
comparable decline in its current account surplus. Japanese imports are largely
primary products that are not especially sensitive to changes in relative prices –
and so a massive increase in household wealth was necessary to bring about the
needed increase in imports.
The surges in asset prices in Japan began to end in the last month of
December 1989 when stock prices peaked; property prices peaked eighteen
months later. The trigger for the decline in asset prices was that the incoming
governor of the Bank of Japan instructed the banks to limit the increase in the
credit for real estate to the rate of growth of total loans. Some of the indebted
borrowers had become dependent on money from new loans to pay some of the
interest on their outstanding loans.
The decline in property prices and stock prices meant that many of the bor-
rowers were unable to pay the interest on their loans. Property prices had increased
so rapidly that the rental rate of return was very small, much less than the interest
rate. These investments were financially attractive only if property prices were to
continue to increase at rates significantly higher than the interest rate.
When property prices began to decline, bankruptcies began to escalate;
Japanese banks incurred large loan losses and their capital declined. These banks
became wards of the government. Their reluctance or inability to increase their
loans to industrial firms meant that these firms could no longer make their
interest payments in a timely way.

EPILOGUE 373
When the supply of new loans declined and the rate of economic growth
slowed, it became evident that industrial productive capacity in Japan was too
large relative to domestic demand. One adjustment was that firms had to shrink,
which meant that the investment in plant and equipment declined sharply. The
Japanese growth rate plummeted. Since then, the Japanese problem has been
that the amounts that households and business firms wish to save is much larger
than the amounts that firms want to invest.
Since the early 1980s, China has experienced a surge in real estate prices
relative to household incomes, which is somewhat similar to the sharp increase
in real estate prices in Japan in the 1980s and especially in the second half of
that decade. The background to the increases in real estate prices in China is
very different from that in Japan. The surge in real estate prices in Japan was
part of a balance of payments adjustment problem, while the surge in real estate
prices in China has been a response to the surge in migration and the search for
a secure store of value. The key question is whether the Chinese experience will
follow that of Japan, and whether a sharp decline in real estate prices will read
to a dramatic decline in its rate of economic growth, much as Japan had after
real estate prices tumbled.
For the past twenty years, the dominant problem in Japan has been that,
together, the household and business saving rates have been higher than domes-
tic investment. Government has absorbed the excess saving with a lot of bridges
to nowhere and massive fiscal deficits.
China also has experienced a remarkable increase in property prices in the
last twenty years, although the cause only partly overlapped with the cause of
the increase in property prices in Tokyo and Osaka. Prices in the property mar-
ket began to increase in the early 1990s soon after the government decreed that
work units should sell the living units to residents for a nominal price relative to
their annual incomes. Because of the massive migration from the countryside to
the city, the prices of these units rose, and some of the sellers who initially had
been gifted units from their employers sold them to more recent migrants from
the countryside and traded up to new and more expensive accommodations.
Initially, the demand for apartments was to provide shelter for those moving
to the cities. As apartment prices increased, it became evident that the ownership
of apartments provided both a secure store of value relative with a much higher
rate of return than the rates of return on currency, bank deposits, and stocks. The
first-time buyers of apartments wanted to ‘get on the train’; they wanted to make
the transition from financial wealth whose purchasing power tended to decline
to owning property because of the continued increase in property prices.
The price of the ticket for getting on the train was increasing more rapidly
than household incomes. The supply of credit available to most first-time home

374 EPILOGUE
buyers was small; most purchases were financed with cash, although some of
the cash may have been borrowed from relatives and friends. The combination
of the rapid increase in house prices and the negative real rates of return on
bank deposits meant that individuals had to save an increasingly large propor-
tion of their incomes because property prices were increasing rapidly. Because
of the rush to buy as soon as possible, it seems like a safe conjecture that house-
holds invested all of their wealth in the apartment at the time of purchase – and
if they had borrowed from family and friends, they invested more than their
wealth.
The continued sharp increase in the price of apartments reflected that the
demand for apartments was increasing more rapidly than the supply. At the end
of 2013, the price of the standard two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment of
about 90 to 100 square meters in Beijing and other Tier I cities was the renminbi
equivalent of $600,000. Per capita income in urban areas was $20,000 so the
prices were twenty to thirty times higher than per capita incomes. An alterna-
tive statement is that the price of an apartment was twenty times the annual
income of a new university graduate. The cost per square foot ranged between
$600 and $800, or three to four times the comparable cost in the United States.
An apartment is a package of embedded labor, concrete glass, steel, other
materials, and land. China has had a virtually unlimited supply of unskilled
construction labor; the increase in the prices of apartments cannot be explained
by higher wage rates. Similarly, the increase in the price of apartments cannot
be explained by the higher costs of the materials that are embedded in the apart-
ments; most of these materials were produced with locally available labor. The
one factor that has been in short supply has been the land that provides the sites
for the apartments, which must be taken from farmers by local governments
who, from time to time, have encountered strong, hostile reactions. The local
governments then either auction the land to developers or instead construct the
apartments on their own.
The major reason that the price of apartments has increased is that the
demand for apartments has increased more rapidly than the supply of land
available for construction. China is a massive country, with an extraordinarily
large number of cities; the bottleneck that contributed significantly to the surge
in prices has been that local governments have encountered various constraints
in displacing farmers from the land rather than the shortage of land.
The paradox is that there is a shortage of housing in China and ten to fifteen
million unoccupied apartments; these apartments had been purchased on the
assumption that apartment prices would continue to increase, which has been
validated for twenty years. It’s as if there is a Chinese proverb, ‘Real estate is a
great investment, the price of real estate never declines’.

EPILOGUE 375
Many million more apartments had been acquired as stores of value and
were rented. The home ownership rate is 90 percent; if the urban housing stock
is 150 million units, then 15 million units are rented. The rental rates of return
are in the range of 1 percent to 1.5 percent a year; these rates are low in percent-
age terms because apartment prices are very high relative to household incomes.
Virgin apartments sell for a premium relative to apartments that have been
occupied by one or several owners, and many owners chose not to rent out their
properties because the rental income is so low relative the projected increase in
the price.
For most of the period since 2008, China has produced ten million hous-
ing units a year. The expenditure on apartments has accounted for 10 percent
of GDP. In recent years perhaps two to three percentage points of this 10 per-
cent represents the demand for apartments that will remain unoccupied. Of the
apartments that have been produced in the last five years, 20 to 30 percent have
been acquired as a store of value.
Because of the spectacular rate of economic growth, urban wages for
unskilled labor have increased, almost certainly because the supply of excess
labor on the farms has been exhausted or nearly exhausted. As a result, China
has lost its low-wage advantage relative to Vietnam, Bangladesh, and other
countries. China’s export growth has slowed. The implication is that migration
will slow dramatically and the demand for accommodation will slow.
As demand for accommodation slows, the price of apartments will increase
less rapidly. Some developers then will reduce prices or otherwise offer incen-
tives to attract buyers. Some developers will go out of business; their unsold
units will be acquired by other developers who believe that they are buying at
bargain prices.
The demand for apartments as a store of value cannot increase more rap-
idly than the supply of land for an unlimited period; at some stage the increase
in demand will decline below the increase in supply of land available for
apartments.
That there are eight or ten or twelve ghost cities suggests that a crossover
point has been reached in a number of regions. A ghost city means an immense
excess supply – and the implication is that apartment prices will decline. As the
anticipation that apartments are a secure store of value becomes clouded, the
demand for apartments as a store of value will decline.
Property developers may own one to two million apartments in their inven-
tories, which is less than two months’ sales at historic rates. Moreover, these
developers may own twenty million apartments in the construction pipeline on
the implicit assumption that it takes two years from the time ground is b roken

376 EPILOGUE
until an apartment is completed. The developers have a massive price risk
because they paid for the land before construction started.
As the prices of apartments decline, so does the demand for apartments
as a store of value. Each decline of production of one million apartments each
year means that the rate of economic growth would decline by two percent-
age points. If individuals have purchased three million apartments each year
as a store of value, then the growth rate would decline by six percentage points,
even before any of the owners of the fifteen million apartments that have been
acquired as a store of value decide to sell.
The arithmetic is that there are thirty million apartments that are com-
pleted or in the construction pipeline. Hence, the supply of vacant apartments
and apartments under construction is 20 percent of the stock of 150 million
apartments.
At some stage, some of the owners of the ten to fifteen million unoccupied
apartments will decide to sell and realize their gains. Similarly, some of the indi-
viduals that have bought apartments as stores of value and have rented them out
will seek to sell one or several of the apartments. The local governments that
own the apartments in the ghost cities will sell them.
The decline in property prices will impact new construction and the GDP
growth rate, household wealth and spending, the capital and solvency of the
banking system, and government finance. Various metrics can be used to esti-
mate the scope of the decline in property prices. The price of a Buick produced
in Shanghai should not differ from the price of one produced in Detroit by
15 or 20 percent, and similarly, the price of an apartment produced in Beijing
should not differ from the price of one produced in Washington by more than
15 or 20 percent. Obviously, apartments are not tradable goods, and there will
be a lot of local variation in prices depending on whether they are near the
center of the city or in distant suburbs. This type of comparison suggests that
prices will decline to 20 to 30 percent of peak prices. Property prices in Japan
at the end of the 1990s were 20 percent of their peak prices at the end of the
1980s. If property prices in China were to decline so that landlords would earn
a competitive rate of return, then at the trough property prices would be one
third of their peak.
As property prices decline annual production will fall. US housing starts
declined from 2.1 million units in 2006 to 550,000 units two years later; the
excess supply of apartments at its peak was slightly more than the demographic
demand associated with one year’s production. Because migration from the
Chinese countryside appears to have declined sharply and the population
growth rate has declined, estimating how long it will take for the excess supply
to be absorbed is not feasible.

EPILOGUE 377
Consider one set of estimates. The cities have stopped growing because
export growth has slowed. If there are ten to fifteen million unoccupied apart-
ments and the twenty million units in the construction pipeline decline to ten
million, then it would take three years of sales at the annual rate of seven mil-
lion units to absorb the excess supply on the assumption that annual production
declines to five million units a year. The larger the impact of the decline in the
growth of cities on the demand for apartments, the larger the number of years
before the excess supply is absorbed. During these three to five years the GDP
growth rate would be modestly negative.
The ownership of apartments may be 70 or 80 percent of household wealth.
As property prices decline, household net worth will decline by 50 to 60 percent.
Household spending will decline, especially on automobiles and other dura-
ble goods. The latent excess capacity in these industries will become apparent.
Firms will reduce prices in the effort to maintain sales, and they will no longer
earn enough to cover fixed costs.
The banks will be between a rock and a hard place; they will be under
instructions from the government to lend freely while they realize that firms
are not earning enough to pay the interest.
The traditional statement is that Chinese banks will not be significantly
impacted by the decline in property prices because most Chinese buyers have
paid cash and, because for all practical purposes, banks are owned by the gov-
ernment. Perhaps. Property developers in China rely extensively on the banks
and on the shadow banks; the various lenders to the property developers will
incur significant loan losses. The local governments that are the developers for
the ghost cities will incur very large losses; these governments probably have
borrowed from the banks to finance construction.
The embedded bank loan losses are immense and will add to the govern-
ment debt.
The Chinese government is pragmatic, and will seek to dampen the impact
of the decline in spending on apartments in terms of the rate of economic
growth.
During the past twenty years, and especially in the last five years, the demand
for apartments as a store of value contributed significantly to the growth rate.
This demand enabled China to delay the adjustments to a disconnect between
national saving and national investment.
The increase in property prices in the United States, Japan, Ireland, Spain,
and numerous other countries resulted from the increases in demand financed
by large amounts of credit. The increase in property prices in China also was
driven by increases in demand as households searched for a secure store of value
because the real rate of return on bank deposits was so modest.

378 EPILOGUE
China’s problem is much like that of Japan’s in the early 1990s; the amount
that households wish to save is much larger than business firms can profitably
invest. The initial adjustment will involve two factors – one is that the private
sector can build more loss-leading toll roads and high-speed railroads, and the
government can spend more on improving the environment and building low-
cost housing. Japan gained modest relief from the excess of intended saving over
intended investment by purchasing US dollar securities.

The ladies and clergymen – in American parlance, ‘widows and orphans’ – may more properly

charitable institutions’ (p. 135); ‘widows, parsons, orphanages, magistrates and civil servants’ (p.

the inevitable widows and orphans’ (p. 202).
In the quotation from Bagehot that constitutes one of the epigraphs of this book, owners of the
blind capital who lacked the wisdom to invest it properly were characterized in the excised portion
as ‘quiet ladies, rural clergymen and country misers’ and again as ‘rectors, authors, grandmoth-
ers’. See Bagehot, ‘Essays on Edward Gibbon’, quoted in Theodore E. Burton, Financial Crises and
Periods of Industrial and Commercial Depression (New York: Appleton, 1902), pp. 321–2.
In his essay on Lord Brougham (1857), Bagehot quotes his subject on the crisis of 1814:
The frenzy, I can call it nothing less ... descended to persons in the humblest circumstances,
and the farthest removed by their pursuits, from commercial cares ... Not only clerks and
labourers, but menial servants, engaged the little sums which they had been laying up for a
provision against old age and sickness ...
The great speculators broke; the middling ones lingered out a precarious existence, deprived
of all means of continuing their dealings either at home or abroad; the poor dupes of the delu-
sion had lost their little hoards and went on the parish (Norman St John-Stevas, ed., Bagehot’s
Historical Essays [New York: New York University Press, 1966], pp. 118–19).
Another British expression for the naive and innocent who were drawn into the last phases of a
bubble is ‘greengrocers and servant girls’. The American 1929 categories were ‘bootblacks and wait-
ers’, whereas a more modern characterization is ‘house painters and office girls’ (John Brooks, The
Go-Go Years [New York: Weybright and Talley, 1973, p. 305]). Classes of current well-to-do ama-
teurish and sometimes badly advised investors in the United States include successful doctors and
dentists and professional athletes.

AFTERWORD
Lord Robert Skidelsky
C
harles Kindleberger had a foot in both economic history and politics. (One
of his many books was entitled Power and Money [1970].) In economics he is
known chiefly as the historian of financial instability, the subject of this absorb-
ing book. Following Keynes’s lead, he championed the role of governments as
stabilizers of the economic system. But there was no world government. How,
therefore, could the international economy be prevented from crashing from
time to time? Out of his study of the Great Depression (The World in Depression
1929–1939 [1973]) he developed his theory of ‘hegemonic stability’ – the theory
for which he is best known in political science. Broadly stated this is the thesis
that ‘for the world economy to be stabilized, there has to be a stabilizer, one sta-
bilizer’. The hegemon is the proxy for the absent world government.
Kindleberger’s contribution here should be coupled with that of Mancur
Olson, whose The Logic of Collective Action: Public Goods and the Theory of
Groups, published in 1965, considers how public goods might be provided in
the absence of compulsory contributions – that is, without taxes or imperial
tribute.
Olson showed how, under specified conditions, the chief of which were the
smallness of the group and an initially large inequality of resources, the cost of
providing a public good like street lighting might be met by the richest house-
hold in the street. Kindleberger applied this insight to the claim that the public
goods of a liberal international economy – which he took to be free trade, sound
money, and fixed exchange rates – can be provided by a preponderantly wealthy
country, which supplies ‘sweeteners’ – essentially financial and trade facilities –
to induce the other countries to follow the ‘rules of the game’.
Kindleberger’s argument grew out of his interpretation of the Great
Depression. The need for stabilizers arises from the existence of contractual
uncertainty which, unless offset, will have a deflationary effect through the

AFTERWORD 405
build-up of inactive balances. The function of the leader or underwriter is to
maintain the global level of activity by satisfying the demand for liquidity and
maintaining the flow of investment finance.
A key feature of Kindleberger’s position is that the provision of public goods
has to be centralized. The existence of competing financial centers, as in the
interwar years, makes stabilization impossible.
Four points in Kindleberger’s model are worth noticing:
1) It sets up a post-imperial game: there is no international or imperial
government.
2) It is a beneficent game: it eliminates the conflict between behaving
rationally and behaving well.
3) It remedies the gap in classical free trade theory, which tended to
assume that its institutional underpinnings were already in place,
and ignored the fact that the general benefit offered by free trade is
an insufficient inducement for individual agents (countries) to play
by free trade rules.
4) It implies that the system is self-liquidating because the costs of the
sweeteners provided by the leader come to exceed the pay-offs. So
it gives us a theoretical explanation of the circulation of hegemons,
focussing particularly on the rise and fall of Britain, and on those
periods of messy transition, in which leadership is contested.
Although financial history is full of banking excesses leading to crashes, one
clear lesson that Kindleberger sought to draw (and which Chapter 13 of this
volume brings out) is that these are not lethal for the economic system if there
exists a single ‘international lender of last resort’. It is the absence of such a
lender which brings economic collapse in the wake of financial collapse. Thus,
the world depression of 1929–33 was so long and deep because Britain could
not, and the USA would not, ‘discount in crisis’. The breakdown of the US-led
Bretton Woods system in the early 1970s suggested to Kindleberger that the
world was about to enter a similarly rocky period.
We are certainly far from having centrally provided public goods in today’s
global economy. From his internationalist perspective, Kindleberger would
have considered the huge global imbalances between the USA and China in
the run-up to the US banking collapse of 2008 as the deepest cause of the Great
Recession. But unlike in the 1930s, there is no successor hegemon or under-
writer waiting in the wings. Germany is in a position to provide Kindlebergian
public goods for the eurozone, but it is reluctant to do so. But China is very far
from taking the place of the United States.

406 AFTERWORD
So we are left with these two questions. Is it necessary for global public
goods to be hegemonically provided, or can they be provided by cooperation?
And if the former is true, is the world economy destined to break up, almost
certainly messily, into a world of regional blocs, as Kindleberger predicted it
would?1
